Snows hid his shoulders; from beneath his chin the founts of rolling streams began their race; a beard of ice hung on his large breast. Here, poised upon his wings, the god descended: then, having rested thus, he plunged downward from the towering height, with precipitate flight, alighted on the seas, and skimmed along the flood. As waterfowl, who seek their fishy food, show less and less to distant prospect; by turns they dance aloft, and dive below: like these, he plied the steerage of his wings, and flew near the surface of the water, until, having passed the seas and crossed the sands, he closed his wings and stooped on Libyan lands: where shepherds had once been housed in homely sheds, now towers advanced their heads within the clouds. Arriving there, he found the Trojan prince raising new ramparts for the town's defense. A purple scarf, embroidered with gold (Queen Dido's gift), he wore about his waist; a sword, diversified with glittering gems, for ornament, not use, hung idly by his side.

Then thus, with winged words, the god began, resuming his own shape: “Degenerate man, woman's property, what are you doing here, raising these foreign walls and Tyrian towers, forgetful of your own? All-powerful Jove, who sways the world below and heaven above, has sent me down with this severe command: what means this lingering of yours in the Libyan land? If glory cannot move a mind so mean, nor future praise wean you from flitting pleasure, regard the fortunes of your rising heir: let young Ascanius wear the promised crown, to whom the Ausonian scepter, and the state of Rome's imperial name, is owed by fate.” So spoke the god; and, speaking, took his flight, wrapped in clouds, and vanished out of sight.

The pious prince was seized with sudden fear; his tongue was mute, and his hair stood upright. Revolving the stern command in his mind, he longed to flee, and loathed the charming land. What should he say? Or how should he begin? What course, alas, remained, to steer between the offended lover and the powerful queen? This way and that he turned his anxious mind, and tried all expedients, and could find none. Fixed on the deed, but doubtful of the means, after long thought he leaned toward this plan: he called three chiefs, and commanded them to repair the fleet, and embark their men with silent care; he bade them find some plausible pretense to color what he secretly designed. He himself, meanwhile, would choose the softest hours, before the love-sick lady heard the news, and would move her tender mind, by slow degrees, to suffer what the sovereign power decreed: Jove would inspire him when, and what, to say. They heard with pleasure, and obeyed with haste.

But the queen soon perceived the thin disguise (what arts can blind a jealous woman's eyes?). She was the first to find out the secret fraud, before the fatal news was blazed abroad. Love hears the first motions of the lover, quick to forebode, and even in safety fears. Nor was impious Fame lacking to report the ships repaired, the Trojans' thick resort, and their purpose to forsake the Tyrian court. Frantic with fear, impatient of the wound, and helpless of mind, she roved round the city. Less wild appear the Bacchanalian dames, when, from afar, they hear their nightly god, and howl about the hills, and shake the wreathed spear. At length she found the dear perfidious man; she prevented his formed excuse, and thus began: “Base and ungrateful! Could you hope to flee, and escape a lover's eye undetected? Could my kindness not move your compassion, nor plighted vows, nor the dearer bonds of love? Or is the death of a despairing queen not worth preventing, though it was foreseen too well? Even when the wintry winds command your stay, you dare the tempests, and defy the sea. False as you are, suppose you were not bound to lands unknown, and foreign coasts to sound; were Troy restored, and Priam's happy reign, would you now dare to tempt the raging main for Troy's sake? See whom you flee! Am I the foe you shun? Now, by those holy vows so lately begun, by this right hand (since I have nothing more to appeal to, except the faith you gave before); I beg you by these tears too truly shed, by the new pleasures of our nuptial bed; if ever Dido, when you were most kind, was pleasing in your eyes, or touched your mind; by these my prayers, if prayers may yet have place, pity the fortunes of a falling race. For you I have provoked a tyrant's hate, incensed both the Libyan and the Tyrian state; for you alone I suffer in my fame, bereft of honor, and exposed to shame. Whom have I now to trust, ungrateful guest? (That only name remains of all the rest!) What have I left? Or where can I flee? Must I endure Pygmalion's cruelty, or wait till Hyarbas shall lead in triumph a queen that proudly scorned his proffered bed? Had you at least deferred your hasty flight, and left behind some pledge of our delight, some babe to bless the mother's mournful sight, some young Aeneas, to supply your place, whose features might express his father's face; I should not then complain to live bereft of all my husband, or be wholly left.”

Here the queen paused. Unmoved, he held his eyes, by Jove's command; nor suffered love to rise, though heaving in his heart; and thus at length replied: “Fair queen, you never can enough recount your boundless favors, or I deny my debt; nor can my mind forget Eliza's name, while vital breath inspires this mortal frame. Let me speak only this in my defense: I never hoped for a secret flight from here, much less pretended to the lawful claim of sacred nuptials, or a husband's name. For, if indulgent Heaven would leave me free, and not submit my life to fate's decree, my choice would lead me to the Trojan shore, to review those relics, adore their dust, and restore Priam's ruined palace. But now the Delphian oracle commands, and fate invites me to the Latian lands. That is the promised place to which I steer, and all my vows are fixed there. If you, a Tyrian, and a stranger born, adorn a Libyan town with walls and towers, why may we not, a foreign race like you, seek shelter in a foreign place like you? As often as night obscures the skies with humid shades, or twinkling stars arise, Anchises' angry ghost appears in my dreams, chides my delay, and fills my soul with fears; and young Ascanius may justly complain of his defrauded and destined reign. Even now the herald of the gods appeared: I saw him waking, and heard his message. He came commissioned from Jove, heavenly bright with radiant beams, and manifest to sight (I attest both the sender and the sent); he entered these walls, and spoke those words. Fair queen, do not oppose what the gods command; forced by my fate, I leave your happy land.”

Thus while he spoke, she had already begun, with sparkling eyes, to view the guilty man; she surveyed his person over from head to foot, nor any longer forbore these outrageous threats: “False as you are, and, worse than false, forsworn! Not sprung from noble blood, nor goddess-born, but hewn from the hardened entrails of a rock! And rough Hyrcanian tigers gave you suck! Why should I fawn? What worse have I to fear? Did he once look, or lend a listening ear? Did he sigh when I sobbed, or shed one kindly tear? All symptoms of a base ungrateful mind, so foul that what is worse it is hard to find. Why should I complain of man's injustice? The gods, and Jove himself, behold in vain triumphant treason; yet no thunder flies, nor does Juno view my wrongs with equal eyes; faithless is earth, and faithless are the skies! Justice has fled, and Truth is now no more! I saved the shipwrecked exile on my shore; I fed his hungry Trojans with needful food; I took the traitor to my throne and bed: fool that I was—it is little to add the rest—I stored and rigged his ruined fleet. I rave, I rave! He pleads a god's command, and makes Heaven accessory to his deeds. Now Lycian lots, and now the Delian god, now Hermes, employed from Jove's abode, to warn him hence—as if the peaceful state of heavenly powers were touched with human fate! But go! I no longer detain your flight; go seek your promised kingdom through the main! Yet, if the heavens will hear my pious vow, the faithless waves, not half so false as you, or secret sands, shall afford sepulchers to your proud vessels and their perjured lord. Then you shall call on injured Dido's name: Dido shall come in a black sulphury flame, when death has once dissolved her mortal frame; shall smile to see the traitor vainly weep: her angry ghost, arising from the deep, shall haunt you waking, and disturb your sleep. At least my shade shall know of your punishment, and Fame shall spread the pleasing news below.”

She stopped abruptly here; then turned away her loathing eyes, and shunned the sight of day. He stood amazed, revolving in his mind what speech to frame, and what excuse to find. Her fearful maids led their fainting mistress, and softly laid her on her ivory bed.

But the good Aeneas, though he much desired to give the pity her grief required; though he much mourned, and labored with his love, resolved at length to obey the will of Jove. He reviewed his forces: with early care they unmoored their vessels and prepared for sea. The fleet was soon afloat in all its pride, and well-caulked galleys rode in the harbor. Then they felled oaks for oars; or, as they stood, they stripped the growing wood of its green arms, studious of flight. The beach was covered all over with Trojan bands, that blackened the whole shore. On every side were seen, descending down, thick swarms of soldiers, loaded from the town. Thus, in battalions, embodied ants march, fearful of winter, and of future wants, invading the corn, and conveying to their cells the plundered forage of their yellow prey. The sable troops, along the narrow tracks, scarcely bear the weighty burden on their backs: some set their shoulders to the ponderous grain; some guard the spoil; some lash the lagging train; all ply their several tasks, and sustain equal toil.

What pangs tore the tender breast of Dido, when, from the tower, she saw the covered shore, and heard the shouts of sailors from afar, mixed with the murmurs of the watery war! All-powerful Love! What changes can you cause in human hearts, subjected to your laws! Once more the tyrant bent her haughty soul: to prayers and mean submissions she descended. No female arts or aids she left untried, nor counsels unexplored, before she died. “Look, Anna! Look! The Trojans crowd to sea; they spread their canvas, and weigh their anchors. The shouting crew binds their ships with garlands, invokes the sea gods, and invites the wind. Could I have thought this threatening blow so near, my tender soul would have been forewarned to bear it. But do not deny me my last request; try your influence with that perfidious man, and bring me news whether I must live or die. You are his favorite; you alone can find the dark recesses of his inmost mind: in all his trusted secrets you have part, and know the soft approaches to his heart. Haste then, and humbly seek my haughty foe; tell him, I did not go with the Grecians, nor did my fleet work against his friends, nor did I swear the ruin of unhappy Troy, nor move his father's dust with profane hands: why then should he reject so just a suit? Whom does he shun, and where would he flee? Can he deny this last, this only prayer? Let him at least delay his dangerous flight, wait better winds, and hope a calmer sea. I urge the nuptials no more, which he disclaims: let him pursue the promised Latian shore. A short delay is all I ask him now; a pause of grief, an interval from woe, until my soft soul is tempered to sustain accustomed sorrows, and inured to pain. If you in pity grant this one request, my death shall glut the hatred of his breast.” Pious Anna bore this mournful message, and seconded her sister's tears with her own; but all her arts were still employed in vain; again she came, and was refused again. His hardened heart neither prayers nor threats moved; Fate, and the god, had stopped his ears to love.

As, when the winds try their airy quarrel, jostling from every quarter of the sky, they bend the mountain oak this way and that, shatter his boughs, and rend his branches; with leaves and falling mast they spread the ground; the hollow valleys echo to the sound: unmoved, the royal plant mocks their fury, or, shaken, clings more closely to the rocks; as far as he shoots his towering head on high, so deep in earth his fixed foundations lie. No lesser storm the Trojan hero bore; he heard thick messages and loud complaints, and bandied words, still beating on his ears. Sighs, groans, and tears proclaimed his inward pains; but the firm purpose of his heart remained.

The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate, at length began to hate the light of heaven, and loathed to live. Then she saw dire portents, to hasten on the death her soul decreed: strange to relate! For when, before the shrine, she poured the purple wine in sacrifice, the purple wine was turned to putrid blood, and the white offered milk converted to mud. This dire presage, revealed to her alone, she concealed from everyone, even her sister. A marble temple stood within the grove, sacred to death, and to her murdered love; that honored chapel she had hung all around with snowy fleeces, and with garlands crowned. Often, when she visited this lonely dome, strange voices issued from her husband's tomb; she thought she heard him summon her away, invite her to his grave, and chide her stay. It is heard hourly, when with a boding note the solitary screech owl strains her throat, and, on a chimney's top, or turret's height, disturbs the silence of the night with obscene songs. Besides, old prophecies augmented her fears; and stern Aeneas appeared in her dreams, as disdainful as by day: alone, she seemed to wander in her sleep through unknown ways, guideless and dark; or, in a desert plain, to seek her subjects, and to seek in vain: like Pentheus, when, distracted with his fear, he saw two suns, and double Thebes, appear; or mad Orestes, when his mother's ghost tossed infernal torches full in his face, and shook her snaky locks: he shuns the sight, flies over the stage, surprised with mortal fright; the Furies guard the door and intercept his flight.

Now, sinking underneath a load of grief, she sought her last relief from death alone; having resolved the time and means within her breast, she thus addressed her mournful sister (dissembling hope, she cleared her cloudy front, and a false vigor appeared in her eyes): “Rejoice!” she said. “Instructed from above, I shall gain my lover, or lose my love. Near rising Atlas, next to the falling sun, long tracts of Ethiopian climates run: there I have found a Massylian priestess, honored for age, renowned for magic arts: the Hesperian temple was her trusted care; she supplied the wakeful dragon's fare. She taught poppy seeds to steep in honey, reclaimed his rage, and soothed him into sleep. She watched the golden fruit; her charms unbind the chains of love, or fix them on the mind: she stops the torrents, leaves the channel dry, repels the stars, and bears back the sky. The yawning earth bellows back to her call, pale ghosts ascend, and mountain ashes fall. Witness, you gods, and you, my better part, how loath I am to try this impious art! Within the secret court, with silent care, erect a lofty pile, exposed in air: hang on the topmost part the Trojan vest, the spoils, the arms, and presents, of my faithless guest. Next, under these, let the bridal bed be placed, where I embraced my ruin in his arms: all relics of the wretch are doomed to fire; for so the priestess and her charms require.”

Thus far she spoke, and forbore further speech; a mortal paleness appeared in her face. Yet the unsuspecting Anna could not discern the secret funeral designed in these rites; nor thought so dire a rage possessed her mind. Unaware of a plan concealed so well, she feared no worse than when Sichaeus fell; and therefore obeyed. They reared the fatal pile within the secret court, exposed in air. The cloven holm oaks and pines were heaped on high, and garlands lay on the hollow spaces. Sad cypress, vervain, and yew composed the wreath, and every baleful green denoting death. The queen, determined to the fatal deed, spread in order the spoils and sword he had left, and the man's image on the nuptial bed.

And now (the sacred altars placed around) the priestess entered, with her hair unbound, and three times invoked the powers below the ground. She proclaimed Night, Erebus, and Chaos, and threefold Hecate, with her hundred names, and three Dianas: next she sprinkled around the hallowed ground with feigned Avernian drops; she gathered hoary simples, found by Phoebe's light, reaped with brazen sickles at the noon of night; then mixed baleful juices in the bowl, and cut the forehead of a newborn foal, robbing the mother's love. The destined queen observed, assisting at the obscene rites; she held a leavened cake in her devoted hands, and stood next to the highest altar: one tender foot was shod, the other bare; her gathered gown was girt, and her hair was loose. Thus dressed, with her dying breath she summoned the heavens and planets conscious of her death, and every power, if any rules above, who minds, or who avenges, injured love.

It was the dead of night, when weary bodies close their eyes in balmy sleep and soft repose. The winds no longer whispered through the woods, nor did murmuring tides disturb the gentle floods. The stars moved around in silent order; and Peace, with downy wings, was brooding on the ground. The flocks and herds, and party-colored fowl, which haunt the woods, or swim the weedy pool, lay stretched securely on the quiet earth, forgetting the past labors of the day. All else partook of nature's common gift: unhappy Dido was alone awake. Neither sleep nor ease could the furious queen find; sleep fled her eyes, as quiet fled her mind. Despair, and rage, and love divided her heart; despair and rage had some, but love the greater part.

Then she said thus within her secret mind: “What shall I do? What succor can I find? Become a suppliant to Hyarbas's pride, and take my turn, to court and be denied? Shall I go with this ungrateful Trojan, forsake an empire, and attend a foe? I sheltered him, and relieved his train; it is true; but am I sure to be received? Can gratitude have place in Trojan souls? Laomedon still lives in all his race! Then, shall I seek alone the churlish crew, or pursue their flying sails with my fleet? What force have I but those whom scarcely before I drew reluctant from their native shore? Will they embark again at my desire, once more sustain the seas, and quit their second Tyre? Rather invade your guilty breast with steel, and take the fortune you yourself have made. Your pity, sister, first seduced my mind, or seconded too well what I designed. Had I never known these dearly bought pleasures, had I continued free, and still my own; avoiding love, I had not found despair, but shared with savage beasts the common air. Like them, I might have led a lonely life, nor mourned the living, nor disturbed the dead.” These thoughts she brooded in her anxious breast. On board, the Trojan found more easy rest. Resolved to sail, he passed the night in sleep; and ordered all things for his early flight.

To whom once more the winged god appeared; he wore his former youthful mien and shape, and invaded his ears with this new alarm: “Do you sleep, O goddess-born? And can you drown your needful cares, so near a hostile town, beset with foes? Nor do you hear the western gales inviting your passage, and inspiring your sails? She harbors a furious hate in her heart, and you shall find the dire effects too late; fixed on revenge, and obstinate to die. Haste swiftly hence, while you have power to flee. The sea will soon be covered with ships, and blazing firebrands shall kindle all the shore. Prevent her rage, while night obscures the skies, and sail before the purple morn arises. Who knows what hazards your delay may bring? Woman is a various and a changeful thing.” Thus Hermes spoke in the dream; then took his flight aloft in air unseen, and mixed with night.

Twice warned by the celestial messenger, the pious prince arose with hasty fear; then roused his drowsy train without delay: “Haste to your banks; weigh your crooked anchors, and spread your flying sails, and stand to sea. A god commands: he stood before my sight, and urged us once again to speedy flight. O sacred power, whatever power you are, I resign my heart to your blest orders. Lead the way; protect your Trojan bands, and prosper the design your will commands.” He said this; and, drawing forth his flaming sword, his thundering arm divided the many-twisted cord. An emulating zeal inspired his train: they ran; they snatched; they rushed into the main. With headlong haste they left the desert shores, and brushed the liquid seas with laboring oars.

Aurora had now left her saffron bed, and beams of early light overspread the heavens, when, from a tower, the queen, with wakeful eyes, saw the day point upward from the rosy skies. She looked to seaward; but the sea was empty, and she could scarcely discern the sailing ships within view. Stung with spite, and furious with despair, she struck her trembling breast, and tore her hair. “And shall the ungrateful traitor go,” she said, “my land forsaken, and my love betrayed? Shall we not arm? Not rush from every street, to follow, sink, and burn his perjured fleet? Haste, haul out my galleys! Pursue the foe! Bring flaming brands! Set sail, and swiftly row! What have I said? Where am I? Fury turns my brain; and my distempered bosom burns. Then, when I gave my person and my throne, this hate, this rage, should have been shown more timely. See now the promised faith, the vaunted name, the pious man, who, rushing through the flame, preserved his gods, and to the Phrygian shore bore the burden of his feeble father! I should have torn him piecemeal; strewn his scattered limbs in the floods, or left them exposed in woods; destroyed his friends and son; and, from the fire, set the reeking boy before the sire. Events are doubtful, which wait on battles: yet where is the doubt, to souls secure of fate? My Tyrians, at their injured queen's command, would have tossed their fires amid the Trojan band; at once extinguished all the faithless name; and I myself, in vengeance of my shame, would have fallen upon the pile, to mend the funeral flame. You, Sun, who view the world below at once; you, Juno, guardian of the nuptial vow; you, Hecate, hearken from your dark abodes! You Furies, fiends, and violated gods, all powers invoked with Dido's dying breath, attend her curses and avenge her death! If so the Fates ordain, and Jove commands, that the ungrateful wretch should find the Latian lands, yet let an untamed race, and haughty foes, oppose his peaceful entrance with dire arms: oppressed with numbers in the unequal field, his men discouraged, and himself expelled, let him sue for succor from place to place, torn from his subjects, and from his son's embrace. First, let him see his friends slain in battle, and lament their untimely fate in vain; and when, at length, the cruel war shall cease, may he buy his peace on hard conditions: nor let him then enjoy supreme command; but fall, untimely, by some hostile hand, and lie unburied on the barren sand! These are my prayers, and this my dying will; and you, my Tyrians, fulfill every curse. Proclaim perpetual hate and mortal wars, against the prince, the people, and the name. Bestow these grateful offerings on my grave; neither league nor love let the hostile nations know! Now, and from here, in every future age, when rage excites your arms, and strength supplies the rage, let some avenger of our Libyan blood arise, to pursue the perjured brood with fire and sword; our arms, our seas, our shores, opposed to theirs; and let the same hate descend on all our heirs!”

Having said this, she weighed in her anxious mind the means of cutting short her odious days. Then to Sichaeus's nurse she briefly said (for, when she had left her country, hers was dead): “Go, Barce, call my sister. Let her prepare the solemn rites of sacrifice; bring the sheep, and all the atoning offerings, sprinkling her body from the crystal spring with living drops; then let her come, and you bind your hoary brow with sacred fillets. Thus will I pay my vows to Stygian Jove, and end the cares of my disastrous love; then cast the Trojan image on the fire, and as that burns, my passions shall expire.”

The nurse moved onward, with officious care, and all the speed her aged limbs could bear. But furious Dido, involved in dark thoughts, shook at the mighty mischief she had resolved. Her face was distinguished by livid spots; her rolling eyes were red, and her pace discomposed; ghastly she gazed, with pain she drew her breath, and nature shivered at approaching death.

Then she passed swiftly to the fatal place, and mounted the funeral pile with furious haste; she unsheathed the sword the Trojan had left behind (not designed for so dire an enterprise). But when she viewed the garments loosely spread, which once he had worn, and saw the conscious bed, she paused, and with a sigh embraced the robes; then cast her trembling body on the couch, repressed the ready tears, and spoke her last: “Dear pledges of my love, while Heaven was so pleased, receive a soul eased of mortal anguish: my fatal course is finished; and I go, a glorious name, among the ghosts below. A lofty city is raised by my hands, Pygmalion is punished, and my lord appeased. What more could my fortune have afforded, had the false Trojan never touched my shore!” Then she kissed the couch, and, “Must I die,” she said, “and unavenged? It is doubly to be dead! Yet even this death I receive with pleasure: on any terms, it is better than to live. May the false Trojan view these flames from afar; may these boding omens pursue his base flight!”

She said this, and struck. The piercing steel entered deep in her side, dyed with reeking purple: the cruel weapon stuck clogged in the wound; the spouting blood came streaming on her hands. Her sad attendants saw the deadly stroke, and with loud cries they shook the sounding palace. Distracted, they fled from the fatal sight, and spread the dismal rumor through the town. First the yell began from the frightened court; redoubled, it ran from house to house. The groans of men, mixed with the shrieks, laments, and cries of women, mounted the vaulted skies. The clamor was no less than if ancient Tyre, or new Carthage, had been set on fire by foes, the rolling ruin, with their loved abodes, enveloping the blazing temples of their gods.

Her sister heard; and, furious with despair, she beat her breast, and tore her yellow hair, and, calling aloud on Eliza's name, ran breathless to the place, and broke through the crowd. “Was all that pomp of woe prepared for this; these fires, this funeral pile, these altars reared? Was all this train of plots contrived,” she said, “only to deceive unhappy me? Which is worse? Did you in death intend to scorn your sister, or delude your friend? Your summoned sister, and your friend, would have come; one sword would have served us both, one common tomb: was I to raise the pile, to invoke the powers, and not to be present at the fatal stroke? You have destroyed both yourself and me at once, your town, your senate, and your colony! Bring water; bathe the wound; while I in death lay my lips close to hers, and catch her flying breath.” Saying this, she mounted the pile with eager haste, and embraced the gasping queen in her arms; she chafed her temples, and tore her own garments, to stanch the streaming blood, and cleanse the gore. Three times Dido tried to raise her drooping head, and, fainting three times, fell groveling on the bed; three times she opened her heavy eyes, and sought the light, but, having found it, sickened at the sight, and closed her lids at last in endless night.

Then Juno, grieving that she should sustain a death so lingering, and so full of pain, sent Iris down, to free her from the strife of laboring nature, and dissolve her life. For since she died, not doomed by Heaven's decree, or her own crime, but by human casualty, and by the rage of love that had plunged her in despair, the Sisters had not cut the topmost hair, which Proserpine and they alone can know; nor made her sacred to the shades below. The various goddess took her flight downward, and drew a thousand colors from the light; then stood above the dying lover's head, and said: “I thus devote you to the dead. I bear this offering to the infernal gods.” Thus while she spoke, she cut the fatal hair: the struggling soul was loosed, and life dissolved in air.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: Aeneas, setting sail from Africa, is driven by a storm onto the coast of Sicily, where he is hospitably received by his friend Acestes, king of part of the island, and born of Trojan parentage. He sets himself to celebrate the memory of his father with divine honors, and accordingly institutes funeral games, and appoints prizes for those who would conquer in them. While the ceremonies are being performed, Juno sends Iris to persuade the Trojan women to burn the ships; who, upon her instigation, set fire to them, which burns four, and would have consumed the rest, had not Jupiter extinguished it by a miraculous shower. Upon this, Aeneas, by the advice of one of his generals and a vision of his father, builds a city for the women, old men, and others who were either unfit for war or weary of the voyage, and sails for Italy. Venus procures of Neptune a safe voyage for him and all his men, except only his pilot Palinurus, who was unfortunately lost.

Meanwhile the Trojan cut his watery way, fixed on his voyage, through the curling sea. Then, casting back his eyes, with dire amazement, he saw on the Punic shore the mounting blaze. The cause was unknown; yet his presaging mind divined the fate of Dido from the fire. He knew the stormy souls of womankind, what secret springs move their eager passions, how capable they are of death for injured love. From this the Trojans drew dire auguries, until they could see neither fires nor shining shores. Now seas and skies alone bounded their prospect: an empty space above, a floating field around. But soon the heavens were overspread with shadows; a swelling cloud hung hovering over their heads: it looked livid, threatening a storm; then night and horror deformed the ocean's face. The pilot, Palinurus, cried aloud: “What gusts of weather from that gathering cloud my thoughts presage! Before the tempest roars, stand to your tackle, mates, and stretch your oars; contract your swelling sails, and luff to windward.” The frightened crew performed the task assigned. Then, to his fearless chief, he said: “Not Heaven, though Jove himself should promise Italy, can stem the torrent of this raging sea. Mark how the shifting winds arise from the west, and what collected night involves the skies! Nor can our shaken vessels live at sea, much less force their way against the tempest. It is fate that diverts our course, and fate we must obey. Not far from here, if I have rightly observed the southing of the stars and the polar light, lies Sicilia, whose hospitable shores we may reach in safety with struggling oars.” Aeneas then replied: “Too surely I find we strive in vain against the seas and wind: now shift your sails; what place can please me more than what you promise, the Sicilian shore, whose hallowed earth contains Anchises' bones, and where a prince of Trojan lineage reigns?” With the course resolved, before the western wind they scudded amain, and made the port assigned. Meanwhile Acestes, from a lofty stand, beheld the fleet descending on the land; and, not unmindful of his ancient race, he ran down from the cliff with an eager pace, and held the hero in a strict embrace. He wore the spoils of a rough Libyan bear, and bore a pointed javelin in either hand. His mother was a dame of Dardan blood; his sire Crinisus, a Sicilian flood. He welcomed his returning friends ashore with plenteous country fare and homely store.

Now, when the following morning had chased away the flying stars, and light had restored the day, Aeneas called the Trojan troops around, and thus addressed them from a rising ground: “Offspring of heaven, divine Dardanian race! The sun, revolving through the ethereal space, has filled the shining circle of the year since this isle first held my father's ashes: and now the rising day renews the year; a day forever sad, forever dear. I would celebrate this with annual games, with gifts piled on altars, and holy flames, though banished to Gaetulia's barren sands, caught on Grecian seas, or on hostile lands. But since this happy storm has driven our fleet (not, as I judge, without the will of Heaven) upon these friendly shores and flowery plains, which hide Anchises and his blessed remains, let us with joy perform his due honors, and pray for prosperous winds, to renew our voyage; let us pray that in towns and temples of our own, the name of great Anchises may be known, and that yearly games may spread the gods' renown. Acestes, of the Trojan race, is pleased to grace our sports with royal gifts: the king bestows two steers on every ship; his gods and ours shall share in your equal vows. Besides, if, nine days hence, the rosy morn shall adorn the skies with unclouded light, that day I mean to grace with solemn sports: light galleys shall run a watery race on the seas; some shall contend in swiftness for the goal, and others try to bend the twanging bow; the strong, armed with iron gauntlets, shall stand opposed in combat on the yellow sand. Let all be present at the prepared games, and let the joyful victors await the just reward. But now assist the rites, crowned with garlands.” He said this, and first bound his brows with myrtle. Then Helymus, led by his example, and old Acestes, each adorned his head; so too did young Ascanius, with a sprightly grace, tie his temples, and all the Trojan race.

Aeneas then advanced amidst the train, followed by thousands through the flowery plain, to great Anchises' tomb; and when he found it, he poured to Bacchus, on the hallowed ground, two bowls of sparkling wine, and two of milk, and two of the purple gore of offered bulls. He then strewed the sepulcher with roses, and thus addressed his father's ghost aloud: “Hail, O holy manes! Hail again, paternal ashes, now reviewed in vain! The gods did not permit that you, with me, should reach the promised shores of Italy, or Tiber's flood, whatever flood it be.” Scarcely had he finished, when, with speckled pride, a serpent began to glide from the tomb; his huge bulk rolled in seven high coils; his back was broad and blue, but streaked with scaly gold: thus riding on his curls, he seemed to pass a rolling fire along, and to singe the grass. More various colors ran through his body than Iris when her bow imbibes the sun. Between the rising altars, and around, the sacred monster shot along the ground; with harmless play amidst the bowls he passed, and with his lolling tongue tried the taste: thus fed with holy food, the wondrous guest retired to rest within the hollow tomb. The pious prince, surprised at what he viewed, renewed the funeral honors with more zeal, doubtful whether this was the genius of the place, or the guardian of his father's sepulcher. He slew five sheep, according to the rites; as many swine, and steers of sable hue; he poured new generous wine from the goblets, and called upon his father's ghost, restored from hell. The glad attendants came in long order, offering their gifts at great Anchises' tomb: some added more oxen; some divided the spoil; some placed the chargers on the grassy soil; some blew the fires, and broiled the offered entrails.

Now came the desired day. The skies were bright with the rosy luster of the rising light: the bordering people, roused by the sounding fame of Trojan feasts and great Acestes' name, filled the crowded shore with acclamations, some to behold, and some to prove their skill. And first they placed the gifts in public view: green laurel wreaths, and palm, the victors' grace; within the circle, arms and tripods lay, ingots of gold and silver, heaped on high, and vests embroidered, of the Tyrian dye. The trumpet's clangor then proclaimed the feast, and all prepared for their appointed games. Four galleys first, bearing equal rowers, advanced, appearing in the watery lists. The speedy Dolphin, that outstrips the wind, bore Mnestheus, author of the Memmian kind: Gyas commanded the vast Chimaera's bulk, which rose like a towering city; three Trojans tugged at every laboring oar; three banks in three degrees bore the sailors; beneath their sturdy strokes the billows roared. Sergesthus, who began the Sergian race, took the leading place in the great Centaur; Cloanthus stood on the sea-green Scylla, from whom Cluentius draws his Trojan blood.

Far in the sea, against the foaming shore, there stands a rock. The raging billows roar above his head in storms; but when the sea is clear, they uncurl their ridgy backs, and appear at his foot. Below, the gentle waters run in peace; the cormorants above lie basking in the sun. On this the hero fixed an oak in sight, as the mark to guide the mariners aright. To bear with this, the seamen stretched their oars; then steered round the rock, and sought the former shores. The lots decided their places. Above the rest, each leader shone in his Tyrian vest; the common crew crowned their temples with wreaths of poplar boughs, and shaded their sweaty brows: their naked shoulders, besmeared with oil, shone. All took their seats, and waited for the sounding sign: they gripped their oars; and every panting breast was raised by turns with hope, and depressed by turns with fear. The clangor of the trumpet gave the sign; at once they started, advancing in a line: with shouts the sailors rent the starry skies; lashed with their oars, the smoky billows rose; the briny main sparkled, and the vexed ocean fried. Exact in time, they rowed with equal strokes: at once the brushing oars and brazen prow dashed up the sandy waves, and opened the depths below. Not fiery coursers in a chariot race invade the field with half so swift a pace; nor does the fierce driver lend the sounding lash with more fury, and before the stroke descends, bend his pliant body low to the wheels. The partial crowd divided its hopes and fears, and aided with eager shouts the favored side. Cries, murmurs, clamors, with a mixing sound, rebounded from woods to woods, from hills to hills.

Amidst the loud applause of the shore, Gyas outstripped the rest, and sprang before: Cloanthus, better manned, pursued him fast, but his overmasted galley checked his haste. The Centaur and the Dolphin brushed the brine with equal oars, advancing in a line; and now the mighty Centaur seemed to lead, and now the speedy Dolphin got ahead; now board to board the rival vessels rowed, the billows laved the skies, and the ocean groaned below. They reached the mark; proud Gyas and his train rode in triumph, the victors of the main. But, steering round, he charged his pilot to stand more close to shore, and skim along the sand. “Let others bear to sea!” Menoetes heard; but he feared the secret shelves too cautiously, and, fearing, sought the deep; and still he steered aloof. With louder cries the captain called again: “Bear to the rocky shore, and shun the main.” He spoke, and, speaking, saw at his stern the bold Cloanthus drawing near the shelvings. Between the mark and him the Scylla stood, and plowed the flood in a closer compass. He passed the mark; and, wheeling, got before: Gyas blasphemed the gods, devoutly swore, cried out in anger, and tore his hair. Mindless of others' lives (so high had grown his rising rage) and careless of his own, he drew the trembling dotard to the deck; then hoisted him up, and threw him overboard: this done, he seized the helm; his fellows cheered; turned short upon the shelves, and madly steered.

Hardly did the plunging pilot raise his head, clogged with his clothes, and encumbered with his years: now dripping wet, he climbed the cliff with pain. The crowd, that saw him fall and float again, shouted from the distant shore; and laughed loudly, to see his heaving breast disgorge the briny draught. The following Centaur, and the Dolphin's crew, renewed their vanished hopes of victory; while Gyas lagged, they kindled in the race, to reach the mark. Sergesthus took the place; Mnestheus pursued; and while they wound around, came up, not half his galley's length behind; then, on the deck, he appeared amidst his mates, and thus cheered their drooping courage: “My friends, and Hector's followers heretofore, exert your vigor; tug the laboring oar; stretch to your strokes, my still unconquered crew, whom I drew from the flaming walls of Troy. In this our common interest, let me find that strength of hand, that courage of mind, as when you stemmed the strong Malean flood, and rowed over the Syrtes' broken billows. I do not now seek the foremost palm to gain; though yet—but, ah! That haughty wish is vain! Let those enjoy it whom the gods ordain. But to be last, the laggards of all the race! Redeem yourselves and me from that disgrace.” Now, one and all, they tugged amain; they rowed at the full stretch, and shook the brazen prow. The sea beneath them sank; their laboring sides were swollen, and sweat ran guttering down in tides. Chance aided their daring with unhoped success; Sergesthus, eager with his beak to press between the rival galley and the rock, shut up the unwieldy Centaur in the lock. The vessel struck; and, with the dreadful shock, shivered her oars, and broke her head. The trembling rowers rose from their banks, and, anxious for themselves, renounced the prize. With iron poles they heaved her off the shores, and gathered their floating oars from the sea. The crew of Mnestheus, with elated minds, urged their success, and called the willing winds; then plied their oars, and cut their liquid way in larger compass on the roomy sea. As, when the dove forsakes her rocky hold, roused in a fright, and shakes her sounding wings; the cavern rings with clattering; out she flies, and leaves her callow care, and cleaves the skies: at first she flutters; but at length she springs to smoother flight, and shoots upon her wings: so Mnestheus in the Dolphin cut the sea; and, flying with a force, that force assisted his way. Sergesthus in the Centaur he soon passed, wedged in the rocky shoals, and sticking fast. In vain the victor Sergesthus implored him with cries, and practiced to row with shattered oars. Then Mnestheus bore upon Gyas, and outflew him: the ship, without a pilot, yielded the prize. Unvanquished Scylla now alone remained; he pursued her, and strained all his vigor. Shouts from the favoring multitude arose; applauding Echo replied to the shouts; shouts, wishes, and applause ran rattling through the skies. The Scylla heard these clamors with disdain, and much grudged the praise, but more the robbed reward: resolved to hold their own, they mended their pace, all obstinate to die, or to gain the race. Raised with success, the Dolphin ran swiftly; for they can conquer who believe they can. Both urged their oars, and fortune supplied both, and both might perhaps have shared an equal prize; when Cloanthus held his hands to the seas, and demanded succor from the watery powers: “Gods of the liquid realms, on which I row! If, given by you, the laurel binds my brow, assist me to make myself guilty of my vow! A snow-white bull shall be slain on your shore; his offered entrails cast into the main, and ruddy wine, thrown from golden goblets, shall own your grateful gift and my return.” The choir of nymphs, and Phorcus, from below, with virgin Panopea, heard his vow; and old Portunus, with his breadth of hand, pushed on, and sped the galley to the land. Swift as an arrow, or a winged wind, she flew, and, darting to the port, obtained the prize.

The herald summoned all, and then proclaimed Cloanthus conqueror of the naval games. The prince crowned the victor's head with laurel, and three fat steers were led to his vessel, the ship's reward; besides generous wine, and sums of silver, which the crew divided. The leaders were distinguished from the rest; the victor was honored with a nobler vest, where gold and purple strove in equal rows, and needlework bestowed its happy cost. There Ganymede was wrought with living art, chasing the trembling hart through Ida's groves: breathless he seems, yet eager to pursue; when from aloft descends, in open view, the bird of Jove, and, pouncing on his prey, bears the boy away with crooked talons. In vain, with lifted hands and gazing eyes, his guards behold him soaring through the skies, and the dogs pursue his flight with imitated cries.

Mnestheus was declared the second victor; and, summoned there, he shared the second prize. A coat of mail, which brave Demoleus bore—more brave Aeneas tore from his shoulders in single combat on the Trojan shore—was ordained for Mnestheus to possess: in war for his defense, for ornament in peace. The gift was rich, and glorious to behold, but yet so ponderous with its plates of gold, that scarcely two servants could sustain the weight; yet, loaded thus, Demoleus over the plain had pursued and lightly seized the Trojan train. The third, succeeding to the last reward, shared two goodly bowls of massy silver, with prominent figures, and richly wrought, and two brass cauldrons brought from Dodona.

Thus all, rewarded by the hero's hands, bound their conquering temples with purple bands; and now Sergesthus, clearing from the rock, brought back his galley shattered with the shock. She looked forlorn, without an aiding oar, and, hooted by the common people, was brought to shore. As when a snake, surprised upon the road, is crushed athwart her body by the load of heavy wheels; or with a mortal wound her belly is bruised, and she is trodden to the ground: in vain, with loosened coils, she crawls along; yet, fierce above, she brandishes her tongue; glares with her eyes, and bristles with her scales; but, groveling in the dust, she trails her unsound parts: so the Centaur tended slowly to the port, but what she lacked in oars, she made up for with sails. Yet, for his saved galley, the grateful prince was pleased to recompense the unhappy chief. Pholoe, the Cretan slave, rewarded his care, beautiful herself, with lovely twins as fair.

From there the Trojan hero bent his way into the neighboring plain, penned in with mountains, whose sides were shaded with surrounding wood. Full in the midst of this fair valley stood a native theater, which, rising slow by just degrees, overlooked the ground below. High on a sylvan throne the leader sat; a numerous train attended in solemn state. Here those who delighted in the rapid course were invited by the desire of honor and the prize. The rival runners stood without order; the Trojans mingled with the Sicilian band. First appeared Nisus, with Euryalus; Euryalus was a boy of blooming years, crowned with sprightly grace and equal beauty; Nisus, renowned for his friendship to the youth. Diores next, of Priam's royal race; then Salius joined with Patron, took their place; but Patron had his birth in Arcadia, and Salius his from Acarnanian earth; then two Sicilian youths, whose names were these: swift Helymus, and lovely Panopes: both jolly huntsmen, both bred in the forest, and acknowledging old Acestes as their head; with several others of more ignoble name, whom time has not delivered over to fame.

To these the hero thus explained his thoughts, in words which gained general approval: “One common largess is designed for all, the vanquished and the victor shall be joined: two darts of polished steel and Gnosian wood, a silver-studded axe, shall be bestowed alike. The foremost three have olive wreaths decreed: the first of these obtains a stately steed, adorned with trappings; and the next in fame, the quiver of an Amazonian dame, well supplied with feathered Thracian arrows: a golden belt shall gird his manly side, which shall be tied with a sparkling diamond. Let the third be content with this Grecian helmet.” He said. They went to their appointed base; with beating hearts they received the expected sign, and, starting all at once, left the barrier. They flew, spread out, as on the winged winds, and seized the distant goal with greedy view. Shot from the crowd, swift Nisus overtook all; nor did storms or thunder equal half his haste. The next, though next, yet far disjoined, came Salius, and Euryalus behind; then Helymus, whom young Diores pressed, step after step, and almost side by side, pressing his shoulders; and, in a longer space, would have won, or at least left the race in doubt.

Now, spent, they almost reached the goal at last, when eager Nisus, hapless in his haste, slipped first, and, slipping, fell upon the plain, soaked with the blood of oxen newly slain. The careless victor had not marked his way; but, treading where the treacherous puddle lay, his heels flew up; and on the grassy floor he fell, besmeared with filth and holy gore. Not mindless then, Euryalus, of you, nor of the sacred bonds of amity, he strove to cross the immediate rival's hope, and caught the foot of Salius as he rose. So Salius lay extended on the plain; Euryalus sprang out, to gain the prize, and left the crowd: applauding peals attended the victor to the goal, who was vanquished by his friend. Next came Helymus; and then Diores, made third in fame by two misfortunes.

But Salius entered, and, exclaiming loud for justice, deafened and disturbed the crowd; he urged that his cause might be heard in court; and pleaded that the prize was wrongfully conferred. But favor appeared for Euryalus; his blooming beauty, with his tender tears, had bribed the judges for the promised prize. Besides, Diores filled the court with cries, who reached in vain for the last reward, if the first palm were conferred on Salius. Then thus the prince: “Let no disputes arise: where fortune placed it, I award the prize. But give me leave to mend fortune's errors, at least to pity my deserving friend.” He said this, and from among the spoils he drew (ponderous with shaggy mane and golden paws) a lion's hide: and gave this to Salius. Nisus saw the gift with envy, and grieved. “If such rewards are due to vanquished men,” he said, “and falling is to rise through you, what prize may Nisus claim from your bounty, who merited the first rewards and fame? In falling, both tried an equal fortune; would that fortune had provided so well for my fall!” With this he pointed to his face, and showed his hand and all his habit smeared with blood. The indulgent father of the people smiled, and caused an ample shield to be produced, of wondrous art, wrought by Didymaon, long since brought in triumph from Neptune's bars. This he gave to Nisus; he then divided the rest, and expressed equal justice in his gifts.

The race thus ended, and the rewards bestowed, once more the prince addressed the attentive crowd: “If there is any here whose dauntless courage dares to fight with gauntlets, with limbs and body bare, to sustain his opposite in open view, let the champion stand forth, and renew the games. Two prizes I propose, and thus divide: a bull with gilded horns, tied with fillets, shall be the portion of the conquering chief; a sword and helm shall cheer the loser's grief.”

Then haughty Dares appeared in the lists; stalking he strode, bearing his head erect: his nervous arms wielded the weighty gauntlets, and loud applause echoed through the field. Dares alone used to stand in combat against mighty Paris, hand to hand; the same, at Hector's funerals, undertook gigantic Butes, of the Amycian stock, and, by the stroke of his resistless hand, stretched the vast bulk upon the yellow sand. Such was Dares; and such he strode along, and drew the wonder of the gazing throng. He showed his brawny back and ample breast; he threw his lifted arms around his head, and dealt in the whistling air his empty blows. He sought a match; but, through the trembling band, not one dared answer to the proud demand. Presuming of his force, with sparkling eyes he already devoured the promised prize. He claimed the bull with awless insolence, and, having seized his horns, accosted the prince: “If none dares oppose my matchless valor, how long shall Dares wait for his dastard foes? Permit me, chief, permit without delay, to lead this uncontended gift away.” The crowd assented, and with redoubled cries demanded the prize for the proud challenger.

Acestes, fired with just disdain to see the palm usurped without a victory, reproached Entellus thus, who sat beside him, and heard and saw, unmoved, the Trojan's pride: “Once, but in vain, a champion of renown, can you so tamely bear the ravished crown, a prize borne in triumph before your sight, and shun, for fear, the danger of the fight? Where is our Eryx now, the boasted name, the god who taught your thundering arm the game? Where now your baffled honor? Where the spoil that filled your house, and the fame that filled our isle?” Entellus thus replied: “My soul is still the same, unmoved with fear, and moved with martial fame; but my chill blood is curdled in my veins, and scarcely the shadow of a man remains. O could I turn to that fair prime again, that prime of which this boaster is so vain, the brave man who defies this decrepit age should feel my force, without the promised prize.”

He said this; and, rising at the word, he threw down two ponderous gauntlets in open view; gauntlets which Eryx used to wield in fight, and sheathe his hands with in the listed field. Seized with fear and wonder, the crowd beheld the gloves of death, with seven distinguished folds of tough bull-hides; the space within was spread with iron, or with loads of heavy lead. Dares himself was daunted at the sight, renounced his challenge, and refused to fight. Astonished at their weight, the hero stood, and poised the ponderous engines in his hands. “What would your wonder have been,” said Entellus, “had you seen the gauntlets of Alcides, or viewed the stern debate on this unhappy green? These that I bear, your brother Eryx bore, still marked with battered brains and mingled gore. With these he long sustained the Herculean arm; and these I wielded while my blood was warm, while better spirits fed this languished frame, before age unstrung my nerves, or time oversnowed my head. But if the challenger refuses these arms, and cannot wield their weight, or dare not use them; if great Aeneas and Acestes join in his request, I resign these gauntlets; let us perform the fight with equal arms, and let him leave off fearing, since I resign my right.”

This said, Entellus prepared for the strife; stripped of his quilted coat, he bared his body; composed of mighty bones and brawn he stood, a goodly towering object on the sands. Then just Aeneas supplied equal arms, which they tied round their shoulders to their wrists. Both stood on tiptoe, at full extent, their arms aloft, their bodies bent inward; they held their heads far from aiming blows; with clashing gauntlets they then provoked the war. One relied on his youth and pliant limbs; one on his sinews and his giant size. The last was stiff with age, his motion slow; he heaved for breath, he staggered to and fro, and clouds of issuing smoke blew loudly from his nostrils. Yet equal in success, they warded, they struck; their ways were different, but their art alike. Before, behind, the blows were dealt; around their hollow sides the rattling thumps resounded. A storm of well-meant strokes flew with fury, and erred about their temples, ears, and eyes. Nor did it always err; for often the gauntlet drew a sweeping stroke along the crackling jaws. Heavy with age, Entellus held his ground, but with his warping body warded the wound. His hand and watchful eye kept even pace; while Dares traversed and shifted his place, and, like a captain who besieges round some strong-built castle on a rising ground, viewed all the approaches with observing eyes: he tried this and that other part in vain, and relied more on industry than force. With hands on high, Entellus threatened the foe; but Dares watched the motion from below, and slipped aside, and shunned the long descending blow. Entellus wasted his forces on the wind, and, thus deluded of the stroke he intended, fell headlong and heavy; his ample breast and weighty limbs pressed his ancient mother. So falls a hollow pine that had long stood on Ida's height, or in Erymanthus's wood, torn from the roots. The different nations rose, and shouts and mingled murmurs rent the skies. Acestes ran with eager haste, to raise the fallen companion of his youthful days. Dauntless he rose, and returned to the fight; his glowing cheeks burned with shame, his eyes with fury. Disdain and conscious virtue fired his breast, and with redoubled force he pressed his foe. He laid on load with either hand, amain, and drove the Trojan headlong over the plain; nor stopped, nor stayed; nor allowed rest or breath; but storms of strokes descended about his brows, a rattling tempest, and a hail of blows. But now the prince, who saw the wild increase of wounds, commanded the combatants to cease, and checked Entellus' wrath, and bade the peace. First he came to the Trojan, spent with toil, and soothed his sorrow for the suffered shame. “What fury seized my friend? The gods,” said he, “propitious to him, and averse to you, have given his arm superior force to yours. It is madness to contend with divine strength.” The gauntlet fight thus ended, from the shore his faithful friends bore unhappy Dares away: his mouth and nostrils poured out a purple flood, and pounded teeth came rushing with his blood. Faintly he staggered through the hissing throng, and hung his head, and trailed his legs along. His train carried the sword and helmet; but the palm and the ox remained with his foe.

The champion then came before Aeneas, proud of his prize, but prouder of his fame: “O goddess-born, and you, Dardanian host, mark with attention, and forgive my boast; learn what I was, by what remains; and know from what impending fate you saved my foe.” Sternly he spoke, and then confronted the bull; and, aiming full on his ample forehead, the deadly stroke, descending, pierced the skull. Down dropped the beast, nor needed a second wound, but sprawled in pangs of death, and spurned the ground. Then, thus: “In Dares' place I offer this. Eryx, accept a nobler sacrifice; take the last gift my withered arms can yield: I resign your gauntlets, and here renounce the field.”

This done, Aeneas ordered, for the close, the strife of archers with contending bows. He raised with his own hands, on the shore, the mast that Sergesthus' shattered galley had borne. They tied a fluttering dove upon the top, the living mark at which their arrows would fly. The rival archers advanced in a line, to receive their turn of shooting from chance. A helmet held their names; the lots were drawn: on the first scroll was read Hippocoon. The people shouted. On the next was found young Mnestheus, lately crowned with naval honors. The third contained Eurytion's noble name, your brother, Pandarus, and next in fame, whom Pallas urged to confound the treaty, and to send a feathered wound among the Greeks. Acestes remained last at the bottom, whom not his age restrained from youthful sports. Soon all with vigor bent their trusty bows, and each chose his arrow from the quiver. Hippocoon's was the first: with forceful sway it flew, and, whizzing, cut the liquid way. Fixed in the mast the feathered weapon stood: the fearful pigeon fluttered in her bonds, and the tree trembled, and the shouting cries of the pleased people rent the vaulted skies. Then Mnestheus drove his arrow to the head, with lifted eyes, and took his aim above, but made a glancing shot, and missed the dove; yet missed so narrowly that he cut the cord that fastened by the foot the flitting bird. The captive thus released, she flew away, and beat with clapping wings the yielding skies. With his bow already bent, Eurytion stood; and, having first invoked his brother god, he sped his winged shaft with eager haste. The fatal message reached her as she fled: she left her life aloft; she struck the ground, and rendered back the weapon in the wound. Acestes, grudging at his lot, remained, without a prize to gratify his pains. Yet, shooting upward, he sent his shaft, to show an archer's art, and boast his twanging bow. The feathered arrow gave a dire portent, from which later augurs judge events. Chafed by the speed, it fired; and, as it flew, drew a trail of following flames ascending: kindling, they mounted, and marked the shiny way; like falling meteors they played across the skies, and vanished into wind, or decayed in a blaze. The Trojans and Sicilians wildly stared, and, trembling, turned their wonder into prayer. The Dardan prince put on a smiling face, and embraced Acestes closely; then, honoring him with gifts above the rest, turned the bad omen, and did not confess his fears. “The gods,” said he, “have wrought this miracle, and ordered you the prize without the lot. Accept this goblet, rough with figured gold, which Thracian Cisseus gave my sire of old: receive this pledge of ancient amity, which I justly give to my second sire.” He said this, and, with the trumpets' cheerful sound, proclaimed him victor, and crowned him with laurel. Nor did good Eurytion envy him the prize, though he had transfixed the pigeon in the skies. He who cut the line was graced with the second gifts; the third was his whose arrow pierced the mast.

The chief, before the games were wholly done, called Periphantes, tutor to his son, and whispered thus: “Find Ascanius with speed; and, if his childish troop is ready joined, let him grace his grandsire's day on horseback, and lead his equals armed in just array.” He said; and, calling out, cleared the circus. The crowd withdrew, and an open plain appeared. And now the noble youths, of form divine, advanced before their fathers in a line; the riders graced the steeds; the steeds shone with glory.

Thus marching on in military pride, shouts of applause resounded from side to side. They wore their helmets adorned with laurel wreaths, each brandishing aloft a cornel spear. Some bore their gilded quivers at their backs; their chains of burnished gold hung down before. They formed three graceful troops upon the green; three graceful leaders were seen at their head; twelve followed every chief, and left a space between. Young Priam led the first; a lovely boy, whose grandsire was the unhappy king of Troy; his race was known to fame in after times, adding new honors to the Latian name; and well the royal boy became his Thracian steed. The fetlocks of his feet were white in front, and on his brow he bore a snowy star. Then beautiful Atys, bred with Iülus, of equal age, led the second squadron. The last in order, but the first in place, first in the lovely features of his face, rode fair Ascanius on a fiery steed, Queen Dido's gift, and of the Tyrian breed. The king ordained sure coursers for the rest, adorned with golden bits, and purple reins.

The pleased spectators renewed peals of shouts, and all the parents saw themselves in the children; their form, their motions, and their sprightly grace, and hopes and fears alternated in their faces.

The unfledged commanders and their martial train first made the circuit of the sandy plain around their sires, and, at the appointed sign, drawn up in beautiful order, formed a line. The second signal sounded, the troop divided into three distinguished parts, with three distinguished guides. Again they closed, and once again they parted; troop to troop opposed, and line to line. They met; they wheeled; they threw their darts afar with harmless rage and well-dissembled war. Then in a round the mingled bodies ran: flying they followed, and pursuing shunned; broken, they broke; and, rallying, they renewed the military show in other forms. At last, in order, undiscerned they joined, and marched together in a friendly line. And, as the Cretan labyrinth of old, with wandering ways and many a winding fold, involved the weary feet, without redress, in a round error, which denied recess; so fought the Trojan boys in warlike play, turned and returned, and still took a different way. Thus dolphins in the deep chase each other in circles, when they swim around the watery race. This game, these carousels, Ascanius taught; and, building Alba, brought them to the Latins; he showed what he had learned: the Latin sires impart the graceful art to their succeeding sons; from these imperial Rome received the game, which they call Troy, and the troop the Trojan troop.

Thus far the sacred sports they celebrated: but Fortune soon resumed her ancient hate. For, while they paid the dead his annual dues, Saturnian Juno viewed those envied rites; and she sent the goddess of the various bow to try new methods of revenge below; she supplied the winds to wing her airy way, where in the port the secure navy lay. Swift as fair Iris descended her arch, and, undiscerned, ended her fatal voyage. She saw the gathering crowd; and, gliding from there, the deserted shore, and the fleet without defense. The Trojan matrons, alone upon the sands, with sighs and tears bemoaned Anchises' death; then, turning their weeping eyes to the sea, their pity for themselves renewed their cries. “Alas!” said one, “what oceans yet remain for us to sail! What labors to sustain!” All took up the word, and, with a general groan, implored the gods for peace, and for places of their own.

The goddess, great in mischief, viewed their pains, and restrained her heavenly limbs in a woman's form. In face and shape she became old Beroe, Doryclus' wife, a venerable dame, once blessed with riches, and a mother's name. Thus changed, she ran amidst the crying crowd, mingled with the matrons, and began these words: “O wretched we, whom neither the Grecian power, nor the flames, destroyed in Troy's unhappy hour! O wretched we, reserved by cruel fate, beyond the ruins of the sinking state! Now seven revolving years are wholly run, since we began this unprosperous voyage; since, tossed from shores to shores, from lands to lands, inhospitable rocks and barren sands, wandering in exile through the stormy sea, we search in vain for flying Italy. Now cast by fortune on this kindred land, what should withstand our rest and rising walls, or hinder us from fixing our banished band here? O country lost, and gods redeemed in vain, if we still remain in endless exile! Shall we no more renew the Trojan walls, or view the streams of some dissembled Simois? Haste, join with me, to consume the unhappy fleet! Cassandra bids it; and I declare her doom. In sleep I saw her; she supplied my hands (for this I more than dreamt) with flaming brands: ‘With these,' she said, ‘destroy these wandering ships: these are your fated seats, and this your Troy.' Time calls you now; employ the precious hour: do not slack the good presage, while Heaven inspires our minds to dare, and gives the ready fires. See! Neptune's altars minister their brands: the god is pleased; the god supplies our hands.” Then she drew a flaming fire from the pile, and, tossed in air, threw it amidst the galleys.

Wrapped in amazement, the matrons wildly stared; then Pyrgo, revered for her hoary hair, Pyrgo, the nurse of Priam's numerous race, cried: “This is no Beroe, though she belies her face! What terrors arise from her frowning brow! Behold a goddess in her ardent eyes! What rays are seen around her heavenly face! Mark her majestic voice, and more than mortal bearing! I just left Beroe, whom, pined with pain, her age and anguish detain from these rites,” she said. The matrons, seized with new amazement, rolled their malignant eyes, and gazed upon the navy. They feared, and hoped, and obeyed neither part: they hoped the fated land, but feared the fatal way. The goddess, having done her task below, mounted up on equal wings, and bent her painted bow. Struck with the sight, and seized with divine rage, the matrons prosecuted their mad design: they shrieked aloud; they snatched, with impious hands, the food of altars; fires and flaming brands. Green boughs and saplings, mingled in their haste, and smoking torches, they cast on the ships. The flame, unstopped at first, gained more fury, and Vulcan rode at large with loosened reins: triumphant he soared to the painted sterns, and seized, in this way, the banks and crackling oars. Eumelus was the first to bear the news, while they still crowded the rural theater. Then, what they heard was witnessed by their eyes: a storm of sparkles and of flames arose. Ascanius took the alarm, while he still led his early warriors on his prancing steed, and, spurring on, soon overpassed his equals; nor could his frightened friends reclaim his haste. As soon as the royal youth appeared in view, he sent his voice before him as he flew: “What madness moves you, matrons, to destroy the last remainders of unhappy Troy? You burn not hostile fleets, but your own hopes, and turn your fatal fury on your friends. Behold your own Ascanius!” While he said this, he drew his glittering helmet from his head, in which he had led the youths to sportful arms. By this, Aeneas and his train appeared; and now the women, seized with shame and fear, dispersed, and took their flight to woods and caverns, abhorred their actions, and avoided the light; they acknowledged their friends, and found their error, and shook the goddess from their altered mind.

Not so did the raging fires cease their fury, but, lurking in the seams, with seeming peace, worked on their way amid the smoldering tow, sure in destruction, but slow in motion. The silent plague ate through the green timber, and vomited out a tardy flame by fits. Down to the keels, and upward to the sails, the fire descended, or mounted, but still prevailed; nor poured buckets, nor the strength of human hand, could withstand the victorious element.

The pious hero rent his robe, and threw his hands to heaven, and with his hands his vows. “O Jove,” he cried, “if prayers can yet have place; if you do not abhor all the Dardan race; if any spark of pity still remains; if gods are gods, and not invoked in vain; yet spare the relics of the Trojan train! Yet free our burning vessels from the flames, or let your fury fall alone on me! Throw your thunder at this devoted head, and send the willing sacrifice below!”

Scarcely had he said this, when southern storms arose: from pole to pole the forked lightning flew; loud rattling shook the mountains and the plain; Heaven bellied downward, and descended in rain. Whole sheets of water were sent from the clouds, which, hissing through the planks, prevented the flames, and stopped the fiery pest. Four ships alone burned to the waist, and atoned for the fleet.

But doubtful thoughts divided the hero's heart: whether he should still reside in Sicily, forgetful of his fates, or tempt the main, in hope of gaining the promised Italy. Then Nautes, old and wise, to whom alone Pallas had foreshown the will of Heaven; versed in portents, experienced, and inspired to tell events, and what the fates required; thus while he stood, inclined to neither part, relieved his laboring mind with cheerful words: “O goddess-born, resigned in every state, bear with patience, push with prudence your fate. By suffering well, we subdue our Fortune; flee when she frowns, and, when she calls, pursue. Your friend Acestes is of Trojan kind; to him disclose the secrets of your mind: trust in his hands your old and useless train; they are too numerous for the ships that yet remain: the feeble, the old, those indulgent of their ease, the dames who dread the dangers of the seas, with all the dastard crew, who dare not stand the shock of battle with your foes by land. Here you may build a common town for all, and, from Acestes' name, call it Acesta.” These reasons, joined with his friend's experience, encouraged him much, but more disturbed his mind.

It was dead of night; when to his slumbering eyes his father's shade descended from the skies, and thus he spoke: “O dearer to me than vital breath, loved while I lived, and dear even after death; O son, tossed in various toils and troubles, the King of Heaven employs my careful ghost on his commands: the god, who saved your flaming fleet from fire, and heard your just desire. Receive the wholesome counsel of your friend, and leave the coward train and the women here: transport the chosen youth, and those who nobly dare, to tempt the dangers of the war. The stern Italians will try their courage; rough are their manners, and their minds are high. But first you shall go to Pluto's palace, and seek my shade among the blessed below: for my soul does not remain with impious ghosts, nor suffer with the damned perpetual pains, but breathes the living air of the soft Elysian plains. The chaste Sibylla shall convey your steps, and the blood of offered victims shall free the way. There you shall know what realms the gods assign, and learn the fates and fortunes of your line. But now, farewell! I vanish with the night, and feel the blast of heaven's approaching light.” He said this, and mixed with shades, and took his airy flight. “Where do you go so fast?” filial duty cried; “and why, ah why, is the wished embrace denied?”

He said this, and rose; as holy zeal inspired him, he raked hot embers, and renewed the fires; then adored his country gods and Vesta with cakes and incense, and implored their aid. Next, he sent for his friends and his royal host, revealed his vision, and the gods' intent, with his own purpose. All, without delay, obeyed the will of Jove and his desires. They listed with women every degenerate name, who dared not hazard his life for future fame. These they cashiered: the brave remaining few renewed the oars, banks, and cables, half consumed. The prince designed a city with the plow; the lots allowed their several tenements. This part is named from Ilium, that from Troy, and the new king ascended the throne with joy; he drew a chosen senate from the people; appointed the judges, and ordained the laws. Then, on the top of Eryx, they began a rising temple to the Paphian queen. Anchises, last, was honored as a god; a priest was added, annual gifts bestowed, and groves were planted round his blessed abode. Nine days they passed in feasts, their temples crowned; and fumes of incense abounded in the shrines. Then from the south arose a gentle breeze that curled the smoothness of the glassy seas; the rising winds afforded a ruffling gale, and called the merry mariners aboard.

Now loud laments resounded along the shores, of parting friends bound in close embraces. The trembling women, the degenerate train, who had shunned the frightful dangers of the main, even those now desired to sail, and to take their share of the rough passage and the promised war; whom good Aeneas cheered, and recommended his fearful friends to their new master's care. On Eryx's altars he laid three fat calves; a new-fallen lamb to the stormy seas; then he slipped his hawsers, and weighed his anchors. High on the deck the godlike hero stood, crowned with olive, a charger in his hands; then cast the reeking entrails in the brine, and poured the sacrifice of purple wine. Fresh gales arose; with equal strokes they vied, and brushed the buxom seas, and flew over the billows.

Meanwhile the mother goddess, full of fears, thus addressed Neptune, with tender tears: “The pride of Jove's imperious queen, the rage, the malice which no sufferings can assuage, compel me to these prayers; since neither fate, nor time, nor pity, can remove her hate: even Jove is thwarted by his haughty wife; still vanquished, yet she still renews the strife. As if it were little to consume the town which awed the world, and wore the imperial crown, she prosecutes the ghost of Troy with pains, and gnaws, even to the bones, the last remains. Let her tell the causes of her hatred; but you can witness its effects too well. You saw the storm she raised on Libyan floods, that mixed the mounting billows with the clouds; when, bribing Aeolus, she shook the main, and moved rebellion in your watery reign. With fury she possessed the Dardan dames, to burn their fleet with execrable flames, and forced Aeneas, when his ships were lost, to leave his followers on a foreign coast. For what remains, I implore your godhead, and trust my son to your protecting power. If neither Jove's nor Fate's decree withstands it, secure his passage to the Latian land.”

Then thus the mighty Ruler of the Main: “What may not Venus hope from Neptune's reign? My kingdom claims your birth; my late defense of your endangered fleet may claim your confidence. Nor less by land than sea do my deeds declare how much your loved Aeneas is my care. I attest you, Xanthus, and you, Simois. When proud Achilles pressed your Trojan troops, and drove them headlong before him on the plain, and dashed the trembling train against the walls; when the floods were filled with bodies of the slain; when crimson Xanthus, doubtful of his way, stood up on ridges to behold the sea; new heaps came tumbling in, and choked his way; when your Aeneas fought, but fought with odds of unequal force, and unequal gods; I spread a cloud before the victor's sight, sustained the vanquished, and secured his flight; even then secured him, when I sought with joy the vowed destruction of ungrateful Troy. My will is the same: fair goddess, fear no more, your fleet shall safely gain the Latian shore; their lives are given; one destined head alone shall perish, and atone for multitudes.” Having thus armed her anxious mind with hopes, Saturnian Neptune joined his finny team, then added the foamy bridle to their jaws, and permitted the laws to the loosened reins. High on the waves he guided his azure car; its axles thundered, and the sea subsided, and the smooth ocean rolled her silent tides. The tempests fled before their father's face, trains of inferior gods graced his triumph, and monster whales played before their master, and choirs of Tritons crowded the watery way. The marshaled powers divided in equal troops to right and left; the gods enclosed his better side, and on the worse the Nymphs and Nereids rode.

Now smiling hope, with sweet vicissitude, renewed his joys within the hero's mind. He called to raise the masts, to display the sheets; the cheerful crew obeyed with diligence; they scudded before the wind, and sailed in open sea. Ahead of all the master pilot steered; and, as he led, the following navy veered. The steeds of Night had traveled half the sky, the drowsy rowers lay on their benches, when the soft God of Sleep, with easy flight, descended, and drew a trail of light behind. You, Palinurus, are his destined prey; he takes his fatal way to you alone. He bears dire dreams to you, and iron sleep; and, lighting on your prow, he wears the form of Phorbas. Then thus the traitor god began his tale: “The winds, my friend, inspire a pleasing gale; the ships, without your care, sail securely.
