Now steal an hour of sweet repose; and I will take the rudder and supply your room.” To whom the yawning pilot, half asleep: “Do you bid me trust the treacherous deep, the harlot smiles of her dissembling face, and commit the Trojan race to her faith? Shall I believe the Siren South again, and, often betrayed, not know the monster main?” He said: his fastened hands kept the rudder, and, fixed on heaven, his eyes repelled invading sleep. The god was wroth, and threw at his temples a branch dipped in Lethe, and drunk with Stygian dew: the pilot, vanquished by the divine power, soon closed his swimming eyes, and lay supine. Scarcely were his limbs extended at their length, when the god, insulting with superior strength, fell heavy on him, plunged him in the sea, and, with the stern, tore away the rudder. Headlong he fell, and, struggling in the main, cried out for helping hands, but cried in vain. The victor daemon mounted obscure in air, while the ship sailed without the pilot's care. On Neptune's faith the floating fleet relied; but what the man forsook, the god supplied, and the navy flew secure over the dangerous deep; it glided by the Sirens' cliffs, a shelvy coast, long infamous for ships and sailors lost, and white with bones. The impetuous ocean roared, and rocks bellowed back from the sounding shores. The watchful hero felt the knocks, and found the tossing vessel sailing on shoaly ground. Sure of his pilot's loss, he himself took the helm, and steered aloof, and shunned the shelf. Inwardly he grieved, and, groaning from his breast, deplored his death; and thus expressed his pain: “For trusting in seas, and in the flattering sky, your naked corpse is doomed to lie on shores unknown.”

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: The Sibyl foretells to Aeneas the adventures he shall meet with in Italy. She attends him to hell; describing to him the various scenes of that place, and conducting him to his father Anchises, who instructs him in those sublime mysteries of the soul of the world and of the transmigration; and shows him that glorious race of heroes which was to descend from him and his posterity.

He said this, and wept; then spread his sails before the winds, and at length reached the Cumaean shore. The anchors dropped, and his crew moored the vessels. They turned their heads to sea, their sterns to land, and greeted the Italian strand with greedy joy. Some struck their fiery seed from clashing flints; some gathered sticks to feed the kindled flames, or searched for hollow trees, and felled the woods, or traced the discovered floods through valleys. Thus, while they fulfilled their several charges, the pious prince ascended the sacred hill where Phoebus is adored, and sought the shade that hid from sight his venerable maid. Deep in a cave the Sibyl makes her abode; from there she returns full of fate, and of the god. Through Trivia's grove they walked; and now they beheld, and now entered, the temple roofed with gold. When Daedalus, to flee the Cretan shore, bore his heavy limbs on jointed pinions (the first who sailed in air, as Fame sings), he came at length to the Cumaean coast, and alighting here, built this costly frame. Inscribed to Phoebus, he hung on high the steerage of his wings that cut the sky: then over the lofty gate his art embossed Androgeos' death, and the offerings to his ghost; the seven youths yearly sent from Athens, to meet the fate appointed by revengeful Crete. And next to these the dreadful urn was placed, in which the destined names were cast by lots: the mournful parents stood around in tears, and rising Crete appeared against their shore. There too, in living sculpture, might be seen the mad affection of the Cretan queen; then how she cheated her bellowing lover's eye; the rushing leap, the doubtful progeny, the lower part a beast, a man above, the monument of their polluted love. Not far from there he engraved the wondrous maze, with a thousand doors, a thousand winding ways: here dwells the monster, hid from human view, not to be found, but by the faithful clue; until the kind artist, moved with pious grief, lent this last relief to the loving maid, and described all those erring paths so well that Theseus conquered and the monster fell. Here hapless Icarus would have found his part, had not the father's grief restrained his art. Twice he tried to cast his son in gold; twice from his hands he dropped the forming mold.

All this Aeneas viewed with wondering eyes; each varying object renewed his delight: eager to read the rest, Achates came, and by his side the mad divining dame, the priestess of the god, Deiphobe by name. “Time does not allow,” she said, “to feed your eyes with empty pleasures; haste to the sacrifice. Choose seven bullocks, still unyoked, for Phoebus, and seven unspotted ewes for Diana.” This said, the servants urged the sacred rites, while she invited the prince to the temple. A spacious cave, within its farthest part, was hewn and fashioned by laborious art through the hill's hollow sides: before the place, a hundred doors, a hundred entries grace it; and as many voices issue forth, and the sound of Sibyl's words rebounds as many times. Now they came to the mouth. Aloud she cried: “This is the time; inquire your destinies. He comes; behold the god!” Thus while she spoke (and shivering she stayed at the sacred entry), her color changed; her face was not the same, and hollow groans came from her deep spirit. Her hair stood up; convulsive rage possessed her trembling limbs, and heaved her laboring breast. She seemed greater than humankind to look upon, and spoke with an accent more than mortal. Her staring eyes rolled with sparkling fury; when all the god came rushing on her soul. Swiftly she turned, and, foaming as she spoke: “Why this delay?” she cried; “invoke the powers! Your prayers alone can open this abode; otherwise my demands are vain, and the god is dumb.”

She said no more. The trembling Trojans listened, overspread with a damp sweat and holy fear. The prince himself, possessed with awful dread, thus addressed his vows to great Apollo: “Indulgent god, propitious power to Troy, swift to relieve, unwilling to destroy, by whose hand directed the Dardan dart pierced the proud Grecian's only mortal part: thus far, by fate's decrees and your commands, through ambient seas and through devouring sands, our exiled crew has sought the Ausonian ground; and now, at length, the flying coast is found. Thus far the fate of Troy has pursued her wandering race from place to place with fury. Here cease, you powers, and let your vengeance end: Troy is no more, and can no more offend. And you, O sacred maid, inspired to see the event of things in dark futurity, give me what Heaven has promised to my fate: to conquer and command the Latian state; to fix my wandering gods, and find a place for the long exiles of the Trojan race. Then my grateful hands shall raise a temple to the twin gods, with vows and solemn prayer; and annual rites, and festivals, and games, shall be performed to their auspicious names. Nor shall you lack your honors in my land; for there your faithful oracles shall stand, preserved in shrines; and every sacred lay which, through your mouth, Apollo shall convey: all shall be treasured by a chosen train of holy priests, and ever shall remain. But O! do not commit your prophetic mind to flitting leaves, the sport of every wind, lest they disperse our empty fate in air; do not write, but relate what the powers ordain.”

Struggling in vain, impatient of her load, and laboring underneath the ponderous god, the more she strove to shake him from her breast, with more and far superior force he pressed; commanded his entrance, and, without control, usurped her organs and inspired her soul. Now, with a furious blast, the hundred doors opened of themselves; a rushing whirlwind roared within the cave, and Sibyl's voice was restored: “Escaped from the dangers of the watery reign, yet more and greater ills remain by land. Your troops shall reach the coast so long desired (nor doubt the event), but, having reached it, shall repent. Wars, horrid wars, I see; a field of blood, and Tiber rolling with a purple flood. Neither Simois nor Xanthus shall be lacking there: a new Achilles shall appear in arms, and he, too, goddess-born. Fierce Juno's hate, added to hostile force, shall urge your fate. To what strange nations will you not resort, driven to solicit aid at every court! The cause is the same that once oppressed Ilium: a foreign mistress, and a foreign guest. But you, secure of soul, unbent by woes, oppose the more, the more your fortune frowns. The dawnings of your safety shall be shown from where you least shall hope—a Grecian town.”

Thus, from the dark recess, the Sibyl spoke, and the resisting air the thunder broke; the cave rebellowed, and the temple shook. The ambiguous god, who ruled her laboring breast, expressed his mind in these mysterious words; some truths he revealed, the rest he left in involved terms. At length her fury fell, her foaming ceased, and, ebbing in her soul, the god decreased. Then thus the chief: “No terror is new to my view, no frightful face of danger can be new. Inured to suffer, and resolved to dare, the Fates, beyond my power, shall be beyond my care. This let me crave, since near your grove the road to hell lies open, and the dark abode which Acheron surrounds, the innavigable flood; conduct me through the regions void of light, and lead me longing to my father's sight. For him, I have sought a thousand dangers, and, rushing where the thickest Grecians fought, brought the sacred burden safe on my back. He, for my sake, endured the raging ocean, and the wrath of Heaven, my still auspicious guide, and bore beyond the strength that decrepit age supplied. Often, since he breathed his last, in the dead of night his reverend image has stood before my sight; charging me to seek his holy shade below; conducted there by your unerring aid. But you, if pious minds are won by prayers, oblige the father, and protect the son. Yours is the power; nor has Proserpine in vain made you priestess of her nightly reign. If Orpheus, armed with his enchanting lyre, could inspire the ruthless king with pity, and redeem his wife from the shades below; if Pollux, offering his alternate life, could free his brother, and can daily go by turns aloft, and by turns descend below: why do I name Theseus, or his greater friend, who trod the downward path, and could ascend upward? No less than theirs is my lineage from Jove; my mother is greater, my descent the same.” So prayed the Trojan prince, and, while he prayed, laid his hand upon the holy altar.

Then thus replied the divine prophetess: “O goddess-born of great Anchises' line, the gates of hell are open night and day; the descent is smooth, and easy is the way: but to return, and view the cheerful skies, in this the task and mighty labor lies. To few does great Jupiter impart this grace, and those of shining worth and heavenly race. Between those regions and our upper light, deep forests and impenetrable night possess the middle space: the infernal bounds Cocytus surrounds with his sable waves. But if so dire a love invades your soul, as to view the trembling shades twice below; if you will undertake so hard a toil, as to pass twice over the innavigable lake; receive my counsel. In the neighboring grove there stands a tree; the queen of Stygian Jove claims it as her own; thick woods and gloomy night conceal the happy plant from human sight. It bears one bough; but wondrous to behold! The ductile rind and leaves of radiant gold: this must be torn from the vulgar branches, and the present borne to fair Proserpine, before leave is given to tempt the nether skies. When the first is thus rent away, a second will arise, and the same metal supplies the same room. Look round the wood, with lifted eyes, to see the lurking gold upon the fatal tree: then rend it off, as holy rites command; the willing metal will obey your hand, following with ease, if favored by your fate, you are foredoomed to view the Stygian state: if not, no labor can constrain the tree; and strength of stubborn arms and steel are vain. Besides, you do not know, while you attend here, the unworthy fate of your unhappy friend: breathless he lies; and his unburied ghost, deprived of funeral rites, pollutes your host. Pay first his pious dues; and, for the dead, let two sable sheep be led around his hearse; then lay living turfs upon his body: this done, securely take the destined way, to find the regions destitute of day.”

She said, and held her peace. Aeneas went sad from the cave, and full of discontent, not knowing whom the sacred Sibyl meant. Achates, the companion of his breast, walked grieving by his side, oppressed with equal cares. Walking, they talked, and fruitlessly divined what friend the priestess designed by those words. But soon they found an object to deplore: Misenus lay extended on the shore; son of the God of Winds: none so renowned for sounding the warrior trumpet in the field; for kindling fierce alarms with breathing brass, and rousing men to dare their fate in honorable arms. He had served great Hector, and was ever near, not only with his trumpet, but with his spear. But when Hector fell by Pelides' arms, he chose Aeneas; and he chose as well. Swollen with applause, and aiming still at more, he now provoked the sea gods from the shore; Triton heard the martial sound with envy, and drowned the bold champion for his challenge; then cast his mangled carcass on the strand: the gazing crowd stood around the body. All wept; but Aeneas most mourned his fate, and hastened to perform the funeral rites. They reared a stately pile in the manner of an altar; the base broad below, and the top advanced in air. The Trojans found an ancient wood, fit for the work designed (the shady covert of the savage kind): the sounding axe was plied; firs, pines, pitch trees, and the towering pride of forest ashes, felt the fatal stroke, and piercing wedges cleaved the stubborn oak. Huge trunks of trees, felled from the steepy crown of the bare mountains, rolled down with ruin. Armed like the rest, the Trojan prince appeared, and urged them on by his pious labor.

Thus, while he wrought, revolving in his mind the ways to compass what his wish designed, he cast his eyes upon the gloomy grove, and then implored the Queen of Love with vows: “O may your power, propitious still to me, conduct my steps to find the fatal tree in this deep forest; since the Sibyl's breath foretold, alas, too truly, Misenus' death.” Scarcely had he said this, when, full before his sight, two doves, descending from their airy flight, alighted secure upon the grassy plain. He knew his mother's birds; and thus he prayed: “Be you my guides, with your auspicious aid, and lead my footsteps, until the branch is found, whose glittering shadow gilds the sacred ground. And you, great parent, with celestial care, be present to my prayer in this distress!” Having said this, he stopped with watchful sight, still observing the motions of their flight, what course they took, what happy signs they showed. They fed, and, fluttering, by degrees withdrew still farther from the place, but still in view: hopping and flying, they thus led him on to the slow lake, whose baleful stench to shun, they winged their flight aloft; then, stooping low, perched on the double tree that bears the golden bough. Through the green leaves the glittering shadows glowed; as the wintry mistletoe on the sacred oak, where the proud mother views her precious brood, and happier branches, which she never sowed. Such was the glittering; such the ruddy rind, and dancing leaves, that wantoned in the wind. He seized the shining bough with griping hold, and rent the lingering gold away with ease; then bore the prize to the Sibyl's palace. Meanwhile the Trojan troops, with weeping eyes, paid their obsequies to dead Misenus. First, from the ground they reared a lofty pile of pitch trees, oaks, and pines, and unctuous fir: they strewed the fabric's front with cypress twigs, and stuck the sides with boughs of baleful yew. The topmost part was adorned with his glittering arms; warm waters, then, borne in brazen cauldrons, were poured to wash his body, joint by joint, and fragrant oils anointed the stiffened limbs. With groans and cries they lamented Misenus: then on a bier, covered over with purple, they laid the breathless body, thus bewailed, and fired the pile, their faces turned away: such reverend rites their fathers were used to pay. They threw pure oil and incense on the fire, and the fat of victims which his friends bestowed. The greedy flames devoured these gifts to dust; then they poured red wine on the living coals; and, last, they disposed the relics by themselves, which the priests enclosed in a brazen urn. Old Corynaeus compassed the crew three times, and dipped an olive branch in holy dew; which he sprinkled round three times, and three times aloud invoked the dead, and then dismissed the crowd. But good Aeneas ordered a stately tomb on the shore, whose top bore a trumpet, a soldier's falchion, and a seaman's oar. Thus was his friend interred; and deathless fame still consigns his name to the lofty cape. These rites performed, the prince, without delay, hastened on his destined way to the nether world. The cave was deep; and, downward as it went from the wide mouth, a rocky rough descent; and here a gloomy grove defends the access, and there the unnavigable lake extends, over whose unhappy waters, void of light, no bird presumes to steer his airy flight; such deadly stenches arise from the depths, and steaming sulphur, that infects the skies. From this, the Grecian bards made their legends, and gave the name Avernus to the lake. The pious hero brought four sable bullocks, untaught in the yoke, for sacrifice. The priestess poured the wine between their horns; then cut the curling hair; that first oblation burned, invoking Hecate to repair there: a powerful name in hell and in the upper air. The sacred priests with ready knives bereaved the beasts of life, and received the streaming blood in full bowls: Aeneas offered a lamb to Hell and Night (the sable wool without a streak of white); and, by fate's decree, a barren heifer, Proserpine, to you. With holocausts he filled Pluto's altar; he killed seven brawny bulls with his own hand; then poured oil on the broiling entrails; which, anointed thus, the raging flame devoured. The nocturnal sacrifice began late, nor ended until the next returning sun. Then the earth began to bellow, trees to dance, and howling dogs to advance in glimmering light, before Hecate came. “Far from here be souls profane!” the Sibyl cried, “and abstain from the grove! Now, Trojan, take the way your fates afford; assume your courage, and unsheathe your sword.” She said, and passed along the gloomy space; the prince pursued her steps with equal pace.
You realms, yet unrevealed to human sight, you gods who rule the regions of the night, you gliding ghosts, permit me to relate the mystic wonders of your silent state!

Obscure they went through dreary shades, that led along the waste dominions of the dead. Thus travelers wander in woods by night, by the moon's doubtful and malignant light, when Jove involves the skies in dusky clouds, and the faint crescent shoots by fits before their eyes.

Just in the gate and in the jaws of hell, revengeful Cares and sullen Sorrows dwell, and pale Diseases, and repining Age, Want, Fear, and Famine's unresisted rage; here Toils, and Death, and Death's half-brother, Sleep, terrible forms to view, keep their sentry; with the anxious Pleasures of a guilty mind, deep Frauds before, and open Force behind; the Furies' iron beds; and Strife, that shakes her hissing tresses and unfolds her snakes. Full in the midst of this infernal road, an elm displays her dusky arms abroad: the God of Sleep there hides his heavy head, and empty dreams are spread on every leaf. Of various forms, unnumbered specters more, Centaurs, and double shapes, besiege the door. Before the passage, horrid Hydra stands, and Briareus with all his hundred hands; Gorgons, Geryon with his triple frame; and vain Chimaera vomits empty flame. The chief unsheathed his shining steel, prepared, though seized with sudden fear, to force the guard, offering his brandished weapon at their face; had not the Sibyl stopped his eager pace, and told him what those empty phantoms were: forms without bodies, and impassive air. Hence to deep Acheron they took their way, whose troubled eddies, thick with ooze and clay, are whirled aloft, and lost in Cocytus. There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast: a sordid god: down from his hoary chin a length of beard descends, uncombed, unclean; his eyes, like hollow furnaces on fire; a girdle, foul with grease, binds his obscene attire. He spreads his canvas; with his pole he steers; he bears the freights of flitting ghosts in his thin bottom. He looked old in years; yet in his years were seen a youthful vigor and autumnal green. An airy crowd came rushing where he stood, which filled the margin of the fatal flood: husbands and wives, boys and unmarried maids, and the more majestic shades of mighty heroes, and youths, entombed before their fathers' eyes, with hollow groans, and shrieks, and feeble cries. Thick as the leaves in autumn strew the woods, or fowls, forced by winter, forsake the floods, and wing their hasty flight to happier lands; such, and so thick, the shivering army stood, and pressed for passage with extended hands. Now these, now those, the surly boatman bore: the rest he drove to a distance from the shore. The hero, who beheld with wondering eyes the tumult mixed with shrieks, laments, and cries, asked of his guide what the rude concourse meant; why the thronging people bent toward the shore; what forms of law were used among the ghosts; why some were ferried over, and some refused.

“Son of Anchises, offspring of the gods,” the Sibyl said, “you see the Stygian floods, the sacred stream by which heaven's imperial state attests in oaths, and fears to violate. The ghosts rejected are the unhappy crew, deprived of sepulchers and funeral due: the boatman, Charon; those, the buried host, he ferries over to the farther coast; nor does his transport vessel dare cross the waves with such whose bones are not composed in graves. A hundred years they wander on the shore; at length, their penance done, they are wafted over.” The Trojan chief repressed his forward pace, revolving anxious thoughts within his breast. He saw his friends, who, overwhelmed beneath the waves, claimed their funeral honors, and asked for their quiet graves. He knew the lost Leucaspis in the crowd, and the brave leader of the Lycian crew, whom the tempests had met on the Tyrrhene seas; the sailors were mastered, and the ship overset.

Amidst the spirits, Palinurus pressed, yet fresh from life, a new-admitted guest, who, while he steered, viewing the stars, and bearing his course from Africa to the Latian shore, fell headlong down. The Trojan fixed his view, and scarcely knew the sullen shadow through the gloom. Then thus the prince: “What envious power, O friend, brought your loved life to this disastrous end? For Phoebus, ever true in all he said, has in your fate alone betrayed my faith. The god foretold that you should not die before you reached the Italian shore, secure from the seas. Is this the unerring power?” The ghost replied: “Phoebus did not flatter, nor did his answers lie; nor have envious gods sent me to the deep: but, while I kept the stars and course of heaven, my wearied eyes were seized with fatal sleep. I fell; and, with my weight, the helm constrained was drawn along, which yet my grip retained. Now by the winds and raging waves I swear, your safety, more than mine, was then my care; lest, bereft of the guide, and the rudder lost, your ship should run against the rocky coast. For three blustering nights, borne by the southern blast, I floated, and at last discovered land: high on a mounting wave I bore my head, forcing my strength, and gathering to the shore. Panting, but past the danger, I now seized the craggy cliffs, and eased my tired limbs. While, encumbered with my dropping clothes, I lay, the cruel nation, covetous of prey, stained with my blood the unhospitable coast; and now, by winds and waves, my lifeless limbs are tossed: avert which, O avert, by yon ethereal light, which I have lost for this eternal night! Or, if you may be won by dearer ties, by your dead sire, and by your living son, redeem my wandering ghost from this reproach; or with your navy seek the Velin coast, and compose my corpse in a peaceful grave; or, if a nearer way your mother shows, without whose aid you would not dare undertake this frightful passage over the Stygian lake, lend your hand to this wretch, and waft him over to the sweet banks of yon forbidden shore.” Scarcely had he said this when the prophetess began: “What hopes delude you, miserable man? Do you think, thus unentombed, to cross the floods, to view the Furies and infernal gods, and to visit, without leave, the dark abodes? Await the term of long revolving years; Fate, and the dooming gods, are deaf to tears. Take this comfort from your dire misfortune: the wrath of Heaven, inflicted for your sake, shall with vengeance pursue the inhuman coast, until they propitiate your offended ghost, and raise a tomb, with vows and solemn prayer; and the place shall bear Palinurus' name.” This calmed his cares; he was soothed with his future fame, and pleased to hear his propagated name.

Now they drew nearer to the Stygian lake: the surly boatman saw them from the shore; observed their passage through the shady wood, and marked their near approach to the flood. Then thus he called aloud, inflamed with wrath: “Mortal, whoever you are, who in arms presume to tread this forbidden path, I charge you, stand, and tell your name, and your business in the land. Know this: the realm of night; the Stygian shore. My boat conveys no living bodies over; nor was I pleased to bear great Theseus once, who forced a passage with his pointed spear, nor strong Alcides, men of mighty fame, whose lineage came from the immortal gods. One tied the barking porter in fetters, and took him trembling from his sovereign's side: two sought by force to seize his beautiful bride.” To whom the Sibyl thus: “Compose your mind; no frauds are contrived here, nor force designed. Still may the dog constrain the wandering troops of airy ghosts, and vex the guilty train, and his lovely queen remain with her grisly lord. The Trojan chief, whose lineage is from Jove, much famed for arms, and more for filial love, is sent to seek his sire in your Elysian grove. If neither piety, nor Heaven's command, can gain his passage to the Stygian strand, this fatal present shall prevail at least.” Then she showed the shining bough, concealed within her vest. No more was needful: for the gloomy god stood mute with awe, to see the golden rod; he admired the destined offering to his queen; a venerable gift, so rarely seen. His fury thus appeased, he put to land; the ghosts forsook their seats at his command: he cleared the deck, received the mighty freight; the leaky vessel groaned beneath the weight. Slowly she sailed, and scarcely stemmed the tides; the pressing water poured within her sides. At length his passengers were wafted over, exposed, in muddy weeds, upon the miry shore.

No sooner had they landed, than in his den they found the triple porter of the Stygian sound, grim Cerberus, who soon began to rear his crested snakes, and armed his bristling hair. The prudent Sibyl had prepared beforehand a sop, steeped in honey, to charm the guard; which, mixed with powerful drugs, she cast before his greedy grinning jaws, just opened to roar. With three enormous mouths he gaped; and straightway, pressed with hunger, devoured the pleasing bait. Long draughts of sleep enslaved his monstrous limbs; he reeled, and, falling, filled the spacious cave. The keeper charmed, the chief without delay passed on, and took the irremeable way. Before the gates, the cries of babes newly born, whom fate had torn from their tender mothers, assaulted his ears: then those, whom the form of laws condemned to die, when traitors judged their cause. Nor do they lack lots, nor judges to review the wrongful sentence, and award a new. Minos, the strict inquisitor, appears; and hears lives and crimes, with his assessors. He rolls the blended balls round in his urn, absolves the just, and dooms the guilty souls. The next, in place and punishment, are they who prodigally throw their souls away; fools, who, repining at their wretched state, and loathing anxious life, suborned their fate. With late repentance now they would retrieve the bodies they forsook, and wish to live; they desire to bear their pains and poverty, to view the light of heaven, and breathe the vital air: but fate forbids; the Stygian floods oppose, and with circling streams enclose the captive souls.

Not far from there, the Mournful Fields appear, so called from lovers who inhabit there. The souls whom that unhappy flame invades, in secret solitude and myrtle shades, make endless moans, and, pining with desire, lament too late their unextinguished fire. Here he found Procris, and Eriphyle here, baring her breast, yet bleeding with the wound made by her son. He saw Pasiphaë there, with Phaedra's ghost, a foul incestuous pair. There Laodamia, with Evadne, moves, unhappy both, but loyal in their loves: Caeneus, once a woman, and once a man, but ending in the sex she first began. Not far from these stood Phoenician Dido, fresh from her wound, her bosom bathed in blood; whom when the Trojan hero hardly knew, obscure in shades, and with a doubtful view, (doubtful as he who sees, through dusky night, or thinks he sees, the moon's uncertain light,) he first approached the sullen shade with tears; and, as his love inspired him, thus he said: “Unhappy queen! Then is the common breath of rumor true, in your reported death, and I, alas, the cause? By Heaven, I vow, and all the powers that rule the realms below, unwilling I forsook your friendly state, commanded by the gods, and forced by fate. Those gods, that fate, whose unresisted might has sent me to these regions void of light, through the vast empire of eternal night. Nor did I dare to presume that, pressed with grief, my flight should urge you to this dire relief. Stay, stay your steps, and listen to my vows: this is the last interview that fate allows!” In vain he thus attempted to move her mind with tears, and prayers, and late-repenting love. Disdainfully she looked; then, turning round, she fixed her eyes unmoved upon the ground, and regarded what he said and swore no more than the deaf rocks, when the loud billows roar; but she whirled away, to shun his hateful sight, hid in the forest and the shades of night; then sought Sichaeus through the shady grove, who answered all her cares, and equaled all her love.

The pitying hero paid some pious tears, and followed the flitting shade with his eyes, then took the forward way, ordained by fate, and, with his guide, attained the farther fields, where, severed from the rest, the warrior souls remained. He met Tydeus, with Meleager's race, the pride of armies, and the soldiers' grace; and pale Adrastus with his ghastly face. Of the Trojan chiefs he viewed a numerous train, all much lamented, all slain in battle; Glaucus and Medon, high above the rest, Antenor's sons, and Ceres' sacred priest. And proud Idaeus, Priam's charioteer, who shook his empty reins, and aimed his airy spear. The gladsome ghosts, in circling troops, attended, and beheld their friend with unwearied eyes; delighted to hover near, and longed to know what business brought him to the realms below. But the Argive chiefs, and Agamemnon's train, when his refulgent arms flashed through the shady plain, fled from his well-known face, with their wonted fear, as when his thundering sword and pointed spear had driven them headlong to their ships, and gleaned the routed rear. They raised a feeble cry, with trembling notes; but the weak voice deceived their gasping throats.

Here he found Priam's son, Deiphobus, whose face and limbs were one continued wound: dishonest, with lopped arms, the youth appeared, spoiled of his nose, and shortened of his ears. He scarcely knew him, striving to disown his blotted form, and blushing to be known; and therefore first began: “O Teucer's race, who dared thus to deface your faultless figure? What heart could wish, what hand inflict, this dire disgrace? It was famed that, in our last and fatal night, your single prowess long sustained the fight, until, tired, not forced, you chose a glorious fate, and fell upon a heap of slaughtered foes. But, in remembrance of so brave a deed, I decreed a tomb and funeral honors; I thrice called your manes on the Trojan plains: the place still retains your armor and your name. I sought your body too, and, had I found it, designed it for burial in your native ground.”

The ghost replied: “Your piety has paid all needful rites, to rest my wandering shade; but cruel fate, and my more cruel wife, betrayed my sleeping life to Grecian swords. These are the monuments of Helen's love: the shame I bear below, the marks I bore above. You know in what deluding joys we passed the night that was decreed by Heaven as our last: for, when the fatal horse, descending down, pregnant with arms, overwhelmed the unhappy town, she feigned nocturnal orgies; left my bed, and, mixed with Trojan dames, led the dances. Then, waving high her torch, she made the signal, which roused the Grecians from their ambuscade. Overworn with watching, oppressed with cares, unhappy, I had laid myself down to rest, and heavy sleep possessed my weary limbs. Meanwhile my worthy wife mislaid our arms, and conveyed away my sword from beneath my head; she unlatched the door, and, with repeated calls, invited her former lord within my walls. Thus she placed her confidence in her crime, and with new treasons would redeem the past. What need I say more? They ran into the room, and basely murdered a defenseless man. Ulysses, basely born, first led the way. Avenging powers! With justice if I pray, may that fortune be their own another day! But answer you; and in your turn relate, what brought you, living, to the Stygian state: were you driven by the winds and errors of the sea, or did you obey Heaven's superior doom? Or tell what other chance conducts your way, to view with mortal eyes our dark retreats, the tumults and torments of the infernal seats.”

While they thus passed the flying hours in talk, the sun had finished more than half his race: and they, perhaps, had spent in words and tears the little time of stay which Heaven had lent; but thus the Sibyl chided their long delay: “Night rushes down, and headlong drives the day: here, in different paths, the way divides; the right guides to Pluto's golden palace; the left tends to that unhappy region which descends to the depth of Tartarus; the seat of profound night, and of punished fiends.” Then thus Deiphobus: “O sacred maid, forbear to chide, and let your will be obeyed! Lo! I retire to the secret shadows, to pay my penance until my years expire. Proceed, auspicious prince, with glory crowned, and born to better fates than I have found.” He said; and, while he said, turned his steps to secret shadows, and mourned in silence.

The hero, looking on the left, spied a lofty tower, and strong on every side with treble walls, which Phlegethon surrounds, whose fiery flood bounds the burning empire; and, pressed between the rocks, the bellowing noise resounds. Wide is the fronting gate, and, raised on high with adamantine columns, threatens the sky. Vain is the force of man, and vain of Heaven, to crush the pillars which sustain the pile. Sublime on these a tower of steel is reared; and dire Tisiphone there keeps the ward, girt in her sanguine gown, by night and day, observant of the souls that pass the downward way. From there are heard the groans of ghosts, the pains of sounding lashes and of dragging chains. The Trojan stood astonished at their cries, and asked his guide from where those yells arose; and what the crimes, and what the tortures were, and the loud laments that rent the liquid air.

She thus replied: “The chaste and holy race are all forbidden this polluted place. But when Hecate gave me to rule the woods, she then led me trembling through these dire abodes, and taught me the tortures of the avenging gods. These are the realms of unrelenting fate; and awful Rhadamanthus rules the state. He hears and judges each committed crime; he inquires into the manner, place, and time. The conscious wretch must reveal all his acts, loath to confess, unable to conceal, from the first moment of his vital breath, to his last hour of unrepenting death. Straight, over the guilty ghost, the Fury shakes the sounding whip and brandishes her snakes, and the pale sinner, with her sisters, takes. Then, of itself, the eternal door unfolds; with dreadful sounds the brazen hinges roar. You see, before the gate, what stalking ghost commands the guard, what sentries keep the post. More formidable Hydra stands within, whose jaws with iron teeth severely grin. The gaping gulf lies low to the center, and is twice as deep as earth is distant from the skies. The rivals of the gods, the Titan race, here, singed with lightning, roll within the unfathomed space. Here lie the Aloean twins (I saw them both), enormous bodies, of gigantic growth, who dared in fight to defy the Thunderer, affect his heaven, and force him from the sky. I found Salmoneus, suffering cruel pains, for emulating Jove; the rattling sound of mimic thunder, and the glittering blaze of pointed lightnings, and their forky rays. Through Elis and the Grecian towns he flew; the audacious wretch drew four fiery coursers: he waved a torch aloft, and, madly vain, sought godlike worship from a servile train. Ambitious fool! With horny hoofs to pass over hollow arches of resounding brass, to rival thunder in its rapid course, and imitate inimitable force! But he, the King of Heaven, obscure on high, bared his red arm, and, launching from the sky his writhen bolt, not shaking empty smoke, struck the flaming felon down to the deep abyss. There Tityus was to be seen, who took his birth from heaven, his nursing from the foodful earth. Here his gigantic limbs, with large embrace, enfold nine acres of infernal space. A ravenous vulture, in his opened side, tried her crooked beak and cruel talons; still for the growing liver dug his breast; the growing liver still supplied the feast; still are his entrails fruitful to their pains: the immortal hunger lasts, the immortal food remains. I could name Ixion and Pirithous, and more Thessalian chiefs of mighty fame. High over their heads a moldering rock is placed, that promises a fall, and shakes at every blast. They lie below, displayed on golden beds; and genial feasts, with regal pomp, are made. The Queen of Furies is set by their sides, and snatches the untasted meat from their mouths, which if they touch, she rears her hissing snakes, tossing her torch, and thundering in their ears. Then, they who disown brothers' better claim, expel their parents, and usurp the throne; defraud their clients, and, sold to lucre, sit brooding on unprofitable gold; who dare not give, and even refuse to lend, to their poor kindred, or to a wanting friend. Vast is the throng of these; nor less the train of lustful youths, for foul adultery slain: hosts of deserters, who sold their honor, and basely broke their faith for bribes of gold. All these remain within the dungeon's depth, despairing pardon, and expecting pain. Ask not what pains; nor seek further to know their process, or the forms of law below. Some roll a weighty stone; some, laid along, and bound with burning wires, on spokes of wheels are hung. Unhappy Theseus, doomed forever there, is fixed by fate on his eternal chair; and wretched Phlegyas warns the world with cries (could warning make the world more just or wise): ‘Learn righteousness, and dread the avenging deities.' Others have sold their country to tyrants, imposing foreign lords for foreign gold; some have repealed old laws, made new statutes, not as the people pleased, but as they paid; with incest some profaned their daughters' bed: all dared the worst of ills, and, what they dared, attained. Had I a hundred mouths, a hundred tongues, and throats of brass, inspired with iron lungs, I could not repeat half those horrid crimes, nor half the punishments those crimes have met. But let us haste to pursue our voyage: the walls of Pluto's palace are in view; the gate, and iron arch above it, stands on anvils labored by the Cyclops' hands. Before the Fates allow our further way, here we must fix on high the golden bough.”

She said, and through the gloomy shades they passed, and chose the middle path. Arrived at last, the prince sprinkled his limbs and body with living water; then approached the door, possessed the porch, and on the front above fixed the fatal bough required by Pluto's love. These holy rites performed, they took their way where long extended plains of pleasure lay: the verdant fields may vie with those of heaven, clothed in ether, and a purple sky; the blissful seats of happy souls below. They know stars of their own, and their own suns; they exercise their airy limbs in sports, and contend on the green for the wrestler's prize. Some divinely sing in heroic verse; others led the ring in artful measures. The Thracian bard, surrounded by the rest, stood conspicuous there in his flowing vest; his flying fingers, and harmonious quill, struck seven distinguished notes, and seven at once filled the air. Here they found Teucer's old heroic race, born to grace better times and happier years. Assaracus and Ilus enjoy perpetual fame here, with him who founded Troy. The chief beheld their chariots from afar, their shining arms, and coursers trained to war: their lances fixed in earth, their steeds around, free from their harness, grazed the flowery ground. The love of horses which they had, alive, and the care of chariots, survive after death. Some cheerful souls were feasting on the plain; some maintained the song, and some the choir, beneath a laurel shade, where mighty Po mounts up to woods above, and hides his head below. Here patriots live, who, for their country's good, were prodigal of blood in fighting fields: priests of unblemished lives here make their abode, and poets worthy of their inspiring god; and searching wits, of more mechanic parts, who graced their age with new-invented arts: those who extended their bounty to worth, and those who knew how to commend that bounty. The heads of these were bound with holy fillets, and all their temples were crowned with garlands.

To these the Sibyl thus addressed her speech, and first to him who, surrounded by the rest, towered in height, and was ample in breast: “Say, happy souls, divine Musaeus, say, where does Anchises live, and where lies our way to find the hero, for whose only sake we sought the dark abodes, and crossed the bitter lake?” To this the sacred poet thus replied: “The happy souls reside in no fixed place. In groves we live, and lie on mossy beds, by crystal streams, that murmur through the meads: but pass that easy hill, and thence descend; the path conducts you to your journey's end.” Saying this, he led them up the mountain's brow, and showed them all the shining fields below. They wound round the hill, and went through the blissful meadows.

But old Anchises, in a flowery vale, reviewed his mustered race, and took the tale: those happy spirits, which, ordained by fate, awaited future beings and new bodies. With studious thought he observed the illustrious throng, in nature's order as they passed along: their names, their fates, their conduct, and their care, in peaceful senates and successful war. When Aeneas appeared on the plain, he met him with open arms, and falling tears. “Welcome,” he said, “the gods' undoubted race! O long expected to my dear embrace! Once more it is given me to behold your face! The love and pious duty which you pay have passed the perils of so hard a way. It is true, computing times, I now believed the happy day was approaching; nor are my hopes deceived. What length of lands, what oceans have you passed; what storms sustained, and on what shores been cast? How have I feared your fate! But I feared it most, when love assailed you, on the Libyan coast.” To this, filial duty thus replied: “Your sacred ghost appeared before my sleeping eyes, and often urged this painful enterprise. After long tossing on the Tyrrhene sea, my navy rides at anchor in the bay. But reach your hand, O parent shade, nor shun the dear embraces of your longing son!” He said; and falling tears bedewed his face: then three times he threw his arms around his neck; and three times the flitting shadow slipped away, like winds, or empty dreams that flee the day.

Now, in a secret vale, the Trojan sees a separate grove, through which a gentle breeze plays with a passing breath, and whispers through the trees; and, just before the confines of the wood, the gliding Lethe leads her silent flood. About the boughs an airy nation flew, thick as the humming bees, that hunt the golden dew; who in summer's heat feed on the tops of lilies, and creep within their bells, to suck the balmy seed: the winged army roams the fields around; the rivers and the rocks remurmur to the sound. Aeneas stood wondering, then asked the cause which drew the crowding people to the stream. Then thus the sire: “The souls that throng the flood are those to whom, by fate, other bodies are owed: in Lethe's lake they taste long oblivion, secure of future life, forgetful of the past. Long has my soul desired this time and place, to set before your sight your glorious race, that this presaging joy may fire your mind to seek the shores designed by destiny.” “O father, can it be, that sublime souls return to visit our terrestrial clime, and that the generous mind, released by death, can covet lazy limbs and mortal breath?”

Anchises then, in order, thus began to clear those wonders to his godlike son: “Know, first, that heaven, and earth's compacted frame, and flowing waters, and the starry flame, and both the radiant lights, are inspired and fed by one common soul, which animates the whole. This active mind, infused through all the space, unites and mingles with the mighty mass. Hence men and beasts obtain the breath of life, and the birds of air, and the monsters of the main. The ethereal vigor is the same in all, and every soul is filled with equal flame; as much as earthy limbs, and the gross alloy of mortal members, subject to decay, do not blunt the beams of heaven and the edge of day. From this coarse mixture of terrestrial parts, desire and fear by turns possess their hearts, and grief, and joy; nor can the groveling mind, confined in the dark dungeon of the limbs, assert the native skies, or own its heavenly kind: nor can death itself wholly wash their stains; but long-contracted filth remains even in the soul. They wear the relics of inveterate vice, and spots of obscene sin appear on every face. For this, various penances are enjoined; and some are hung to bleach upon the wind, some plunged in waters, others purged in fires, until all the dregs are drained, and all the rust expires. All have their manes, and those manes bear: the few, so cleansed, repair to these abodes, and breathe, in ample fields, the soft Elysian air. Then they are happy, when by length of time the scurf of each committed crime is worn away; no speck is left of their habitual stains, but the pure ether of the soul remains. But, when a thousand rolling years have passed (so long do their punishments and penance last), whole droves of minds are, by the driving god, compelled to drink the deep Lethaean flood, to steep in large forgetful draughts the cares of their past labors, and their irksome years, that, unremembering its former pain, the soul may suffer mortal flesh again.”

Thus having said, the father spirit led the priestess and his son through swarms of shades, and took a rising ground, from which to see the long procession of his progeny. “Survey,” the sire pursued, “this airy throng, as they pass along, offered to your view. These are the Italian names, which fate will join with ours, and graft upon the Trojan line. Observe the youth who appears first in sight, and holds the nearest station to the light; already he seems to snuff the vital air, and leans just forward, on a shining spear: he is Silvius, your last-begotten race, but sent first in order, to fill your place; an Alban name, but mixed with Dardan blood, born in the covert of a shady wood: fair Lavinia, your surviving wife, shall breed him in groves, to lead a solitary life. In Alba he shall fix his royal seat, and, born a king, shall beget a race of kings. Then Procas, honor of the Trojan name, Capys, and Numitor, of endless fame. After these, a second Silvius appears; Silvius Aeneas, for he bears your name; equally renowned for arms and justice, who, late restored, shall be crowned in Alba. How great they look! How vigorously they wield their weighty lances, and sustain the shield! But those who appear crowned with oaken wreaths shall rear the Gabian walls and strong Fidena; shall found Nomentum, Bola, with Pometia; and raise Collatian towers on rocky ground. All these shall then be towns of mighty fame, though now they lie obscure, and as lands without a name. See Romulus the great, born to restore the crown which once his injured grandsire wore. A priestess of your blood shall bear this prince, and he shall appear in arms like his sire. Two rising crests adorn his royal head; born from a god, himself born to godhead: his sire already signs him for the skies, and marks the seat amidst the deities. Auspicious chief! Your race, in times to come, shall spread the conquests of imperial Rome. Rome, whose ascending towers shall invade heaven, enveloping earth and ocean in her shade; high as the Mother of the Gods in place, and proud, like her, of an immortal race. Then, when in pomp she makes the Phrygian round, with golden turrets crowned on her temples; a hundred gods supply her sweeping train; all her offspring, and all command the sky.

“Now fix your sight, and stand intent, to see your Roman race, and the Julian progeny. The mighty Caesar awaits his vital hour, impatient for the world, and grasps his promised power. But next behold the youth of form divine, Caesar himself, exalted in his line; Augustus, often promised, and long foretold, sent to the realm that Saturn ruled of old; born to restore a better age of gold. Africa and India shall obey his power; he shall extend his propagated sway beyond the solar year, without the starry way, where Atlas turns the rolling heavens around, and his broad shoulders are crowned with their lights. At his foreseen approach, already quake the Caspian kingdoms and the Maeotian lake: their seers behold the tempest from afar, and threatening oracles denounce the war. Nile hears him knocking at his sevenfold gates, and seeks his hidden spring, and fears his nephew's fates. Nor did Hercules know more lands or labors, not even when he slew the brazen-footed hind, freed Erymanthus from the foaming boar, and dipped his arrows in Lernaean gore; nor Bacchus, turning from his Indian war, drawn triumphant in his car by tigers, descending from Nisus' top to the plains, with curling vines around his purple reins. And do we yet doubt, through dangers, to pursue the paths of honor, and a crown in view? But who is the man, who appears from afar? His head crowned with olive, his hand bears a censer, his hoary beard and holy vestments bring his lost idea back: I know the Roman king. He shall ordain new laws for peaceful Rome, called from his humble abode to sustain a scepter. Next in dignity him, Tullus succeeds, an active prince, and prone to martial deeds. He shall prepare his troops for fighting fields, disused to toils, and triumphs of war. By dint of sword he shall increase his crown, and scour his armor from the rust of peace. Whom Ancus follows, with a fawning air, but vain within, and proudly popular. Next view the Tarquin kings, the avenging sword of Brutus, justly drawn, and Rome restored. He first renews the rods and severe axe, and gives the consuls royal robes to wear. His sons, who seek to sustain the tyrant, and long for arbitrary lords again, are scourged with ignominy, in open sight; he dooms them to deserved death, asserting public right. Unhappy man, to break the pious laws of nature, pleading in his children's cause! However the doubtful fact is understood, it is love of honor, and his country's good: the consul, not the father, sheds the blood. Behold Torquatus pursuing the same track; and, next, view the two devoted Decii: the Drusian line, Camillus loaded home with standards well redeemed, and foreign foes overcome. The pair you see shine in equal armor, now, friends below, joined in close embraces; but, when they leave the shady realms of night, and, clothed in bodies, breathe your upper light, they shall pursue each other with mortal hate: what wars, what wounds, what slaughter shall ensue! From the Alpine heights the father first descends; his daughter's husband awaits him on the plain: his daughter's husband arms his eastern friends. Embrace again, my sons, be foes no more; nor stain your country with her children's gore! And you, the first, lay down your lawless claim, you, of my blood, who bear the Julian name! Another comes, who shall ride in triumph, and guide his chariot to the Capitol, from conquered Corinth, rich with Grecian spoils. And yet another, famed for warlike toils, shall impose the Roman laws on Argos, and avenge the Trojan cause on the Greeks; he shall drag their Achillean race in chains; he shall vindicate his ancestors' disgrace, and Pallas, for her violated place. Great Cato there, for gravity renowned, and conquering Cossus go crowned with laurels. Who can omit the Gracchi? Who can declare the Scipios' worth, those thunderbolts of war, the double bane of Carthage? Who can see, without esteem for virtuous poverty, severe Fabricius, or cease to admire the plowman consul in his coarse attire? Tired as I am, the Fabii claim my praise; and you, great hero, greatest of your name, ordained in war to save the sinking state, and, by delays, to put a stop to fate! Let others better mold the running mass of metals, and inform the breathing brass, and soften into flesh a marble face; plead better at the bar; describe the skies, and tell when the stars descend, and when they rise. But, Rome, it is yours alone, with awful sway, to rule mankind, and make the world obey, disposing peace and war by your own majestic way; to tame the proud, to free the fettered slave: these are imperial arts, and worthy of you.”

He paused; and, while they viewed the passing spirits with wondering eyes, thus renewed his speech: “See great Marcellus! How, untired in toils, he moves with manly grace, how rich with regal spoils! When his country, threatened with alarms, requires his courage and his conquering arms, he shall more than once affright the Punic bands; shall kill the Gaulish king in single fight; then move to the Capitol in triumph, and the third spoils shall grace Feretrian Jove.” Aeneas here beheld, of form divine, a godlike youth shining in glittering armor, keeping equal pace with great Marcellus; but his eyes were gloomy, his face dejected. He saw, and, wondering, asked his airy guide, what he was and from whence, who pressed the hero's side: “His son, or one of his illustrious name? How like the former, and almost the same! Observe the crowds that compass him around; all gaze, and all admire, and raise a shouting sound: but hovering mists are spread around his brows, and night, with sable shades, involves his head.” “Seek not to know,” the ghost replied with tears, “the sorrows of your sons in future years. This youth (the blissful vision of a day) shall just be shown on earth, and snatched away. The gods had raised the Roman state too high, had their gifts been as permanent as great. What groans of men shall fill the Martian field! How fierce a blaze his flaming pile shall yield! What funeral pomp shall floating Tiber see, when, rising from his bed, he views the sad solemnity! No youth shall give equal hopes of glory, no youth afford so great a cause to grieve; the Trojan honor, and the Roman boast, admired when living, and adored when lost! Mirror of ancient faith in early youth! Undaunted worth, inviolable truth! No foe, unpunished, in the fighting field shall dare you, foot to foot, with sword and shield; much less in arms oppose your matchless force, when your sharp spurs shall urge your foaming horse. Ah! Could you break through fate's severe decree, a new Marcellus shall arise in you! Bring full canisters of fragrant lilies, mixed with the purple roses of the spring; let me strew his body with funeral flowers; this gift which parents owe to their children, this unavailing gift, at least, I may bestow!” Thus having said, he led the hero round the confines of the blessed Elysian ground; which when Anchises had shown to his son, and fired his mind to mount the promised throne, he tells him the future wars, ordained by fate; the strength and customs of the Latian state; the prince, and people; and forearms his care with rules, to push his fortune, or to bear.

Two gates adorn the silent house of Sleep; this of polished ivory, that of transparent horn: true visions arise through the transparent horn; deluding lies pass through polished ivory. Discoursing of various things as he passed, Anchises bent his steps here at last. Then, through the gate of ivory, he dismissed his valiant offspring and his divining guest. Straightway Aeneas took his way to the ships, embarked his men, and skimmed along the sea, still coasting, until he gained Caieta's bay. At length he moored his galleys on oozy ground; their heads were turned to sea, their sterns to shore.

chapters.title: Book VII
paragraphs: King Latinus entertains Aeneas, and promises him his only daughter, Lavinia, the heiress of his crown. Turnus, being in love with her, and favored by her mother, by Juno, and by Alecto, breaks the treaty that had been made, and engages in his quarrel Mezentius, Camilla, Messapus, and many other of the neighboring princes, whose forces, and the names of their commanders, are particularly related.

And you, O matron of immortal fame, here dying, have left your name to the shore. The place is still called Caieta from you, the nurse of the infancy of great Aeneas. Here your bones rest in the rich plains of Hesperia; your name (which is all a ghost can have) remains.

Now, when the prince had paid her funeral rites, he plowed the Tyrrhene seas with sails displayed. A gentle breeze arose from the land by night; the stars shone serenely, the moon was bright, and the sea trembled with her silver light. Now they ran near the shelves of Circe's shores (Circe, the rich, the daughter of the Sun)—a dangerous coast: the goddess wastes her days in joyous songs; the rocks resound her lays; in spinning, or at the loom, she spends the night, and cedar brands supply her father's light. From there were heard, rebellowing to the main, the roars of lions that refuse the chain, the grunts of bristled boars, and the groans of bears, and the herds of howling wolves that stun the sailors' ears. These, from their caverns, at the close of night, fill the sad island with horror and fright. In the darkness they mourn their fate, whom Circe's power (who watched the moon and the planetary hour), with words and wicked herbs, had altered from humankind and confined in brutal shapes. Lest the Trojans' pious host should bear these monsters or touch upon the enchanted coast, propitious Neptune steered their course by night with rising gales that sped their happy flight. Supplied with these, they skimmed the sounding shore, and heard the swelling surges vainly roar. Now, when the rosy morn began to rise, and waved her saffron streamer through the skies; when Thetis blushed in a purple not her own, and the breathing winds were blown from her face, a sudden silence sat upon the sea, and sweeping oars, with struggling, urged their way. From the main, the Trojan beheld a wood, which stood thick with shades and a brown horror; between the trees the Tiber took his course, dimpled with whirlpools, and with downward force, which drove the sand along, he took his way, and rolled his yellow billows to the sea. About him, and above, and round the wood, the birds that haunt the borders of his flood, that bathed within, or basked upon his side, applied their narrow throats to tuneful songs. The captain gave the command; the joyful train glided through the gloomy shade, and left the main.

Now, Erato, inspire your poet's mind, and fill his soul with your celestial fire! Relate what Latium was; tell of her ancient kings; declare the past and present state of things, when the Trojan fleet first sought Ausonia, and how the rivals loved, and how they fought. These are my theme, and how the war began, and how it was concluded by the godlike man. For I shall sing of battles, blood, and rage, which princes and their people did engage; and haughty souls, who, moved with mutual hate, pursued and found their fate in fighting fields; that roused the Tyrrhene realm with loud alarms, and involved peaceful Italy in arms. A larger scene of action is displayed; and, rising hence, a greater work is weighed.

Latinus, old and mild, had long possessed the Latin scepter, and had blessed his people. His father was Faunus; his mother a Laurentian dame, fair Marica by name. But Faunus came from Picus; Picus drew his birth from Saturn, if records be true. Thus King Latinus, in the third degree, had Saturn as author of his family. But this old peaceful prince, as Heaven decreed, was blessed with no male issue to succeed: his sons in blooming youth were snatched by fate; one only daughter inherited the royal state. Fired with her love, and led by ambition, the neighboring princes courted her nuptial bed. Among the crowd, but far above the rest, young Turnus addressed himself to the beauteous maid. Turnus, for high descent and graceful mien, was first, and favored by the Latian queen; with him she strove to join Lavinia's hand, but dire portents withstood the purposed match.

Deep in the palace, of long growth, there stood the trunk of a laurel, a venerable wood; where divine rites were paid, whose holy hair was kept and cut with superstitious care. Latinus, when he walled his town, then found this plant, and from the tree called it Laurentum; and last, in honor of his new abode, he vowed the laurel to the laurel's god. It happened once (a boding prodigy) that a swarm of bees, which cut the liquid sky, unknown from where they took their airy flight, alighted in clouds on the topmost branch. There with their clasping feet they clung together, and a long cluster hung from the laurel. An ancient augur prophesied from this: "Behold on Latian shores a foreign prince! From the same parts of heaven his navy comes, to the same parts on earth; his army lands; the town he conquers, and commands the tower."

Yet more: when fair Lavinia fed the fire before the gods, and stood beside her sire, strange to relate, the flames, involved in the smoke of incense, broke from the sacred altar, and caught her disheveled hair and rich attire. Her crown and jewels crackled in the fire; from there the fuming trail began to spread, and lambent glories danced about her head. This new portent the seer viewed with wonder; then, pausing, he thus renewed his prophecy: "The nymph, who scatters flaming fires around, shall shine with honor, shall herself be crowned; but, caused by her irrevocable fate, war shall waste the country, and change the state."

Latinus, frightened with this dire omen, went for counsel to his father Faunus, and sought the shades renowned for prophecy, which lie near Albunea's sulphurous fountain. To these the Latian and the Sabine land flee, when distressed, and from thence demand relief. The priest takes his ease on the skins of offerings, and sees nightly visions in his slumber; a swarm of thin aerial shapes appears, and, fluttering round his temples, deafens his ears. These he consults, to know the future fates from the powers above, and from the fiends below. Here Latinus flew for the gods' advice, offering a hundred sheep for sacrifice. Their woolly fleeces, as the rites required, he laid beneath him, and retired to rest. No sooner were his eyes bound in slumber, when from above, a more than mortal sound invaded his ears; and thus the vision spoke: "Do not seek, my offspring, to yoke our fair Lavinia in Latian bonds, nor provoke the gods. A foreign son descends upon your shore, whose martial fame extends from pole to pole. His race, renowned in arms and in arts of peace, neither Latium shall contain, nor Europe bound: theirs shall be whatever the sun surveys." These answers, received in the silent night, the king himself divulged, and the land believed. Fame flew through all the neighboring nations, when now the Trojan navy was in view.

Beneath a shady tree, the hero spread his table on the turf, with cakes of bread; and with his chiefs, he fed on forest fruits. They sat, and (not without the gods' command), having dispatched their homely fare, the hungry band invaded their trenchers next, and soon devoured, to mend the scanty meal, their very cakes of flour. Ascanius observed this, and, smiling, said: "See, we devour the plates on which we fed!" The speech had an omen in it, that the Trojan race should find rest, and that this was the time and place. Aeneas took up the word, and thus replied, confessing fate with wonder in his eyes: "All hail, O earth! All hail, my household gods! Behold the destined place of your abodes! For thus Anchises prophesied of old, and foretold this our fatal place of rest: 'When, on a foreign shore, instead of meat, forced by famine, you shall eat your trenchers, then ease will attend your weary Trojans, and the long labors of your voyage shall end. Remember, on that happy coast, to build, and to enclose the fruitful field with a trench.' This was that famine, and this the fatal place, which ends the wandering of our exiled race. Then, on tomorrow's dawn, employ your care to search the land, and where the cities lie, and what the men are; but give this day to joy. Now pour libations to Jove; and, after Jove is blessed, call great Anchises to the genial feast. Crown the goblets high with a cheerful draught; enjoy the present hour; adjourn the future thought."

Thus having said, the hero bound his brows with leafy branches; then performed his vows, adoring first the genius of the place; then Earth, the mother of the heavenly race; the nymphs, and native godheads yet unknown; and Night, and all the stars that gild her sable throne; and ancient Cybele, and Idaean Jove; and last his sire below, and his mother queen above. Then heaven's high monarch thundered three times aloud, and three times shook a golden cloud aloft. Soon through the joyful camp a rumor flew that the time had come for them to renew their city. Then every brow was crowned with cheerful green; the feasts were doubled, and the bowls went round.

When next the rosy morn disclosed the day, the scouts divided their way to several parts, to learn the names of the natives, to explore their towns, and the coasts and bends of the crooked shore: here flows Tiber, and here stands Numicus; here warlike Latins hold the happy lands. The pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways to found his empire and to raise his town, selected a hundred youths from all his train, and directed their course to the Latian court (the spacious palace where their prince resides), and veiled all their heads with wreaths of olive. They went commissioned to ask for peace, and to carry presents to procure access. Thus while they hastened their pace, the prince designed his newly elected seat, and drew the lines. The Trojans cast a rampart round the place, and set palisades about the trenches.

Meanwhile the train, proceeding on their way, surveyed the town and the lofty towers from afar. At length they approached the walls. Outside the gate, they saw the boys and Latian youth contend for the martial prizes on the dusty plain: some drove the cars, some reined the coursers; some bent the stubborn bow for victory, and some tried their active sinews with darts. A posting messenger, dispatched from there, advised their aged prince of this fair troop, that foreign men of mighty stature had come, uncouth in habit, and unknown in name. The king ordained their entrance, and ascended his regal seat, surrounded by his friends.

The palace built by Picus, vast and proud, stood supported by a hundred pillars, and was surrounded by a rising wood. The pile overlooked the town, and drew the sight, surprising at once with reverence and delight. There kings received the marks of sovereign power; in state the monarchs marched; the lictors bore their awful axes, and the rods before. Here the tribunal stood, the house of prayer, and here the sacred senators repaired; all set at large tables in long order, a ram their offering, and a ram their meat. Above the portal, carved in cedar wood, stood their godlike grandsires placed in their ranks: old Saturn, with his crooked scythe on high; and Italus, who led the colony; and ancient Janus, with his double face, and bunch of keys, the porter of the place. There good Sabinus, planter of the vines, reclined his head on a short pruning hook, and studiously surveyed his generous wines. Then warlike kings, who fought for their country, and brought honorable wounds from battle. Around the posts hung helmets, darts, and spears, and captive chariots, axes, shields, and bars, and broken beaks of ships, the trophies of their wars. Above the rest, as chief of all the band, was placed Picus, with a buckler in his hand; his other hand waved a long divining wand. The hero sat girt in his Gabine gown, yet he could not with his art avoid his fate: for Circe had long loved the youth in vain, till love, refused, converted to disdain. Then, mixing powerful herbs with magic art, she changed his form, since she could not change his heart; she constrained him into a bird, and made him fly as a chattering magpie, with party-colored plumes.

In this high temple, on a chair of state, the seat of audience, old Latinus sat; then gave admission to the Trojan train, and thus began with pleasing accents: "Tell me, you Trojans (for that name you own, nor is your course unknown upon our coasts), say what you seek, and where you were bound. Were you cast aground by stress of weather, such dangers as are often seen at sea, and often befall miserable men? Or have you come to lay your shipping in our ports, spent and disabled by so long a way? Say what you want; you shall find the Latians not forced to goodness, but inclined by will; for, since the time of Saturn's holy reign, we retain his hospitable customs. I call to mind (though time has worn the tale) that the Aurunci said that Dardanus, though born on Latian plains, yet sought the Phrygian shore, and Samothracia, formerly called Samos. From Tuscan Corythus he claimed his birth; but afterwards, when exempt from mortal earth, he ascended from there to his kindred skies, a god, and, as a god, augments their sacrifice."

He said. Ilioneus made this reply: "O king, of Faunus' royal family! Neither did wintry winds force our way to Latium, nor did the stars betray our wandering course. Willingly we sought your shores; and, bound here, we at length found the long-desired port; expelled from our sweet homes and ancient realms, once as great as the greatest the sun beheld. The god who rules above began our line; and, as our race, our king descends from Jove; and here we have come, by his command, to crave admission in your happy land. How dire a tempest, poured from Mycenae, devoured our plains, our temples, and our town; what was the waste of war, what fierce alarms shook Asia's crown with European arms—even such have heard of it, if any such there be, whose earth is bounded by the frozen sea, and such as, born beneath the burning sky and sultry sun, lie between the tropics. From that dire deluge, through the watery waste, having past such length of years and various perils, we have at last escaped, and we repair to Latium, to beg what you without your own want may spare: the common water, and the common air; and sheds which we ourselves will build, and mean abodes, fit to receive and serve our banished gods. Nor shall our admission disgrace your realm, nor shall length of time efface our gratitude. Besides, what endless honor shall you gain, to save and shelter Troy's unhappy train! Now, by my sovereign, and by his fate, I swear—renowned for faith in peace, for force in war—often our alliance has been desired by other lands, and what we seek of you has been required of us. Do not despise, then, that in our hands we bear these holy boughs, and sue with words of prayer. Fate and the gods, by their supreme command, have doomed our ships to seek the Latian land. Apollo sends our fleet to these abodes; here Dardanus was born, and here he tends; where Tuscan Tiber rolls with rapid force, and where Numicus opens his holy source. Besides, our prince presents, with his request, some small remains of what his sire possessed: this golden charger, snatched from burning Troy, Anchises employed in sacrifice; old Priam wore this royal robe and this tiara, and bore this golden scepter in full assemblies, and in solemn games; these purple vests were woven by Dardan dames."

Thus while he spoke, Latinus rolled his eyes around, and fixed them for a while upon the ground. He seemed intent, and anxious in his breast; not moved by the scepter or the kingly vest, but pondering future things of wondrous weight: succession, empire, and his daughter's fate. On these he mused within his thoughtful mind, and then revolved what Faunus had divined. This was the foreign prince, decreed by fate to share his scepter and Lavinia's bed; this was the race that sure portents foreshow would sway the world, and subdue land and sea. At length he raised his cheerful head, and spoke: "The powers," he said, "the powers we both invoke, to you, and to yours, and to mine, may they be propitious, and confirm our purpose with their augury! Have what you ask; I receive your presents; land, where and when you please, with ample leave; partake and use my kingdom as your own; all shall be yours, while I command the crown. And, if my wished alliance pleases your king, tell him he should not send the peace, but bring it. Then let him not fear a friend's embraces; the peace is made when I behold him here. Besides this answer, tell my royal guest, I add my own request to his commands: one only daughter inherits my crown and state, whom neither our oracles, nor Heaven, nor fate, nor frequent prodigies, permit to join with any native of the Ausonian line. A foreign son-in-law shall come from far (such is our doom), a chief renowned in war, whose race shall bear aloft the Latian name, and diffuse our fame through the conquered world. That he himself is the man the fates require, I firmly judge, and, what I judge, I desire."

He said, and then bestowed a steed on each. Three hundred horses, fed in high stables, stood ready, all shining, and smoothly dressed. Of these he chose the fairest and the best, to mount the Trojan troop. At his command, the steeds stood caparisoned with purple, with golden trappings, glorious to behold, and champed the foaming gold between their teeth. Then to his absent guest the king decreed a pair of coursers born of heavenly breed, which breathed ethereal fire from their nostrils—which Circe had stolen from her celestial sire, by substituting mares produced on earth, whose wombs had conceived a more than mortal birth. These drew the chariot which Latinus sent, and commended the rich present to the prince. Borne sublime on stately steeds, the Trojans returned to their expecting lord with peace.

But jealous Juno, from the height of Pachynus, as she took her airy flight from Argos, beheld with envious eyes this hateful sight. She saw the Trojan and his joyful train descending upon the shore, deserting the main, designing a town, and, with unhoped success, the ambassadors returning with a promised peace. Then, pierced with pain, she shook her haughty head, sighed from her inward soul, and thus she said: "O hated offspring of my Phrygian foes! O fates of Troy, that oppose Juno's fates! Could they not fall unpitied on the plain, but revive slain, and, taken, escape again? When execrable Troy lay in ashes, through fires and swords and seas they forced their way. Then vanquished Juno must contend in vain, her rage disarmed, her empire at an end. Is all my fury spent, breathless and tired? Or does my glutted spleen at length relent? As if it were too little to chase them from their town, I pursued their exiled race through the seas; I engaged the heavens, opposed the stormy main; but billows roared, and tempests raged in vain. What have my Scyllas and my Syrtes done, when they overpass these, and shun those? On Tiber's shores they land, secure of fate, triumphant over the storms and over Juno's hate. Mars could bathe the Centaurs in mutual blood, and Jove himself gave way to Cynthia's wrath, who sent the tusky boar to Calydon; what great offense had either people done? But I, the consort of the Thunderer, have waged a long and unsuccessful war, with various arts and arms have toiled in vain, and at length am foiled by a mortal man. If native power does not prevail, shall I doubt to seek needful succor from without? If Jove and Heaven deny my just desires, Hell shall supply the power of Heaven and Jove. Grant that the Fates have firmed, by their decree, that the Trojan race shall reign in Italy; at least I can defer the nuptial day, and delay the peace with protracted wars. The dear alliance shall be bought with blood, and both peoples brought near destruction; so shall the son-in-law and father join, with ruin, war, and the waste of either line. O fatal maid, your marriage is endowed with Phrygian, Latian, and Rutulian blood! Bellona leads you to your lover's hand; another queen brings forth another brand, to burn another land with foreign fires! A second Paris, differing only in name, shall fire his country with a second flame."

Thus having said, she sinks beneath the ground, with furious haste, and shoots across the Stygian sound, to rouse Alecto from the infernal seat of her dire sisters, and from their dark retreat. This Fury, fit for her intent, she chose—one who delights in wars and human woes. Even Pluto hates his own misshapen race; her sister Furies fly her hideous face; so frightful are the forms the monster takes, so fierce the hissings of her speckled snakes. Juno finds her, and thus inflames her spite: "O virgin daughter of eternal Night, give me this once your labor, to sustain my right, and to execute my just disdain. Let not the Trojans, with a feigned pretense of proffered peace, delude the Latian prince. Expel that odious name from Italy, and let not Juno suffer in her fame.
