First, from the quarter of the morn, sprang a light that signed the heavens, and shot along; then from a cloud, fringed round with golden fires, timbrels were heard, and Berecynthian choirs; and, last, a voice, with more than mortal sounds, wounded both hosts, opposed in arms, with equal horror: "O Trojan race, forbear your needless aid, and know, my ships are my peculiar care. With greater ease the bold Rutulian may, with hissing brands, attempt to burn the sea, than to singe my sacred pines. But you, my charge, loosed from your crooked anchors, launch at large, exalted, each a nymph; forsake the sand, and swim the seas, at Cybele's command." No sooner had the goddess ceased to speak, when, behold, the obedient ships broke their hawsers; and, strange to tell, like dolphins, they plunged their prows in the main, and dove, and sprang again: as many beauteous maids swept the billows, as before had ridden tall vessels on the deep.

The foes, surprised with wonder, stood aghast; Messapus curbed his fiery courser's haste; old Tiber roared, and, raising up his head, called back his waters to their oozy bed. Turnus alone, undaunted, bore the shock, and thus bespoke his trembling troops with these words: "These monsters are meant for the Trojans' fate, and are sent by Jove for black presages. He takes away the cowards' last relief; for fly they cannot, and, constrained to stay, must yield unfought, a base inglorious prey. The liquid half of all the globe is lost; heaven shuts the seas, and we secure the coast. Theirs is no more than that small spot of ground which myriads of our martial men surround. I fear not their fates, nor vain oracles. It was given to Venus that they should cross the seas, and land secure upon the Latian plains; their promised hour is past, and mine remains. It is in the fate of Turnus to destroy, with sword and fire, the faithless race of Troy. Shall such affronts as these inflame the Grecian brothers, and the Grecian name, alone? My cause and theirs is one; a fatal strife, and final ruin, for a ravished wife. Was it not enough that they fell, punished for the crime? But will they fall a second time? One would have thought they had paid enough before, to curse the costly sex, and dared offend no more. Can they securely trust their feeble wall, a slight partition, a thin interval, between their fate and them; when Troy, though built by divine hands, yet perished by their guilt? Lend me, for once, my friends, your valiant hands, to force these dastard bands out of their lines. Less than a thousand ships will end this war; nor does Vulcan need prepare his fated arms. Let all the Tuscans, all the Arcadians, join! Neither these nor those shall frustrate my design. Let them not fear the treasons of the night, the robbed Palladium, the pretended flight: our onset shall be made in open light. No wooden engine shall betray their town; fires they shall have around, but fires by day. No Grecian babes appear before their camp, whom Hector's arms detained to the tenth tardy year. Now, since the sun is rolling to the west, let us give the silent night to needful rest: refresh your bodies, and prepare your arms; the morn shall end the small remains of war."

The post of honor fell to Messapus, to keep the nightly guard, to watch the walls, to pitch the fires at distances around, and to close the Trojans in their scanty ground. Twice seven Rutulian captains stood ready, and these chiefs commanded twice seven hundred horse. All, clad in shining arms, invested the works, each with a radiant helm and waving crest. Stretched at their length, they pressed the grassy ground; they laughed, they sang (the jolly bowls went round), with lights and cheerful fires they renewed the day, and passed the wakeful night in feasts and play.

The Trojans, from above, beheld their foes, and filled all the ramparts with armed legions. Seized with affright, they first explored their gates; they joined works to works with bridges, tower to tower: thus all things needful for defense abounded. Mnestheus and brave Seresthus walked the round, commissioned by their absent prince to share the common danger, and divide the care. The soldiers drew their lots, and, as they fell, by turns relieved each other on the wall.

Near where the foes advanced their utmost guards, the chance of watching the gate fell to warlike Nisus. His father was Hyrtacus, of noble blood; his mother was a huntress of the wood, who sent him to the wars. Well could he bear his lance in fight, and dart the flying spear, but was better skilled to send unerring shafts. Beside him stood Euryalus, his friend: Euryalus, than whom no fairer face, or sweeter air, the Trojan host could boast. Scarcely had the down begun to shade his cheeks. One was their care, and their delight was one: they shared one common hazard in the war, and now were both by choice upon the guard.

Then Nisus thus: "Do the gods inspire this warmth, or do we make gods of our desire? A generous ardor boils within my breast, eager for action, enemy to rest. This urges me to fight, and fires my mind to leave a memorable name behind. You see the foe secure; how faintly shine their scattered fires! Most of them, supine, lie along the ground in sleep, an easy conquest; the wakeful few ply the fuming flagon; all is hushed around. Now hear what I revolve—a thought unripe, and scarcely yet resolved. Both camp and council mourn our absent prince; both would hasten his return with a message. If they will confer on you what I demand (for fame is recompense enough for me), methinks I have spied, beneath yon hill, a way that will safely guide my passage."

Euryalus stood listening while he spoke, struck with the love of praise and with noble envy. Then he exposed his mind to his ardent friend: "All this, alone, and leaving me behind! Am I unworthy, Nisus, to be joined with you? Do you think I can yield my share of glory, or send you unassisted to the field? Not so did my father teach my childhood arms; I was born in a siege, and bred among alarms! Nor is my youth unworthy of my friend, nor of the heaven-born hero I attend. The thing called life I can disclaim with ease, and think it overvalued if it must be paid to purchase fame."

Then Nisus thus: "Alas! Your tender years would minister new matter to my fears. So may the gods, who view this friendly strife, restore me to your loved embrace with life, and condemn me to pay my vows (as surely I trust)—this request of yours is cruel and unjust. But if some chance (as many chances are, and doubtful hazards, in the deeds of war) should reach my head, there let it fall, and spare your life; I would not perish all. Your blooming youth deserves a longer date; live, to mourn your love's unhappy fate; to bear my mangled body from the foe, or buy it back, and bestow funeral rites. Or, if hard fortune shall deny those dues, you may at least supply an empty tomb. O, let me not renew the widow's tears! Nor let a mother's curse pursue my name—your pious parent, who, for love of you, forsook the coasts of friendly Sicily, committing her age to the seas and winds, when every weary matron stayed behind." To this, Euryalus: "You plead in vain, and but protract the cause you cannot gain. No more delays, but haste!" With that, he woke the nodding watch; each took to his office. The guard relieved, the generous couple went to find the council at the royal tent.

All other creatures forgot their daily care, and shared the common gift of nature, sleep; except the Trojan peers, who sat wakeful in nightly council for the endangered state. They voted a message to their absent chief, to show their distress, and to beg swift relief. Amid the camp they chose a silent seat, remote from clamor, and secure from foes. On their left arms they bore their ample shields, their right reclining upon the bending spear. Now Nisus and his friend approached the guard, and begged admission, eager to be heard: the affair was important, not to be deferred. Ascanius bade them be conducted in, ordering the more experienced to begin. Then Nisus thus: "Fathers, lend your ears; nor judge our bold attempt beyond our years. The foe, securely drenched in sleep and wine, neglects their watch; the fires shine but thinly; and where the smoke flies in cloudy vapors, covering the plain, and curling to the skies, between two paths that divide at the gate, close by the sea, we have spied a passage which will guide our way to great Aeneas. Expect every hour to see him safe again, loaded with spoils of foes slain in battle. Let us snatch the lucky minute while we may; nor can we be mistaken in the way; for, hunting in the vale, we both have seen the rising turrets, and the stream between, and know the winding course, with every ford."

He ceased; and old Alethes took up the word: "Our country gods, in whom we place our trust, will yet save the Trojan race from ruin, while we behold such dauntless worth appear in dawning youth, and souls so void of fear." Then he broke into tears of joy; he took each of them by turns in his longing arms; panted and paused; and thus he spoke again: "You brave young men, what equal gifts can we decree in recompense of such merit? The greatest, surely, and the best you can receive, the gods and your own conscious worth will give. The rest our grateful general will bestow, and young Ascanius shall owe it until he reaches his manhood."

"And I, whose welfare lies in my father," Ascanius added, "by the great deities, by my dear country, by my household gods, by hoary Vesta's rites and dark abodes, I adjure you both (on you my fortune stands; I plight that, and my faith, into your hands), make me but happy in his safe return, whose wanted presence I can only mourn. Your common gift shall be two large goblets of silver, wrought with curious imagery, and highly embossed, which, when old Priam reigned, my conquering sire gained at sacked Arisba; and besides, two tripods cast in antique mold, with two great talents of the finest gold; besides a costly bowl, engraved with art, which Dido gave, when first she gave her heart. But, if we reign in conquered Italy, when the victor shall obtain the spoils by lot—you saw the courser pressed by proud Turnus: that, Nisus, and his arms, and his nodding crest, and his shield, exempt from chance, shall be your share; twelve laboring slaves, twelve handmaids young and fair, all clad in rich attire, and trained with care; and, last, a Latian field with fruitful plains, and a large portion of the king's domains. But you, whose years are more allied to mine, no fate shall divide my vowed affection from you, heroic youth! Be wholly mine; take full possession; all my soul is yours. One faith, one fame, one fate, shall attend us both; my life's companion, and my bosom friend: my peace shall be committed to your care, and my concerns in war to your conduct."

Then thus the young Euryalus replied: "Whatever fortune, good or bad, betide, the same shall be my age, as now my youth; no time shall find me wanting to my truth. Only let me gain this from your goodness (and without this, all rewards are vain): my mother came of Priam's royal race—surely the best that ever bore the name—whom neither Troy nor Sicily could hold from departing with me, but, overspent and old, she followed my fate. Ignorant of this (whatever) danger, I leave her, neither taking a parting kiss, nor a pious blessing; and in this only act of all my life I deceive her. By this right hand and by conscious night I swear, my soul could not bear so sad a farewell. Be her comfort; fill my vacant place (permit me to presume so great a grace); support her age, forsaken and distressed. That hope alone will fortify my breast against the worst of fortunes, and of fears." He said. The moved assistants melted into tears.

Then thus Ascanius, wonderstruck to see that image of his filial piety: "So great beginnings, in so green an age, exact the faith which I again engage. Your mother shall justly claim all the dues Creusa had, and want only the name. Whatever event your bold attempt shall have, it is merit to have borne so brave a son. Now by my head I swear a sacred oath (my father used it): what I prepare for yourself, crowned with success, returning here, shall be shared by your beloved mother, if you fail."

He said, and, weeping while he spoke the word, drew from his broad belt a shining sword, magnificent with gold. Lycaon made it, and sheathed the blade in an ivory scabbard. This was his gift. Great Mnestheus gave his friend a lion's hide, to defend his body; and good Alethes furnished him, besides, with his own trusty helm, of tempered metal.

Thus armed they went. The noble Trojans awaited their issuing forth, and followed to the gate with prayers and vows. Above the rest Ascanius appeared, manly far beyond his years, and entrusted them with messages, all of which were lost in winds and flitting air.

First they passed the trenches; then they took their way where their proud foes lay in pitched pavilions—fatal to many, before they themselves were slain. They found the careless host dispersed upon the plain, who, gorged, and drunk with wine, supinely snored. Unharnessed chariots stood along the shore: amidst the wheels and reins, the goblet by, a medley of debauch and war, they lay. Observing this, Nisus showed his friend the sight: "Behold a conquest gained without a fight. Occasion offers, and I stand prepared; there lies our way; be you upon the guard, and look around, while I securely go, and hew a passage through the sleeping foe." Softly he spoke; then, striding, took his way, with his drawn sword, to where haughty Rhamnes lay; his head raised high on tapestry beneath, and heaving from his breast, he drew his breath; a king and prophet, beloved by King Turnus; but fate cannot be removed by prescience. Him and his sleeping slaves he slew; then he spied where Remus, with his rich retinue, lay. His armor-bearer first, and next he killed his charioteer, entrenched between the wheels and his beloved horses; last he invaded their lord: full on his neck he drove the fatal sword; the gasping head flew off; a purple flood flowed from the trunk, that weltered in the blood, which, dispersed by the spurning heels, besprinkled the bed and bedewed the ground. Lamus the bold, and Lamyrus the strong, he slew, and then Serranus, fair and young. The youth had retired from dice and wine to rest, and puffed the fumy god out of his breast: even then he dreamt of drink and lucky play—more lucky, had it lasted till the day. The famished lion thus, with hunger bold, overleaps the fences of the nightly fold, and tears the peaceful flocks: with silent awe, trembling they lie, and pant beneath his paw.

Nor with less rage did Euryalus employ the wrathful sword, or destroy fewer foes; but on the ignoble crowd his fury flew; he slew Fadus, Hebesus, and Rhoetus. The former fell oppressed with heavy sleep, but Rhoetus was wakeful, and observing all: he slunk behind a spacious jar for fear; the fatal iron found and reached him there; for, as he rose, it pierced his naked side, and, reeking, returned from there, dyed in crimson. The wound pours out a stream of wine and blood; the purple soul comes floating in the flood.

Now they arrived where Messapus had quartered. The fires were fainting there, and just alive; the warrior horses, tied in order, fed. Nisus observed the discipline, and said: "Our eager thirst of blood may betray us both; see the scattered streaks of dawning day, foe to nocturnal thefts. No more, my friend; let our glutted execution end here. We have made a lane through slaughtered bodies." Bold Euryalus, though loth, obeyed. They found a precious load of arms, and arras, and of plate; but these they left behind. Yet, fond of gaudy spoils, the boy would stay to make the rich caparison his prey, which lay on the steed of conquered Rhamnes. Nor did his eyes less longingly behold the girdle-belt, with nails of burnished gold. This present Caedicus the rich had bestowed on Remulus, when first they vowed friendship, and, though absent, joined in hospitable ties; he, dying, bequeathed the prize to his heir, until, oppressed by the conquering Ardean troops, he fell; and they possessed the glorious gift. These glittering spoils (now made the victor's gain) he fitted to his body, but fitted in vain: he found Messapus' helm among the rest, and laced it on, and wore the waving crest. Proud of their conquest, and prouder of their prey, they left the camp, and took the ready way.

But they had not passed far, before they spied three hundred horse, with Volscens for their guide. The queen had sent a legion to King Turnus; but the swift horse forestalled the slower foot, and now, advancing, sought the leader's tent. They saw the pair; for, through the doubtful shade, the shining helm of Euryalus betrayed them, on which the moon played in full reflection. "It is not for nothing," cried Volscens from the crowd, "that these men go there." Then he raised his voice aloud: "Stand! Stand! Why thus in arms? And whither bent? From where, to whom, and on what errand sent?" Silent, they scudded away, and hasted their flight to neighboring woods, and trusted themselves to night. The speedy horse beset all the passages, and spurred their smoking steeds to cross their way, and watched each entrance of the winding wood. Black was the forest: it stood thick with beech, horrid with fern, and intricate with thorn; few paths of human feet, or tracks of beasts, were worn. The darkness of the shades, his heavy prey, and fear, misled the younger from his way. But Nisus hit the turns with happier haste, and, thoughtless of his friend, passed the forest, and the Alban plains (so called from Alba's name), where King Latinus then stabled his oxen; till, at length, turning, he stood his ground, and missed his friend, and cast his eyes around: "Ah, wretch!" he cried, "where have I left behind the unhappy youth? Where shall I hope to find him? Or what way shall I take?" Again he ventured back, and trod the mazes of his former track. He winds the wood, and, listening, heard the noise of tramping coursers, and the riders' voices. The sound approached; and suddenly he viewed the foes enclosing, and his friend pursued, forelaid and taken, while he strove in vain to gain the shelter of the friendly shades. What should he next attempt? What arms employ, what fruitless force, to free the captive boy? Or should he, desperate, rush and lose his life, oppressed with odds, in such unequal strife?

Resolved at length, he shook his pointed spear; and, casting on the moon a mournful look: "Guardian of groves, and goddess of the night, fair queen," he said, "direct my dart aright. If ever my pious father, for my sake, made grateful offerings on your altars, or I increased them with my sylvan toils, and hung your holy roofs with savage spoils, grant me to scatter these." Then from his ear he poised, and aimed, and launched the trembling spear. The deadly weapon, hissing from the grove, drove impetuously on the back of Sulmo; pierced his thin armor, drank his vital blood, and left the broken wood within his body. He staggers round; his eyeballs roll in death, and with short sobs he gasps away his breath. All stood amazed—a second javelin flew with equal strength, and quivered through the skies. This forced its way through your temples, Tagus, and warmly buried itself in the brainpan. Fierce Volscens foamed with rage, and, gazing round, descried not him who gave the fatal wound, nor knew where to fix revenge: "But you," he cried, "shall pay for both," and at the prisoner flew with his drawn sword. Then, struck with deep despair, the lover could not bear that cruel sight, but rushed from his covert into open view, and sent his voice before him as he flew: "Me! Me!" he cried—"turn all your swords alone on me—the fact is confessed, the fault my own. He neither could nor dared, the guiltless youth: you moon and stars, bear witness to the truth! His only crime (if friendship can offend) is too much love to his unhappy friend." Too late he speaks: the sword, guided by fury, driven with full force, had pierced his tender sides. Down fell the beauteous youth: the yawning wound gushed out a purple stream, and stained the ground. His snowy neck reclined upon his breast, like a fair flower pressed by the keen plowshare; like a white poppy sinking on the plain, whose heavy head is overcharged with rain. Despair, and rage, and vengeance justly vowed, drove Nisus headlong onto the hostile crowd. He seeks Volscens; on him alone he bends: borne back, and hemmed in by his surrounding friends, onward he pressed, and kept him still in sight; then whirled his sword aloft with all his might: the unerring steel descended while he spoke, pierced his wide mouth, and broke through his weasand. Dying, he slew; and, staggering on the plain, with swimming eyes he sought his lover slain; then quietly fell on his bleeding bosom, content, in death, to be revenged so well.
O happy friends! For, if my verse can give immortal life, your fame shall ever live, fixed as the Capitol's foundation lies, and spread, wherever the Roman eagle flies!

The conquering party first divided the prey, then conveyed their slain leader to the camp. With wonder, as they went, the troops were filled, to see such numbers whom so few had killed. They found Serranus, Rhamnes, and the rest: vast crowds surrounded the dying and the dead; and the still reeking blood overflowed the ground. All knew the helmet which Messapus had lost, but mourned a purchase that had cost so dear. Now rose the ruddy morn from Tithon's bed, and with the dawn of day overspread the skies; nor did the sun long withhold his daily course, but added colors to the world revealed: when early Turnus, waking with the light, all clad in armor, called his troops to fight. He fired his martial men with fierce harangue, and inspired his own ardor in their souls. This done—to give new terror to his foes, he showed the heads of Nisus and his friend, raised high on pointed spears—a ghastly sight. Loud peals of shouts ensued, and barbarous delight.

Meanwhile the Trojans ran, where danger called; they lined their trenches, and they manned their walls. In front they stood extended to the left; safe was the right, surrounded by the flood. But, casting a frightful view from their towers, they saw the faces, which too well they knew, though then disguised in death, and smeared all over with obscene filth, and dropping putrid gore. Soon hasty fame bore through the sad city the mournful message to the mother's ears. An icy cold benumbed her limbs; she shook; the blood forsook her cheeks, and her hand forsook the web. She ran round the ramparts amidst the war, nor feared the flying darts; she rent her hair, and filled the liquid air with loud laments. "So, then, my loved Euryalus appears! Thus looks the prop of my declining years! Was it on this face my famished eyes I fed? Ah, how unlike the living is the dead! And could you leave me, cruel, thus alone? Not one kind kiss from a departing son! No look, no last adieu before he went, in an ill-boding hour, to slaughter sent! Cold on the ground, and pressing foreign clay, he lies, a prey to Latian dogs and fowls! Nor was I near to close his dying eyes, to wash his wounds, to weep his obsequies, to call his crying friends about his corpse, or spread the mantle (made for other ends) on his dear body, which I wove with care, nor did I spare my daily pains or nightly labor. Where shall I find his corpse? What earth sustains his dismembered trunk, and his cold remains? For this, alas, I left my needful ease, exposed my life to winds and winter seas! If any pity touches Rutulian hearts, here empty all your quivers, all your darts; or, if they fail, you, Jove, conclude my woe, and send me thunderstruck to the shades below!" Her shrieks and clamors pierced the Trojans' ears, unmanned their courage, and augmented their fears; nor could young Ascanius sustain the sight, nor old Ilioneus restrain his tears, but Actor and Idaeus were jointly sent, to bear the madding mother to her tent.

And now the trumpets terribly, from afar, with rattling clangor, roused the sleepy war. The soldiers' shouts succeeded the brazen sounds; and heaven, from pole to pole, rebounded with the noise. The Volscians bore their shields upon their heads, and, rushing forward, formed a moving shed. These filled the ditch; those pulled the bulwarks down; some raised the ladders; others scaled the town. But, where void spaces appeared on the walls, or thin defense, they poured their forces there. With poles and missile weapons, from afar, the Trojans kept aloof the rising war. Taught, by their ten years' siege, defensive fight, they rolled down ribs of rocks, an unresisted weight, to break the penthouse with the ponderous blow, which yet the patient Volscians underwent; but they could not bear the unequal combat long, for, where the Trojans found the thickest throng, the ruin fell: their shattered shields gave way, and their crushed heads became an easy prey. They shrank for fear, abated of their rage, nor any longer dared to engage in a blind fight; contented now to gall them from below with darts and slings, and with the distant bow.

Elsewhere Mezentius, terrible to view, threw a blazing pine within the trenches. But brave Messapus, Neptune's warlike son, broke down the palisades, won the trenches, and loudly called for ladders, to scale the town.

Calliope, begin! You sacred Nine, inspire your poet in his high design, to sing what slaughter manly Turnus made, what souls he sent below the Stygian shade, what fame the soldiers share with their captain, and the vast circuit of the fatal war; for you excel in singing martial facts; you best remember, and alone can tell.

There stood a tower, amazing to the sight, built up of beams, and of stupendous height: art, and the nature of the place, conspired to furnish all the strength that war required. To level this, the bold Italians joined; the wary Trojans obviated their design; with weighty stones they overwhelmed their troops below, shot through the loopholes, and threw sharp javelins. Turnus, the chief, tossed from his thundering hand a flaming brand against the wooden walls: it stuck, the fiery plague; the winds were high; the planks were seasoned, and the timber dry. Contagion caught the posts; it spread along, scorched, and drove the scattered throng to a distance. The Trojans fled; the fire pursued amain, still gathering fast upon the trembling train; till, crowding to the corners of the wall, down fell the defense and the defenders. The mighty crash made heaven itself resound: the dead and dying Trojans strewed the ground. The tower, that followed on the fallen crew, whelmed over their heads, and buried whom it slew: some were stuck upon the darts themselves had sent; all underwent the same equal ruin.

Young Lycus and Helenor alone escaped; saved (how, they knew not) from the steepy leap. Helenor, the elder of the two, by birth on one side royal, and on one a son of earth, whom Licymnia bore to the Lydian king, and sent her boasted bastard to the war (a privilege which none but freemen share). His arms were slight, a sword and silver shield; no marks of honor charged its empty field. As light as he fell, so light the youth arose, and, rising, found himself amidst his foes; no flight was left, nor hopes to force his way. Emboldened by despair, he stood at bay; and, like a stag, whom all the troop of eager huntsmen and invading hounds surround, resolved on death, he dissipates his fears, and bounds aloft against the pointed spears. So dares the youth, secure of death, and throws his dying body on his thickest foes. But Lycus, swifter of foot by far, ran, doubled, wound, and turned amidst the war; he sprang to the walls, and left his foes behind, and snatched at the beam he first could find; looked up, and leaped aloft at all the stretch, in hopes to reach the helping hand of some kind friend. But Turnus followed hard his hunted prey (his spear had almost reached him in the way, short of his reins, and scarce a span behind). "Fool," said the chief, "though fleeter than the wind, could you presume to escape, when I pursue?" He said, and drew the trembling dastard down by the feet; at the tug he fell; vast ruins came along, rent from the smoking walls. Thus on some silver swan, or timorous hare, Jove's bird comes souring down from upper air; her crooked talons truss the fearful prey; then out of sight she soars, and wings her way. So the grim wolf seizes the tender lamb, in vain lamented by the bleating dam.
Then, rushing onward with a barbarous cry, the troops of Turnus flew to the combat. The ditch was filled with fagots, the daring foe threw firebrands on the steepy turrets.

Ilioneus, as bold Lucetius came to force the gate, and to feed the kindling flame, rolled down the fragment of a rock so truly, that it crushed him double underneath the weight. Young Liger and Asylas slew two more: young Liger knew better how to bend the bow; Asylas best threw the pointed javelin. Brave Caeneus laid Ortygius on the plain; the victor Caeneus was slain by Turnus. By the same hand, Clonius and Itys fell, Sagar, and Ida, standing on the wall. From the arms of Capys, Privernus met his fate: hurt first by Themilla (but slight the wound), his shield thrown by, to mitigate the smart, he clapped his hand upon the wounded part; the second shaft came swift and unespied, and pierced his hand, and nailed it to his side, transfixed his breathing lungs and beating heart: the soul came issuing out, and hissed against the dart.

The son of Arcens shone amid the rest, in glittering armor and a purple vest (fair was his face, his eyes inspiring love), bred by his father in the Martian grove, where the fat altars of Palicus flame, and sent in arms to purchase early fame. When the Tuscan king spied him from afar, he laid by the lance, and took to the sling; three times he whirled the thong around his head, and threw: the heated lead half melted as it flew; it pierced his hollow temples and his brain; the youth came tumbling down, and spurned the plain.

Then young Ascanius, who, before this day, had been wont in woods to shoot the savage prey, first bent the twanging bow in martial strife, and exercised it against a human foe. With this he bereft Numanus of his life, who had taken Turnus' younger sister to wife. Proud of his realm, and of his royal bride, vaunting before his troops, and lengthening with a stride, in these insulting terms he defied the Trojans:

"Twice-conquered cowards, now your shame is shown—cooped up a second time within your town! You who dare not issue forth in open field, but hold your walls before you as a shield. Is this how you make war? Is this how you force our alliance? What gods, what madness, steered your course here? You shall not find the sons of Atreus here, nor need you fear the frauds of sly Ulysses. Strong from the cradle, of a sturdy brood, we bear our newborn infants to the flood; there, bathed amid the stream, we hold our boys, hardened by winter, and inured to cold. They wake before the day to range the wood, kill before they eat, nor taste unconquered food. They know no sports but those that belong to war: to break the stubborn colt, to bend the bow. Our youth, patient of labor, earn their bread; they work hard, fed with a frugal diet. Sent from plows and harrows to seek renown, they fight in fields, and storm the shaken town. No part of life is free from the toils of war, no change in age, or difference in degree. We plow and till in arms; our oxen feel, instead of goads, the spur and pointed steel; the inverted lance makes furrows in the plain. Even time, that changes all, yet changes us in vain: the body, not the mind; nor can it control the immortal vigor, or abate the soul. Our helms defend the young, and disguise the gray; we live by plunder, and delight in prey. Your vests, embroidered with rich purple, shine; in sloth you glory, and in dances join. Your vests have sweeping sleeves; with female pride your turbans are tied beneath your chins. Go, Phrygians, back to your Dindymus! Go, less than women, in the shapes of men! Go, mixed with eunuchs, in the Mother's rites, where the flute invites with unequal sound; sing, dance, and howl, by turns, in Ida's shade: resign the war to men, who know the martial trade!"

Ascanius could not hear this foul reproach with patience, or forbear a vowed revenge. At the full stretch of both his hands he drew, and almost joined the horns of the tough yew. But first, before the throne of Jove he stood, and thus, with lifted hands, invoked the god: "Great Jupiter, succeed my first attempt! An annual offering shall bleed in your grove; a snow-white steer, led before your altar, who, like his mother, bears aloft his head, butts with his threatening brows, and stands bellowing, and dares the fight, and spurns the yellow sands."

Jove bowed the heavens, and lent a gracious ear, and thundered on the left, amidst the clear. The bow sounded at once; and swiftly flew the feathered death, and hissed through the skies. The steel forced its way through both his temples: extended on the ground, Numanus lay. "Go now, vain boaster, and scorn true valor! The Phrygians, twice subdued, yet make this third return." Ascanius said no more. The Trojans shook the heavens with shouting, and took new vigor.

Apollo then bestrode a golden cloud, to view the feats of arms, and the fighting crowd; and thus he bespoke the beardless victor aloud: "Advance, illustrious youth, increase in fame, and widely extend your name from east to west; offspring of gods yourself, and Rome shall owe to you a race of demigods below. This is the way to heaven: the divine powers date the Julian line from this beginning. To you, to them, and to their victorious heirs, the conquered war is due, and the vast world is theirs. Troy is too narrow for your name." He said, and, plunging downward, shot his radiant head; he dispelled the breathing air, that broke his flight: shorn of his beams, he became a man to mortal sight. He took the form of old Butes, Anchises' squire, now left by his sire to rule Ascanius: he wears his wrinkled face, and his hoary hairs, his mien, his habit, and his arms; and thus salutes the boy, too forward for his years: "Be content, worthy son of your father, you have already won the warlike prize. The god of archers gives a part of his own praise to your youth, nor envies equal art. Now tempt the war no more." He said, and flew, obscure in air, and vanished from their view. The Trojans, by his arms, knew their patron, and heard the twanging of his heavenly bow. Then they used dutiful force, and Phoebus' name, to keep from the fight the youth too fond of fame. Undaunted, they themselves shun no danger; from wall to wall the shouts and clamors run. They bend their bows; they whirl their slings around; heaps of spent arrows fall, and strew the ground; and helms, and shields, and rattling arms resound. The combat thickens, like the storm that flies from westward, when the showery Kids arise; or like pattering hail pouring down on the main, when Jupiter descends in hardened rain, or bellowing clouds burst with a stormy sound, and strew the ground with an armed winter.

Pandarus and Bitias, thunderbolts of war, whom Hiera bore to bold Alcanor on Ida's top, two youths of height and size like firs that rise on their mother mountain, presuming on their force, unbarred the gates, and of their own accord invited the war. With fates averse, against their king's command, armed, on the right and on the left they stood, and flanked the passage: they wore shining steel, and waving crests appeared above their heads. Thus two tall oaks that adorn the banks of the Po lift up to heaven their unshorn leafy heads, and, overpressed with nature's heavy load, dance to the whistling winds, and nod at each other. In flows a tide of Latians, when they see the gate set open, and the passage free; bold Quercens, with rash Tmarus, rushing on, Equicolus, who shone in bright armor, and Haemon first; but soon repulsed they flew, or died in the well-defended pass. These were fired with success, and those with rage, and each at length engaged on equal terms. Drawn from their lines, and issuing on the plain, the Trojans maintained the fight hand to hand.

Fierce Turnus fought in another quarter, when suddenly the unhoped-for news was brought that the foes had left the fastness of their place, had prevailed in fight, and had his men in chase. He quit the attack, and, to prevent their fate, ran to where the giant brothers guarded the gate. The first he met was Antiphates the brave, but base-begotten on a Theban slave, son of Sarpedon. He slew him: the deadly dart found passage through his breast, and pierced his heart. The Italian cornel stood fixed in the wound, warmed in his lungs, and in his vital blood. Aphidnus next, and Erymanthus, died, and Meropes, and the gigantic size of Bitias, threatening with his ardent eyes. Not by the feeble dart he fell oppressed (a dart would have been lost within that roomy breast), but from a knotted lance, large, heavy, strong, which roared like thunder as it whirled along; not two bull hides could withstand the impetuous force, nor coat of double mail, with scales of gold. Down sank the monster bulk, and pressed the ground; his arms and clattering shield sounded on the vast body. Not with less ruin than the Bajan mole, raised on the seas to control the surges, comes tumbling down at once the rocky wall; the stones, disjointed, fall prone into the deep from the vast pile; the scattered ocean flies; black sands, discolored froth, and mingled mud arise; the frighted billows roll, and seek the shores; then Prochyta trembles, then Ischia roars; Typhoeus, thrown beneath by Jove's command, astonished at the flaw that shakes the land, soon shifts his weary side, and, scarce awake, with wonder feels the weight press lighter on his back.
The warrior god inspired the Latian troops; he strung their sinews anew, and fired their courage, but chilled the Trojan hearts with cold affright: then black despair precipitated their flight.

When Pandarus beheld his brother killed, and the town filled with fear and wild confusion, he turned the hinges of the heavy gate with both his hands, and added his shoulders to the weight. He enclosed some happier friends within the walls; the rest were shut out, exposed to certain death. Fool as he was, and frantic in his care, to admit young Turnus, and include the war! He thrust amid the crowd, securely bold, like a fierce tiger pent amid the fold. Too late they descried his blazing buckler, and the sparkling fires that shot from either eye, his mighty members, and his ample breast, his rattling armor, and his crimson crest.

Far from that hated face the Trojans fled, all but the fool who sought his destiny. Mad Pandarus stepped forth, with vengeance vowed for Bitias' death, and threatened thus aloud: "These are not Ardea's walls, nor is this the town Amata proffers with Lavinia's crown: it is hostile earth you tread. Bereft of hope, no means of safe return by flight are left." To whom, with countenance calm, and soul sedate, thus Turnus: "Then begin, and try your fate: bear my message to the ghost of Priam; tell him a new Achilles sent you there."

The Trojan threw a lance of tough ground ash, rough in the rind, and knotted as it grew: with his full force he first whirled it around; but the soft yielding air received the wound: imperial Juno turned its course before, and fixed the wandering weapon in the door.

"But do not hope," said Turnus, "when I strike, to shun your fate: our force is not alike, nor is your steel tempered by the Lemnian god." Then rising, he stood at his utmost stretch, and aimed from high: the full descending blow cleaved the broad front and beardless cheeks in two. Down sank the giant with a thundering sound: his ponderous limbs oppressed the trembling ground; blood, brains, and foam gushed from the gaping wound; the keen steel divided scalp, face, and shoulders, and the shared visage hung on equal sides. The Trojans fled from their approaching fate; and had the victor then secured the gate, and unclosed the bars to his troops without, one lucky day would have ended all his wars. But boiling youth, and blind desire of blood, pushed on his fury to pursue the crowd. Hamstrung behind, unhappy Gyges died; then Phalaris was added to his side. He drew the pointed javelins from the dead, and threw their friends' arms against their fellows. Strong Halys stood in vain; weak Phlegys fled; Saturnia, still at hand, supplied new force and fire. Then Halius, Prytanis, Alcander fell—engaged against the foes who scaled the wall: but whom they feared without, they found within. At last, though late, he was seen by Lynceus. He called new succors, and assaulted the prince; but his force was weak, and their defense was vain. Turned to the right, the hero drew his sword, and at one blow slew the bold aggressor. He lopped the neck; and, with a stroke so strong, the helm flew off, and bore the head along. Next him, he killed the huntsman Amycus, skilled in envenomed darts and in poison. Then Clytius fell beneath his fatal spear, and Cretheus, whom the Muses held so dear: he fought with courage, and he sang the fight; arms were his business, verses his delight.

The Trojan chiefs beheld, with rage and grief, their slaughtered friends, and hastened their relief. Bold Mnestheus first rallied the broken train, whom brave Seresthus and his troop sustained. To save the living, and to revenge the dead, they led all Troy against one warrior's arms. "O, void of sense and courage!" Mnestheus cried. "Where can you hope to hide your coward heads? Ah, where, beyond these ramparts, can you run? You shun one man, enclosed in your own camp! Shall then a single sword boast such slaughter, and pass unpunished from a numerous host? Forsaking honor, and renouncing fame, you shame your gods, your country, and your king!" This just reproach excited their virtue: they stood, they joined, they thickened for the fight.

Now Turnus doubts, and yet disdains to yield, but with slow paces measures back the field, and inches to the walls, where Tiber's tide, washing the camp, defends the weaker side. The more he loses, the more they advance, and tread in every step he trod before. They shout; they bear him back; and, whom by might they cannot conquer, they oppress with weight.

As, compassed with a wood of spears around, the lordly lion still maintains his ground; grins horribly, retires, and turns again; threatens his distended paws, and shakes his mane; he loses while in vain he presses on, nor will his courage let him dare to run: so Turnus fares, and, unresolved of flight, moves tardily back, and just recedes from the fight. Yet twice, enraged, he renews the combat, twice breaks through, and twice pursues his broken foes. But now they swarm, and, with fresh troops supplied, come rolling on, and rush from every side: nor does Juno, who sustained his arms before, dare with new strength to supply the exhausted store; for Jove, with sour commands, sent Iris down, to force the invader from the frighted town.

Spent with labor, he could no longer wield the heavy falchion, or sustain the shield, overwhelmed with darts, which they flung from afar: the weapons rang around his hollow temples; his golden helm gave way, battered with stony blows, and flat, and beaten to his brows. His crest was dashed away; his ample shield was falsified, and filled round with javelins.

The foe, now faint, the Trojans overwhelm; and Mnestheus lays hard load upon his helm. Sick sweat succeeds; he drops at every pore; with driving dust his cheeks are pasted over; shorter and shorter every gasp he takes; and he makes vain efforts and hurtless blows. Plunged in the flood, he made the waters fly. The yellow god bore the welcome burden, and wiped the sweat, and washed away the gore; then gently wafted him to the farther coast, and sent him safe to cheer his anxious host.

chapters.title: Book X
paragraphs: Jupiter, calling a council of the gods, forbids them to engage on either side. At Aeneas' return there is a bloody battle: Turnus kills Pallas; Aeneas kills Lausus and Mezentius. Mezentius is described as an atheist; Lausus as a pious and virtuous youth. The different actions and deaths of these two are the subject of a noble episode.

The gates of heaven unfold: Jove summons all the gods to council in the common hall. Sublimely seated, he surveys from far the fields, the camp, the fortune of the war, and all the inferior world. From first to last, the sovereign senate are placed in their degrees.

Then thus the almighty sire began: "You gods, natives or denizens of blessed abodes, where do these murmurs come from, and this change of mind—this backward fate from what was first designed? Why this protracted war, when my commands pronounced a peace, and granted the Latian lands? What fear or hope divides our heavens on either side, and arms our powers on different sides? A lawful time of war shall come at length (nor need your haste anticipate its doom), when Carthage shall contend with Rome for the world, shall force the rigid rocks and Alpine chains, and, like a flood, come pouring on the plains. Then shall be your time for faction and debate, for partial favor, and permitted hate. Now let your immature dissension cease; sit quiet, and compose your souls to peace."

Thus Jupiter in few unfolds the charge; but lovely Venus replies at length: "O immense power, eternal energy (for to what else can we fly for protection?), do you see the proud Rutulians, how they dare, unpunished in the fields, to insult my care? How lofty Turnus vaunts amidst his train, triumphant in shining arms on the plain? Even within their lines and trenches the Trojans contend, and their walls scarcely defend their troops: the town is filled with slaughter, and overflows their increasing moats with a red deluge. Aeneas, ignorant, and far from there, has left a camp exposed, without defense. Shall they still sustain this endless outrage? Shall Troy, renewed, be forced and fired again? My banished issue fears a second siege, and a new Diomede appears in arms. One more audacious mortal will be found; and I, your daughter, await another wound. Yet, if with averse fates, without your leave, the Latian lands receive my progeny, let them bear the pains of violated law, and your protection withdraw from their aid. But if the gods foretell their sure success; if those of heaven consent with those of hell, to promise Italy—who dares debate the power of Jove, or fix another fate? What should I tell of tempests on the main, of Aeolus usurping Neptune's reign? Of Iris sent, with Bacchanalian heat, to inspire the matrons, and destroy the fleet? Now Juno descends to the Stygian sky, solicits hell for aid, and arms the fiends. That example was still wanted above: an act that well became the wife of Jove! Alecto, raised by her, inflames with rage the peaceful bosoms of the Latian dames. Imperial sway no more exalts my mind (such hopes I had indeed, while Heaven was kind); now let my happier foes possess my place, whom Jove prefers before the Trojan race, and let those conquer whom you grace with conquest. Since from all your wide command you can spare no spot of earth, no hospitable land, to receive my wandering fugitives (since haughty Juno will not give you leave), then, father (if I may still use that name), by ruined Troy, yet smoking from the flame, I beg you, let Ascanius, by my care, be freed from danger, and dismissed from the war. Let him live inglorious, without a crown. The father may be cast on unknown coasts, struggling with fate; but let me save the son. Cythera is mine, mine are the Cyprian towers; in those recesses, and those sacred bowers, let him rest obscurely; let him resign his right to promised empire and to his Julian line. Then Carthage may destroy the Ausonian towns, nor fear the race of a rejected boy. What does it profit my son to escape the fire, armed with his gods, and loaded with his sire; to pass the perils of seas and winds; to evade the Greeks, and leave the war behind; to reach the Italian shores—if, after all, our second Pergamus is doomed to fall? He had much better have curbed his high desires, and hovered over his ill-extinguished fires. Restore the fugitives to Simois' banks, and give them back to war, and to all the woes before."

Deep indignation swelled Saturnia's heart: "And must I own," she said, "my secret smart—what would with more decency be kept in silence, and, but for this unjust reproach, had slept? Did god or man advise your favorite son to surprise the Latians with an unhoped-for war? By fate, you boast, and by the gods' decree, he left his native land for Italy! Confess the truth: by mad Cassandra, more than by Heaven, inspired, he sought a foreign shore! Did I persuade him to trust his second Troy to the raw conduct of a beardless boy, with unfinished walls, which he himself forsook, and to take a wandering voyage through the waves? When did I urge him meanly to demand the Tuscan aid, and to arm a quiet land? Did I, or Iris, give this mad advice, or did the fool himself make the fatal choice? You think it hard, the Latians should destroy with swords your Trojans, and with fires your Troy! Hard and unjust indeed, for men to draw their native air, nor to take a foreign law! That Turnus is still permitted to live, to whom his birth gives a god and a goddess! But yet is it just and lawful for your line to drive their fields, and by fraud force them to join; to divide realms, not your own, among your clans, and to tear the promised bride from the bridegroom; to petition, while you prepare public arms; to pretend peace, and yet provoke a war? It was given to you, your darling son, to shroud, to draw the dastard from the fighting crowd, and, for a man, to put forward an empty cloud. You turned the fire away from flaming fleets, and changed the ships to daughters of the sea. But is it my crime—does the Queen of Heaven offend, if she presume to save her suffering friends? Your son, not knowing what his foes decree, you say, is absent: absent let him be. Yours is Cythera, yours the Cyprian towers, the soft recesses, and the sacred bowers. Why, then, do you prepare these needless arms, and thus provoke a people prone to war? Did I deface the Trojan town with fire, or hinder your exiled race from return? Was I the cause of mischief, or the man whose lawless lust began the fatal war? Think on whose faith the adulterous youth relied; who promised, who procured, the Spartan bride? When all the united states of Greece combined to purge the world of the perfidious kind, then was your time to fear the Trojan fate: your quarrels and complaints are now too late."

Thus Juno. Murmurs rose, with mixed applause, just as they favored or disliked the cause. So winds, when they still lie unfledged in woods, first try their tender voices in whispers, then issue on the main with bellowing rage, and presage storms to trembling mariners.

Then thus the imperial god replied to both, he who shakes heaven's axles with his awful nod. (When he begins, the silent senate stands with reverence, listening to the dread command: the clouds dispel; the winds restrain their breath; and the hushed waves lie flat on the main.) "Celestials, incline your attentive ears!" said the god. "Since the Trojans must not join in wished alliance with the Latian line; since endless jarrings and immortal hate tend only to discompose our happy state; the war henceforward be resigned to fate; each to his proper fortune stand or fall; equal and unconcerned, I look on all. Rutulians, Trojans, are the same to me; and both shall draw the lots their fates decree. Let these assault, if Fortune be their friend; and, if she favors those, let those defend. The Fates will find their way." The Thunderer said, and shook the sacred honors of his head, attesting Styx, the inviolable flood, and the black regions of his brother god. The poles of heaven trembled, and earth confessed the nod. This end the session had: the senate rose, and through the skies waited their sovereign to his palace.
Meanwhile, intent upon their siege, the foes enclose the Trojan host within their walls. They wound, they kill, they watch at every gate; they renew the fires, and urge their happy fate.

The Aeneans wished in vain for their wanted chief, hopeless of flight, more hopeless of relief. Thin on the towers they stood; and even those few were a feeble, fainting, and dejected crew. Yet some stood in the face of danger: the two bold brothers of Sarpedon's blood, Asius and Acmon; both Assaraci; young Haemon, and, though young, resolved to die. With these were joined Clarus and Thymoetes; Tibris and Castor, both of Lycian kind. From the hands of Acmon came a rolling stone, so large, it half deserved the name of a mountain. Strong-sinewed was the youth, and big of bone; his brother Mnestheus could not have done more, nor the great father of the intrepid son. Some threw firebrands, some sent flights of arrows; and some defended with darts, and some with stones.

Amid the press appeared the beauteous boy, the care of Venus, and the hope of Troy. His lovely face was unarmed, his head bare; in ringlets over his shoulders hung his hair. His forehead was circled with a diadem; distinguished from the crowd, he shone like a gem, enchased in gold, or set in polished ivory, amidst the meaner foil of sable jet.

Nor was Ismarus wanting to the war, directing pointed arrows from afar, and death armed with poison—born in Lydia, where plenteous harvests adorn the fat fields; where proud Pactolus floats the fruitful lands, and leaves a rich manure of golden sands. There were Capys, author of the Capuan name, and Mnestheus too, increased in fame, since he cast Turnus from the camp with shame.

Thus mortal war was waged on either side. Meanwhile the hero cut the nightly tide: for, anxious, when he went from Evander, he sought the Tyrrhene camp, and Tarchon's tent; he exposed the cause of his coming to the chief; he told his name and country, and asked relief; he proposed the terms; he declared his own small strength; what vengeance proud Mezentius had prepared; what bold and violent Turnus had designed; then he showed the slippery state of humankind, and fickle fortune; he warned him to beware, and to his wholesome counsel added prayer. Tarchon, without delay, signed the treaty, and joined the Tuscan forces to the Trojan troops.

They soon set sail; nor now did the fates withstand; their forces entrusted to a foreign hand. Aeneas leads; upon his stern appear two lions carved, which rising Ida bears—Ida, ever dear to wandering Trojans. Under their grateful shade Aeneas sat, revolving the events of war, and various fate. On his left, young Pallas kept, fixed to his side, and often inquired of winds, and of the tide; often of the stars, and of their watery way; and of what he had suffered both by land and sea.
Now, sacred sisters, open all your spring! Sing the Tuscan leaders and their army, which followed great Aeneas to the war; declare their arms, their numbers, and their names.

A thousand youths obeyed brave Massicus, borne in the Tiger through the foaming sea; brought from Asium and Cosa by his care; for arms, they bear light quivers, bows, and shafts. Fierce Abas was next: his men wore bright armor; his stern bore Apollo's golden statue. Six hundred Populonia sent along, all skilled in martial exercise, and strong. Three hundred more Ilva joined for battle, an island renowned for steel, and for inexhausted mines. Asylas appeared third on his prow, who interprets the heavens, and the wandering stars; from offered entrails he expounds prodigies, and peals of thunder with presaging sounds. A thousand spears stood in warlike order, sent by the Pisans under his command.

Fair Astur follows in the watery field, proud of his managed horse and painted shield. Gravisca, noisome from the neighboring fen, and his own Caere, sent three hundred men; with those whom Minio's fields and Pyrgi gave, all bred in arms, unanimous, and brave.

You, Muse, renew the name of Cinyras, and brave Cupavo, followed but by few; whose helm confessed the lineage of the man, and bore, with wings displayed, a silver swan. Love was the fault of his famed ancestry, whose forms and fortunes fly in his ensigns. For Cycnus loved unhappy Phaeton, and sung his loss in poplar groves, alone, beneath the sister shades, to soothe his grief. Heaven heard his song, and hastened his relief, and changed his hoary hair to snowy plumes, and winged his flight, to chant aloft in air. His son Cupavo brushed the briny flood: upon his stern stood a brawny Centaur, who heaved a rock, and, threatening still to throw, alarmed the seas below with lifted hands; they seemed to fear the formidable sight, and rolled their billows on, to speed his flight.

Ocnus was next, who led his native train of hardy warriors through the watery plain: the son of Manto by the Tuscan stream, from which the Mantuan town derives its name—an ancient city, but of mixed descent: three several tribes compose the government; four towns are under each; but all obey the Mantuan laws, and own the Tuscan sway.

Hate of Mezentius armed five hundred more, whom Mincius bore from his sire Benacus: Mincius, with wreaths of reeds covered over his forehead. Grave Auletes leads these: a hundred at once sweep the glassy deep with stretching oars. The Triton bears him and his martial train; high on his poop the sea-green god appears: frowning, he seems to sound his crooked shell, and at the blast the billows dance around. He shows a hairy man above the waist; a porpoise tail grows beneath his belly, and ends as a fish: his breast divides the waves, and froth and foam augment the murmuring tides.
Full thirty ships transport the chosen train for Troy's relief, and scour the briny main.

Now was the world forsaken by the sun, and Phoebe had run half her nightly race. The careful chief, who never closed his eyes, himself held the rudder, and supplied the sails. A choir of Nereids met him on the flood, once his own galleys, hewn from Ida's wood; but now, as many nymphs, they swept the sea, as before had ridden tall vessels on the deep. They knew him from afar; and in a ring they enclosed the ship that bore the Trojan king. Cymodoce, whose voice excelled the rest, above the waves advanced her snowy breast; her right hand stopped the stern; her left divided the curling ocean, and corrected the tides. She spoke for all the choir, and thus began, with pleasing words, to warn the unknowing man: "Does our beloved lord sleep? O goddess-born, awake! Spread every sail, pursue your watery track, and haste your course. We were once your navy, descending from Ida's height to the sea; till Turnus, as we stood fixed at anchor, presumed to violate our holy wood. Then, loosed from shore, we fled his profane fires (unwillingly we broke our master's chain), and have since sought you through the Tuscan main. The mighty Mother changed our forms to these, and gave us life immortal in the seas. But young Ascanius, distressed in his camp, is hard pressed by your insulting foes. The Arcadian horsemen, and the Etrurian host, advance in order on the Latian coast: the Daunian chief designs to cut their way, before their troops can reach the Trojan lines. When the rosy morn restores the light, you, first, arm your soldiers for the ensuing fight; yourself wield the fated sword of Vulcan, and bear aloft the impenetrable shield. Tomorrow's sun, unless my skill be vain, shall see huge heaps of foes in battle slain." Departing, she spoke; and with immortal force pushed on the vessel in her watery course; for well she knew the way. Impelled behind, the ship flew forward, and outstripped the wind. The rest make up. Unknowing of the cause, the chief admires their speed, and draws happy omens.

Then thus he prayed, and fixed his eyes on heaven: "Hear me, great Mother of the deities, crowned with turrets! (On Ida's holy hill, fierce tigers, reined and curbed, obey your will.) Confirm your own omens; lead us on to fight; and let your Phrygians conquer by your right."

He said no more. And now the renewing day had chased the shadows of the night away. He charged the soldiers with preventing care to follow their flags, and to prepare their arms; he warned them of the ensuing fight, and bade them hope for war. Now, from his lofty poop, he viewed below his camp enclosed, and the enclosing foe. His blazing shield, embraced, he held on high; the camp received the sign, and with loud shouts replied. Hope armed their courage: from their towers they threw their darts with double force, and drove the foe. Thus, at the signal given, the cranes arise before the stormy south, and blacken all the skies.

King Turnus wondered at the fight renewed, till, looking back, he viewed the Trojan fleet, the seas covered with swelling canvas, and the swift ships descending on the shore. The Latians saw from afar, with dazzled eyes, the radiant crest that seemed to rise in flames, and to dart diffusive fires around the field, and the keen glittering of the golden shield. Thus threatening comets, when they rise by night, shoot sanguine streams, and sadden all the skies: so Sirius, flashing forth sinister lights, frights pale humankind with plagues and with dry famine.

Yet Turnus, with undaunted mind, is bent to man the shores, and hinder their descent, and thus awakens the courage of his friends: "What you have so long wished, kind Fortune sends: to meet the invading foe in ardent arms. You find, and find him now at advantage. Yours is the day: you need only dare; your swords will make you masters of the war. Your sires, your sons, your houses, and your lands, and dearest wives, are all within your hands. Be mindful of the race from which you came, and emulate your fathers' fame in arms. Now take the time, while they still stand staggering, with feet unfirm, and prepossess the strand: Fortune befriends the bold." He said no more, but balanced whom to leave, and whom to lead; then he selected these to prevent the landing, and left those to keep the city pent.

Meanwhile the Trojan sends his troops ashore: some are exposed by boats, more by bridges. With laboring oars they bore along the strand where the tide languishes, and leap a-land. Tarchon observes the coast with careful eyes, and, where he finds no ford, where the water does not fry, nor the billows roar with unequal murmurs, but slide smoothly along and swell the shore, he steered that course, and thus gave command: "Here ply your oars, and at all hazard land; force on the vessel, that her keel may wound this hated soil, and furrow the hostile ground. Let me securely land—I ask no more; then sink my ships, or shatter them on the shore."

This fiery speech inflamed his fearful friends: they tugged at every oar, and every stretcher bent; they ran their ships aground; the vessels knocked (thus forced ashore), and trembled with the shock. Only Tarchon's was lost, which stood stranded, stuck on a bank, and beaten by the flood: she broke her back; the loosened sides gave way, and plunged the Tuscan soldiers in the sea. Their broken oars and floating planks withstood their passage, while they labored to the land, and ebbing tides bore them back upon the uncertain sand.

Now Turnus led his troops without delay, advancing to the margin of the sea. The trumpets sounded: Aeneas first assailed the newly raised and raw clowns, and soon prevailed. Great Theron fell, an omen of the fight; great Theron, large of limbs, of giant height. He first defied the prince in open field: but armor scaled with gold was no defense against the fated sword, which opened wide his plated shield, and pierced his naked side. Next, Lichas fell, who, not like others born, was ripped and torn from his wretched mother; sacred, O Phoebus, to you from his birth, for his beginning life was free from biting steel. Not far from him was Gyas laid along, of monstrous bulk, with fierce and strong Cisseus: vain bulk and strength! For, when the chief assailed, neither valor nor Herculean arms availed, nor their famed father, wont to go in war with great Alcides, while he toiled below. The noisy Pharos next received his death: Aeneas twisted his dart, and stopped his bawling breath. Then wretched Cydon would have received his doom, who courted Clytius in his beardless bloom, and sought polluted joys with obscene lust; the Trojan sword would have cured his love of boys, had not his seven bold brethren stopped the course of the fierce champion, with united force. Seven darts were thrown at once; and some rebounded from his bright shield, some sounded on his helmet; the rest would have reached him, but his mother's care prevented those, and turned them aside in air.

The prince then called Achates, to supply the spears that knew the way to victory—"those fatal weapons which, inured to blood, stood in Grecian bodies under Ilium. Not one of those shall my hand toss in vain against our foes, on this contended plain." He said; then seized a mighty spear, and threw, which, winged with fate, flew through Maeon's buckler, pierced all the brazen plates, and reached his heart: he staggered with intolerable smart. Alcanor saw; and reached, but reached in vain, his helping hand, to sustain his brother. A second spear, which kept the former course, from the same hand, and sent with equal force, pierced his right arm, and holding on, bereft him of the use of both, and pinioned down his left. Then Numitor drew the ill-omened spear from his dead brother, and threw it at the Trojan: preventing fate directed the lance awry, which, glancing, only marked Achates' thigh.

In pride of youth the Sabine Clausus came, and, from afar, took his aim at Dryops. The spear flew hissing through the middle space, and pierced his throat, directed at his face; it stopped at once the passage of his wind, and resigned the free soul to flitting air: his forehead was the first to strike the ground; lifeblood and life rushed mingled through the wound. He slew three brothers of the Borean race, and three whom their native place Ismarus had sent to war, but all the sons of Thrace. Halesus, next, led the bold Aurunci: the son of Neptune came to his aid, conspicuous on his horse. On either hand, these fight to keep, and those to win, the land. With mutual blood the Ausonian soil is dyed, while on its borders each decides their claim. As wintry winds, contending in the sky, try their titles with equal force of lungs: they rage, they roar; the doubtful rack of heaven stands without motion, and the tide undriven: each bent to conquer, neither side to yield, they long suspend the fortune of the field. Both armies thus perform what courage can; foot set to foot, and mingled man to man.

But, in another part, the Arcadian horse engaged the Latin force with ill success: for, where the impetuous torrent, rushing down, had thrown huge craggy stones and rooted trees, they left their coursers, and, unused to fight on foot, were scattered in a shameful flight. Pallas, who had viewed with disdain and grief his foes pursuing, and his friends pursued, used threatenings mixed with prayers, his last resource, to move their minds with the former, and to fire their force with the latter: "Which way, companions? Where would you run? By yourselves, and by mighty battles won, by my great sire, by his established name, and by the early promise of my future fame; by my youth, emulous of equal right to share his honors—shun ignoble flight! Do not trust your feet: your hands must hew a way through yon black body, and that thick array: it is through that forward path that we must come; there lies our way, and that our passage home. Neither powers above, nor destinies below, oppress our arms: with equal strength we go, with mortal hands to meet a mortal foe. See on what foot we stand: a scanty shore, the sea behind, our enemies before; no passage left, unless we swim the main, or, forcing these, gain the Trojan trenches." This said, he strode with eager haste along, and bore amidst the thickest of the throng. Lagus, the first he met, with fate to foe, had heaved a stone of mighty weight, to throw: stooping, the spear descended on his chine, just where the bone distinguished either loin: it stuck so fast, so deeply buried lay, that the victor scarcely forced the steel away. Hisbon came on; but while he moved too slow for wished revenge, the prince prevented his blow; for, warding his at once, at once he pressed, and plunged the fatal weapon in his breast. Then lewd Anchemolus he laid in the dust, who had stained his stepmother's bed with impious lust. And, after him, the Daucian twins were slain, Laris and Thymbrus, on the Latian plain; so wondrously alike in feature, shape, and size, as to cause an error in their parents' eyes—a grateful mistake! But soon the sword decided the nice distinction, and divided their fate: for Thymbrus' head was lopped off; and Laris' hand, dismembered, sought its owner on the strand; the trembling fingers still strained the falchion, and still threatened the intended stroke in vain.

Now, to renew the charge, the Arcadians came: the sight of such deeds, and the sense of honest shame, and grief, mixed with anger, inflamed their minds. Then, with a casual blow, Rhoeteus was slain, who chanced, as Pallas threw, to cross the plain: the flying spear had been sent after Ilus; but Rhoeteus happened on a death unmeant. As he fled from Teuthras and Tyres, the lance laid him dead across his body: rolled from his chariot with a mortal wound, and intercepted fate, he spurned the ground. As when, in summer, welcome winds arise, the watchful shepherd flies to the forest, and fires the midmost plants; contagion spreads, and catching flames infect the neighboring heads; around the forest flies the furious blast, and all the leafy nation sinks at last, and Vulcan rides in triumph over the waste; the shepherd, pleased with his dire victory, beholds the satiate flames ascend to the sky in sheets: so Pallas' troops united their scattered strength, and, pouring on their foes, delighted their prince.

Halesus came, fierce with desire of blood; but first he stood collected in his arms: advancing then, he plied the spear so well that Ladon, Demodocus, and Pheres fell. He tossed his glittering brand around his head, and from Strymonius hewed his better hand, held up to guard his throat; then he hurled a stone at Thoas' ample front, and pierced the bone: it struck beneath the space of either eye; and blood, and mingled brains, together flew. Deeply skilled in future fates, Halesus' sire had retired with the youth to lonely groves; but, when the father's mortal race was run, dire destiny laid hold upon the son, and hauled him to the war, to find, beneath the Evandrian spear, a memorable death. Pallas seeks the encounter, but, before he throws, he addresses his vows to Tuscan Tiber thus: "O sacred stream, direct my flying dart, and grant me to pass through proud Halesus' heart! Your holy oak shall bear his arms and spoils." Pleased with the bribe, the god received his prayer: for, while Halesus' shield protects a distressed friend, the dart came driving on, and pierced his breast.

But Lausus, no small portion of the war, did not permit panic fear to reign too far, caused by the death of so renowned a knight; but he cheered the fight by his own example. Fierce Abas he first slew; Abas, the stay of Trojan hopes, and hindrance of the day. The Phrygian troops had escaped the Greeks in vain: they, and their mixed allies, now loaded the plain. To the rude shock of war both armies came; their leaders equal, and their strength the same. The rear so pressed the front, they could not wield their angry weapons, to dispute the field. Here Pallas urges on, and Lausus there: both appear of equal youth and beauty, but both by fate forbid to breathe their native air. Great Jove withstands their meeting in the field: both doomed to fall, but fall by greater hands.

Meanwhile Juturna warns the Daunian chief of Lausus' danger, urging swift relief. With his driven chariot he divides the crowd, and, making to his friends, thus calls aloud: "Let none presume to join his needless aid; retire, and clear the field; the fight is mine: to this right hand alone is Pallas due; O were his father here, to view my just revenge!" From the forbidden space his men retired. Pallas admired their awe, and his stern words; surveyed him over and over with wondering sight, struck with his haughty mien, and towering height. Then to the king: "Forbear your empty vaunts; I hope for success, and cannot fear fate; alive or dead, I shall deserve a name; Jove is impartial, and to both the same." He said, and advanced his pace toward the open space: pale horror sat on each Arcadian face. Then Turnus, leaping light from his chariot, addressed himself on foot to single fight. And, as a lion—when he spies from afar a bull that seems to meditate war, bending his neck, and spurning back the sand—runs roaring downward from his hilly stand: imagine eager Turnus no less swift to rush from on high upon his unequal foe.

Young Pallas, when he saw the chief advance within due distance of his flying lance, prepared to charge him first, resolved to try if fortune would supply his want of force; and thus he addressed Heaven and Hercules: "Alcides, once on earth Evander's guest, his son adjures you by those holy rites, that hospitable board, those genial nights: assist my great attempt to gain this prize, and let proud Turnus view, with dying eyes, his ravished spoils." It was heard, the vain request; Alcides mourned, and stifled sighs within his breast. Then Jove, to soothe his sorrow, thus began: "Short bounds of life are set to mortal man. It is virtue's work alone to stretch the narrow span. So many sons of gods, in bloody fight, around the walls of Troy have lost the light: my own Sarpedon fell beneath his foe; nor could I, his mighty sire, ward the blow. Even Turnus shall shortly resign his breath, and stands already on the verge of death." This said, the god permits the fatal fight, but averts his sight from the Latian fields.

Now with full force young Pallas threw his spear, and, having thrown, drew his shining falchion. The steel just grazed along the shoulder joint, and marked it slightly with the glancing point. Fierce Turnus first drew to nearer distance, and poised his pointed spear, before he threw: then, as the winged weapon whizzed along, "See now," he said, "whose arm is better strung." The spear kept on the fatal course, unstayed by plates of iron, which were laid over the shield: through folded brass and tough bull hides it passed, pierced his corslet, and at last reached his heart. In vain the youth tugs at the broken wood; the soul comes issuing with the vital blood: he falls; his arms sound upon his body; and with his bloody teeth he bites the ground.

Turnus bestrode the corpse: "Arcadians, hear," he said; "bear my message to your master: such as the sire deserved, I send the son; it costs him dear to be the Phrygians' friend. Tell him, I bestow the lifeless body, unasked, to rest his wandering ghost below." He said, and trampled down with all the force of his left foot, and spurned the wretched corpse; then snatched the shining belt, inlaid with gold—the belt which Eurytion's artful hands had made, where fifty fatal brides, expressed to sight, all in the compass of one mournful night, had deprived their bridegrooms of returning light.

In an ill hour insulting Turnus tore those golden spoils, and in a worse he wore them. O mortals, blind in fate, who never know how to bear high fortune, or endure the low! The time shall come when Turnus, but in vain, shall wish the trophies of the slain were untouched; shall wish the fatal belt were far away, and curse the dire remembrance of the day.

The sad Arcadians, from the unhappy field, bore back the breathless body on a shield. O grace and grief of war! At once restored, with praises, to your sire, at once deplored! One day first sent you to the fighting field, beheld whole heaps of foes killed in battle; one day beheld you dead, and borne upon your shield. This dismal news, not from uncertain fame, but from sad spectators, came to the hero: his friends stand upon the brink of ruin, unless relieved by his victorious hand. He whirls his sword around, without delay, and hews through adverse foes an ample way, to find fierce Turnus, proud of his conquest: Evander, Pallas, all that friendship owed to large deserts, are present to his eyes; his plighted hand, and hospitable ties.

Four sons of Sulmo, and four whom Ufens bred, he took in fight, and led as living victims, to please the ghost of Pallas, and to expire in sacrifice, before his funeral fire. Next he threw at Magus: he stooped below the flying spear, and shunned the promised blow; then, creeping, clasped the hero's knees, and prayed: "By young Iulus, by your father's shade, O spare my life, and send me back to see my longing sire, and tender progeny! I have a lofty house, and wealth untold, in silver ingots, and in bars of gold: all these, and sums besides, which see no day, shall pay the ransom of this one poor life. If I survive, will Troy prevail any less? A single soul's too light to turn the scale." He said. The hero sternly thus replied: "Leave your bars and ingots, and the sums besides, for your children's lot. Your Turnus broke all rules of war by one relentless stroke, when Pallas fell: so deems, nor deems alone, my father's shadow, but my living son." Thus having said, bereft of kind remorse, he seized his helm, and dragged him with his left hand; then, with his right, while he wreathed his neck, he sheathed his shining falchion up to the hilts.

Emonides, Apollo's priest, was near; his holy fillets appeared on his front; glittering in arms, he shone amidst the crowd; proud of his god, more of his purple. The fierce Trojan followed him through the field: the holy coward fell; and, forced to yield, the prince stood over the priest, and, at one blow, sent him as an offering to the shades below. Serestus bears his arms on his shoulders, designed a trophy for the God of Wars.

Vulcanian Caeculus renews the fight, and Umbro, born upon the mountains' height. The champion cheers his troops to encounter those, and seeks revenge himself on other foes. He drove at Anxur's shield; and, at the blow, both shield and arm went to the ground together. Anxur had boasted much of magic charms, and thought he wore impenetrable arms, so made by muttered spells; and, from the spheres, had secured, in vain, life for a length of years. Then Tarquitus trod the field in triumph; a nymph his mother, his sire a god. Exulting in bright arms, he braves the prince: with his protended lance he makes defense; bears back his feeble foe; then, pressing on, arrests his better hand, and drags him down; stands over the prostrate wretch, and, as he lay, inventing vain tales, and prepared to pray, mows off his head: the trunk stood a moment, then sunk, and rolled along the sand in blood. The vengeful victor thus upbraids the slain: "Lie there, proud man, unpitied, on the plain; lie there, inglorious, and without a tomb, far from your mother and your native home, exposed to savage beasts, and birds of prey, or thrown for food to monsters of the sea."

On Lycas and Antaeus next he ran, two chiefs of Turnus, who led his van.
