They fled for fear; with these, he chased along Camers the yellow-locked, and Numa the strong; both great in arms, and both were fair and young. Camers was son to Volscens lately slain, surpassing all the Latian train in wealth, and in Amycla had fixed his silent easy reign. And, as Aegaeon, when he strove with heaven, stood opposite in arms to mighty Jove; moved all his hundred hands, provoked the war, defied the forky lightning from afar; at fifty mouths his flaming breath expires, and flash for flash returns, and fires for fires; in his right hand he wields as many swords, and takes the thunder on as many shields: with strength like his, the Trojan hero stood; and soon the fields were strewed with falling corpses, when once his falchion had found the taste of blood. With fury scarce to be conceived, he flew against Niphaeus, whom four coursers drew. They, when they saw the fiery chief advance, and pushing his pointed lance at their chests, wheeled with so swift a motion, mad with fear, that they threw their master headlong from the chair. They stare, they start, nor stop their course, before they bear the bounding chariot to the shore.

Now Lucagus and Liger scour the plains, with two white steeds; but Liger holds the reins, and Lucagus maintains the lofty seat: bold brethren both. The former waved in air his flaming sword: Aeneas couched his spear, unused to threats, and more unused to fear. Then Liger thus: "Your confidence is vain to escape from here, as from the Trojan plain: these are not the steeds that Diomede bestrode, nor is this the chariot where Achilles rode; nor is Venus' veil here, nor Neptune's shield; your fatal hour is come, and this the field." Thus Liger vainly vaunts: the Trojan peer returned his answer with his flying spear. As Lucagus bends to lash his horses, prone to the wheels, and protends his left foot, prepared for fight, the fatal dart arrives, and drives through the borders of his buckler; it passed through and pierced his groin: the deadly wound cast him from his chariot, and rolled him on the ground. Whom the chief thus upbraids with scornful spite: "Blame not the slowness of your steeds in flight; no vain shadows forced their swift retreat; but you yourself forsake your empty seat." He said, and seized the loosened rein at once; for Liger lay already on the plain, by the same shock. Then, stretching out his hands, the recreant thus demands his wretched life: "Now, by yourself, O more than mortal man! By her and him from whom your breath began, who formed you thus divine, I beg you, spare this forfeit life, and hear your suppliant's prayer." This much he spoke, and more he would have said; but the stern hero turned aside his head, and cut him short: "I hear another man; you did not talk thus before the fight began. Now take your turn; and, as a brother should, attend your brother to the Stygian flood." Then through his breast he sent his fatal sword, and the soul issued at the gaping vent.
As storms the skies, and torrents tear the ground, thus raged the prince, and scattered deaths around. At length Ascanius and the Trojan train broke from the camp, so long besieged in vain.

Meanwhile the King of Gods and Mortal Men held conference with his queen, and thus began: "My sister goddess, and well-pleasing wife, do you still think that Venus' aid supports the strife—sustains her Trojans—or that they alone, with inborn valor, force their fortune on? How fierce in fight, with courage undecayed! Judge if such warriors want immortal aid." To whom the goddess with the charming eyes, soft in her tone, submissively replies: "Why, O my sovereign lord, whose frown I fear, and cannot, unconcerned, bear your anger; why do you urge my grief thus? When, if I still (as once I was) were mistress of your will, from your almighty power your pleasing wife might gain the grace of lengthening Turnus' life, securely snatch him from the fatal fight, and give him to his aged father's sight. Now let him perish, since you hold it good, and glut the Trojans with his pious blood. Yet he derives his name from our lineage, and, in the fourth degree, came from the god Pilumnus; yet he devoutly pays you divine rites, and offers daily incense at your shrine."

Then shortly thus the sovereign god replied: "Since in my power and goodness you confide, if for a little space, a lengthened span, you beg a reprieve for this expiring man, I grant you leave to take your Turnus from here, away from instant fate, and can so far dispense. But if some secret meaning lies beneath, to save the short-lived youth from destined death, or if you entertain a further thought to change the fates, you feed your hopes in vain." To whom the goddess thus, with weeping eyes: "And what if that request, which your tongue denies, your heart should grant; and not a short reprieve, but length of certain life, give to Turnus? Now speedy death attends the guiltless youth, if my presaging soul divines with truth; which, O! I wish, might err through causeless fears, and that you (for you have power) might prolong his years!"

Thus having said, involved in clouds, she flies, and drives a storm before her through the skies. Swiftly she descends, alighting on the plain, where the fierce foes maintain a dubious fight. Soon she made a spectre of condensed air; and what Aeneas was, such seemed the shade. Adorned with Dardan arms, the phantom bore his head aloft; he wore a plumy crest; this hand appeared to wield a shining sword, and that sustained an imitated shield. With manly mien he stalked along the ground, nor wanted voice belied, nor vaunting sound. (Thus haunting ghosts appear to waking sight, or dreadful visions in our dreams by night.) The spectre seems to dare the Daunian chief, and flourishes his empty sword in air. At this, advancing, Turnus hurled his spear: the phantom wheeled, and seemed to fly for fear. Deluded Turnus thought the Trojan fled, and fed his haughty fancy with vain hopes. "Whither, O coward?" (thus he calls aloud, nor did he find he was speaking to wind, and chasing a cloud), "Why thus forsake your bride! Receive from me the fated land you sought so long by sea." He said, and, brandishing at once his blade, with eager pace pursued the flying shade. By chance a ship was fastened to the shore, which King Osinius bore from old Clusium: the plank was ready laid for safe ascent; for shelter there the trembling shadow bent, and skipped and skulked, and went under hatches. Exulting Turnus, with regardless haste, ascended the plank, and passed to the galley. Scarcely had he reached the prow: Saturnia's hand cut the hawsers, and shot the ship from land. With wind in poop, the vessel plowed the sea, and measured back with speed her former way. Meanwhile Aeneas seeks his absent foe, and sends his slaughtered troops to the shades below.

The guileful phantom now forsook the shroud, and flew sublime, and vanished in a cloud. Too late young Turnus found the delusion, far on the sea, still making from the ground. Then, thankless for a life redeemed by shame, stung with the sense of honor, and of forfeit fame, and fearful besides of what in fight had passed, he cast his hands and haggard eyes to heaven: "O Jove!" he cried, "for what offense have I deserved to bear this endless infamy? From where am I forced, and whither am I borne? How, and with what reproach, shall I return? Shall I ever behold the Latian plain, or see Laurentum's lofty towers again? What will they say of their deserting chief? The war was mine: I fly from their relief; I led them to slaughter, and in slaughter leave them; and even from here I receive their dying groans. Here, overmatched in fight, in heaps they lie; there, scattered over the fields, they fly ignobly. Gape wide, O earth, and draw me down alive! Or, O you pitying winds, relieve a wretch! Drive the splitting vessel on sands or shelves; or set me shipwrecked on some desert shore, where no Rutulian eyes may see me more, unknown to friends, or foes, or conscious Fame, lest she should follow, and proclaim my flight."

Thus Turnus raved, and revolved various fates: the choice was doubtful, but the death resolved. Now the sword, and now the sea, took place, that to revenge, and this to purge disgrace. Sometimes he thought to swim the stormy main, by stretch of arms to gain the distant shore. Three times he essayed the sword, and three times the flood; but Juno, moved with pity, withstood both. And three times she repressed his rage; strong gales supplied, and pushed the vessel over the swelling tide. At length she lands him on his native shores, and restores him to his father's longing arms.

Meanwhile, by Jove's impulse, Mezentius armed, succeeding Turnus, warmed his fainting friends with his ardor, reproached their shameful flight, repelled the victors, and renewed the fight. The Tuscan troops conspire against their king; such is their hate, and such their fierce desire of wished revenge: on him, and on him alone, all hands are employed, and all their darts are thrown. He, like a solid rock enclosed by seas, opposed to raging winds and roaring waves, looking down from his proud summit, disdains their empty menace, and remains unmoved.

Beneath his feet fell haughty Hebrus dead, then Latagus, and Palmus as he fled. At Latagus he flung a weighty stone: his face was flattened, and his helmet rang. But Palmus received his wound from behind; hamstrung, he fell, and groveled on the ground: his crest and armor, torn from his body, adorn your shoulders, Lausus, and your head. Evas and Mimas, both of Troy, he slew. Mimas drew his birth from fair Theano, born on that fatal night when the queen, big with fire, produced young Paris to his sire; but Paris was slain in the Phrygian fields, unthinking Mimas on the Latian plain.

And, as a savage boar, bred on mountains, fed with forest mast and fattening marshes, when once he sees himself enclosed in toils, opposed by huntsmen and their eager hounds, he whets his tusks, and turns, and dares the war; the invaders dart their javelins from afar; all keep aloof, and safely shout around; but none presume to give a nearer wound: he frets and foams, erects his bristled hide, and shakes a grove of lances from his side: not otherwise the troops, inspired with hate, and fired with just revenge against the tyrant, drive their darts with clamor at a distance, and only keep the languished war alive.

From Corythus came Acron to the fight, who had left his betrothed spouse, and unconsummate night. Mezentius sees him ride through the squadrons, proud of the purple favors of his bride. Then, as a hungry lion, who beholds a gamesome goat, who frisks about the folds, or a beamy stag, that grazes on the plain—he runs, he roars, he shakes his rising mane, he grins, and opens wide his greedy jaws; the prey lies panting underneath his paws: he fills his famished maw; his mouth runs over with unchewed morsels, while he churns the gore: so proud Mezentius rushes on his foes, and first overthrows unhappy Acron: stretched at his length, he spurns the swarthy ground; the lance, besmeared with blood, lies broken in the wound. Then with disdain the haughty victor viewed Orodes flying, nor pursued the wretch, nor thought the dastard's back deserved a wound; but, running, he gained the advantage of the ground; then turning short, he met him face to face, to give his victory the better grace. Orodes falls, oppressed in equal fight: Mezentius fixed his foot upon his breast, and rested his lance; and thus he cries aloud: "Lo! Here the champion of my rebels lies!" The fields around ring with Io Paean! and peals of shouts applaud the conquering king. At this the vanquished, with his dying breath, thus faintly spoke, and prophesied in death: "Nor shall you, proud man, remain unpunished: like death attends you on this fatal plain." Then, sourly smiling, thus the king replied: "For what belongs to me, let Jove provide; but die first, whatever chance ensue." He said, and drew the weapon from the wound. A hovering mist came swimming over his sight, and sealed his eyes in everlasting night.

By Caedicus, Alcathous was slain; Sacrator laid Hydaspes on the plain; Orses the strong must yield to greater strength; he, with Parthenius, were killed by Rapo. Then brave Messapus slew Ericetes, who drew his lineage from Lycaon's blood. But Ericetes found his fate from his headstrong horse, who threw his master, as he made a bound: the chief, alighting, stuck him to the ground. Then Clonius, hand to hand, on foot assails; the Trojan sinks, and Neptune's son prevails. Agis the Lycian, stepping forth with pride, defied the boldest foe to single fight; whom Tuscan Valerus by force overcame, and did not belie his mighty father's fame. Salius sent the great Antronius to death; but the victor underwent the same fate, slain by the hand of Nealces, well-skilled to throw the flying dart, and draw the far-deceiving bow.

Thus equal deaths are dealt with equal chance; by turns they quit their ground, by turns advance; victors and vanquished, in the various field, neither wholly overcome, nor wholly yield. The gods from heaven survey the fatal strife, and mourn the miseries of human life. Above the rest, two goddesses appear, concerned for each: here Venus, Juno there. Amidst the crowd, infernal Ate shakes her scourge aloft, and her crest of hissing snakes.

Once more the proud Mezentius, with disdain, brandished his spear, and rushed into the plain, where he stood towering in the midmost rank, like tall Orion stalking over the flood (when with his brawny breast he cuts the waves, his shoulders scarce the topmost billow laves), or like a mountain ash, whose roots are spread, deep fixed in earth, while in clouds he hides his head.

The Trojan prince beheld him from afar, and dauntless undertook the doubtful war. Collected in his strength, and like a rock poised on its base, Mezentius stood the shock. He stood, and, measuring first with careful eyes the space his spear could reach, aloud he cries: "My strong right hand, and sword, assist my stroke! (Those only gods Mezentius will invoke.) His armor, torn from the Trojan pirate, shall be worn by my triumphant Lausus." He said; and with his utmost force he threw the massy spear, which, hissing as it flew, reached the celestial shield, that stopped its course; but, glancing from there, the yet unbroken force took a new bent obliquely, and between the side and bowels fixed famed Anthores. Anthores had traveled far from Argos, Alcides' friend, and a brother of war; till, tired with toils, he chose fair Italy, and sought repose in Evander's palace. Now, falling by another's wound, he cast his eyes to heaven, thought on Argos, and died.

The pious Trojan then sent his javelin; the shield gave way; through treble plates it went, of solid brass, of linen trebly rolled, and three bull hides that fold round the buckler. It passed all these, resistless in its course, transpierced his thigh, and spent its dying force. The gaping wound gushed out a crimson flood. The Trojan, glad with the sight of hostile blood, drew his falchion, addressed himself to closer fight, and with new force oppressed his fainting foe.

Lausus viewed his father's peril with grief; he sighed, he wept, he ran to his relief. And here, heroic youth, it is here I must be just to your immortal memory, and sing an act so noble and so new, posterity will scarcely believe it is true. Pained with his wound, and useless for the fight, the father sought to save himself by flight: encumbered, slow he dragged the spear along, which pierced his thigh, and hung in his buckler. The pious youth, resolved on death, springs below the lifted sword to face the foe; protects his parent, and prevents the blow. Shouts of applause rang ringing through the field, to see the son shield the vanquished father. All, fired with generous indignation, strive, and with a storm of darts drive to distance the Trojan chief, who, held at bay from far, sustained the war on his Vulcanian orb.

As, when thick hail comes rattling in the wind, the plowman, passenger, and laboring hind fly for shelter to the neighboring covert, or lie housed, or safe, in hollow caverns; but, when it has blown over, when heaven above them smiles, they return to travel, and renew their toils. Aeneas thus, overwhelmed on every side, abided undaunted the storm of darts; and thus to Lausus he loudly cried with friendly threatening: "Why will you rush to certain death, and rage in rash attempts, beyond your tender age, betrayed by pious love?" Nor, thus forborne, did the youth desist, but with insulting scorn provoked the lingering prince, whose patience, tired, gave place; and all his breast was fired with fury. For now the Fates prepared their sharpened shears; and lifted high the flaming sword appears, which, full descending with a frightful sway, forced its impetuous way through shield and corslet, and lay buried deep in his fair bosom. The purple streams forced through the thin armor, and drenched the embroidered coat his mother wove; and life at length forsook his heaving heart, loth from so sweet a mansion to depart.

But when, with blood and paleness all overspread, the pious prince beheld young Lausus dead, he grieved; he wept; the sight brought an image of his own filial love, a sadly pleasing thought: then he stretched his hand to hold him up, and said: "Poor hapless youth! What praises can be paid to love so great, to such transcendent store of early worth, and sure presage of more? Accept whatever Aeneas can afford: your arms untouched, your sword untaken; and all that pleased you living, still remain inviolate, and sacred to the slain. I bestow your body on your parents, to rest your soul, at least, if shadows know, or have a sense of human things below. There tell your fellow ghosts, with glory: 'It was by the great Aeneas' hand I fell.'" With this, he beckoned his distant friends near, provoked their duty, and prevented their fear; he himself assisted to lift him from the ground, with clotted locks, and blood that welled from out the wound.

Meanwhile, his father, now no father, stood, and washed his wounds by Tiber's yellow flood: oppressed with anguish, panting, and overspent, he leaned his fainting limbs against an oak. A bough sustained his brazen helmet; his heavier arms lay scattered on the plain: a chosen train of youth stood around him; his drooping head was rested on his hand: his grisly beard sought his pensive bosom; and all his restless thought ran on Lausus. Careful, concerned to prevent his danger, he inquired much, and sent many a message to warn him from the field—alas, in vain! Behold, his mournful followers bear him slain! Over his broad shield still gushed the yawning wound, and drew a bloody trail along the ground. Far off he heard their cries, far off divined the dire event, with a foreboding mind. With dust he first sprinkled his hoary head; then he spread both his lifted hands to heaven; last, embracing the dear corpse, he thus said: "What joys, alas! Could this frail being give, that I have been so covetous to live? To see my son, and such a son, resign his life, a ransom for preserving mine! And am I then preserved, and are you lost? How much too dear has that redemption cost! It is now my bitter banishment I feel: this is a wound too deep for time to heal. My guilt defamed your growing virtues; my blackness blotted your unblemished name. Chased from a throne, abandoned, and exiled for foul misdeeds, were punishments too mild: I owed my people these, and, from their hate, I could have borne my fate with less resentment. And yet I live, and yet sustain the sight of hated men, and of more hated light: but I will not long." With that he raised from ground his fainting limbs, that staggered with his wound; yet, with a mind resolved, and unappalled with pains or perils, he called for his courser, well-mouthed, well-managed, whom he himself had dressed with daily care, and mounted with success; his aid in arms, his ornament in peace.

Soothing his courage with a gentle stroke, the steed seemed sensible, while thus he spoke: "O Rhoebus, we have lived too long for me—if life and long were terms that could agree! This day you shall either bring back the head and bloody trophies of the Trojan dead; this day you shall either revenge my woe, for murdered Lausus, on his cruel foe; or, if inexorable fate deny our conquest, die with your conquered master: for, after such a lord, I rest secure, you will endure no foreign reins, or Trojan load." He said; and straightway the officious courser kneels, to take his wonted weight. He fills his hands with pointed javelins; on his head he laced his glittering helm, which was terribly graced with waving horsehair, nodding from afar; then he spurred his thundering steed amidst the war. Love, anguish, wrath, and grief, wrought to madness, despair, and secret shame, and conscious thought of inborn worth, oppressed his laboring soul, rolled in his eyes, and raged within his breast. Then loud he called Aeneas three times by name: the loud repeated voice came to glad Aeneas. "Great Jove," he said, "and the far-shooting god, inspire my mind to make good your challenge!" He spoke no more, but hastened, void of fear, and threatened with his long protended spear.

To whom Mezentius thus: "Your vaunts are vain. My Lausus lies extended on the plain: he is lost! Your conquest is already won; the wretched sire is murdered in the son. Nor do I fear fate, but defy all the gods. Forbear your threats: my business is to die; but first receive this parting legacy." He said; and straightway he sent a whirling dart; another after, and another went. Round in a spacious ring he rides the field, and vainly plies the impenetrable shield. Three times he rode round; and three times Aeneas wheeled, turned as he turned: the golden orb withstood the strokes, and bore about an iron wood. Impatient of delay, and weary grown still to defend, and to defend alone; to wrench out the darts which alight in his buckler; urged and over-labored in unequal fight; at length, resolved, he throws with all his force full at the temples of the warrior horse. Just where the stroke was aimed, the unerring spear made way, and stood transfixed through either ear. Seized with unwonted pain, surprised with fright, the wounded steed curvets, and, raised upright, lights on his feet before; his hoofs behind spring up in air aloft, and lash the wind. Down comes the rider headlong from his height; his horse came after with unwieldy weight, and, floundering forward, pitching on his head, overlaid his lord's encumbered shoulder.

From either host, the mingled shouts and cries of Trojans and Rutulians rend the skies. Aeneas, hastening, waved his fatal sword high over his head, with this reproachful word: "Now, where are your vaunts, the fierce disdain of proud Mezentius, and the lofty strain?"

Struggling, and wildly staring on the skies, with scarce recovered sight he thus replies: "Why these insulting words, this waste of breath, to souls undaunted, and secure of death? It is no dishonor for the brave to die, nor did I come here with hope of victory; nor do I ask life, nor did I fight with that design: as I have used my fortune, use yours. My dying son contracted no such bond; the gift is hateful from his murderer's hand. For this, this only favor let me sue, if pity can be due to conquered foes: do not refuse it; but let my body have the last retreat of humankind, a grave. Too well I know the insulting people's hate; protect me from their vengeance after my fate: provide this refuge for my poor remains, and lay my much-loved Lausus by my side." He said, and applied his throat to the sword. The crimson stream stained his arms around, and the disdainful soul came rushing through the wound.

chapters.title: Book XI
paragraphs: Aeneas erects a trophy of the spoils of Mezentius, grants a truce for burying the dead, and sends home the body of Pallas with great solemnity. Latinus calls a council, to propose offers of peace to Aeneas; which occasions great animosity between Turnus and Drances. Meanwhile there is a sharp engagement of the horse, wherein Camilla signalizes herself, is killed, and the Latin troops are entirely defeated.

Scarcely had the rosy Morning raised her head above the waves, and left her watery bed, when the pious chief, attended by double cares—for his unburied soldiers, and for his friend—yet first performed a victor's vows to Heaven. He stripped an ancient oak of all her boughs; then on a rising ground he placed the trunk, which he graced with the spoils of his dead foe. The coat of arms worn by proud Mezentius, now borne in triumph on a naked snag, was hung on high, and glittered from afar, a trophy sacred to the God of War. Above his arms, fixed on the leafless wood, appeared his plumy crest, besmeared with blood; his brazen buckler was seen on the left; truncheons of shivered lances hung between; and on the right was placed his corslet, bored; and to the neck was tied his unavailing sword.

A crowd of chiefs enclose the godlike man, who, thus conspicuous in the midst, began: "Our toils, my friends, are crowned with sure success; the greater part performed, achieve the less. Now follow cheerfully to the trembling town; press but an entrance, and presume it won. Fear is no more, for fierce Mezentius lies, as the first fruits of war, a sacrifice. Turnus shall fall extended on the plain, and, in this omen, is already slain. Prepared in arms, pursue your happy chance; that none unwarned may plead ignorance, and I, at Heaven's appointed hour, may find your warlike ensigns waving in the wind. Meanwhile prepare the rites and funeral pomps due to your dead companions of the war: the last respect the living can bestow, to shield their shadows from contempt below. Let that conquered earth be theirs, for which they fought, and which for us with their own blood they bought. But first send the corpse of our unhappy friend to the sad city of Evander, who, not inglorious, in the bloom of his age, was hurried hence by too severe a doom."

Thus, weeping as he spoke, he took his way to where, new in death, lamented Pallas lay. Acoetes watched the corpse; whose youth deserved the father's trust, and who now served the son with equal faith, but with less auspicious care. The attendants of the slain share his sorrow. A troop of Trojans mixed with these appears, and mourning matrons with disheveled hair. As soon as the prince appears, they raise a cry; all beat their breasts, and echoes rend the sky. They rear his drooping forehead from the ground; but when Aeneas viewed the grisly wound that Pallas bore in his manly bosom, and the fair flesh stained with purple gore, the pious man first melted into tears, deplored so sad a sight, then thus began: "Unhappy youth! When Fortune gave the rest of my full wishes, she refused the best! She came; but did not bring you along, to bless my longing eyes, and to share in my success. She grudged your safe return, and the triumphs due to prosperous valor in the public view. Not thus I promised, when your father lent your needless succor with a sad consent, embraced me as I parted for the Etrurian land, and sent me to possess a large command. He warned, and from his own experience told, that our foes were warlike, disciplined, and bold. And now perhaps, in hopes of your return, rich odors burn on his loaded altars, while we, with vain officious pomp, prepare to send him back his portion of the war: a bloody breathless body, which can owe no further debt, but to the powers below. The wretched father, before his race is run, shall view the funeral honors of his son. These are my triumphs of the Latian war, the fruits of my plighted faith and boasted care! And yet, unhappy sire, you shall not see a son whose death disgraced his ancestry; you shall not blush, old man, however grieved: your Pallas received no dishonest wound. He died no death to make you wish, too late, that you had not lived to see his shameful fate: but what a champion has the Ausonian coast, and what a friend have you, Ascanius, lost!"

Thus having mourned, he gave the word around to raise the breathless body from the ground; and he chose a thousand horse, the flower of all his warlike troops, to wait upon the funeral, to bear him back and share Evander's grief: a well-becoming, but a weak relief. Of oaken twigs they twist an easy bier, then rear the sad burden on their shoulders. The body is borne on this rural hearse; strewn leaves and funeral greens adorn the bier. He lies all pale, and looks like a lovely flower, newly cropped by virgin hands to dress the bower: unfaded yet, but yet unfed below, owing nothing more to mother earth or to the green stem. Then the Trojan hero brought two fair vests, of wondrous work and cost, of purple woven, and embossed with gold, for ornament—which Sidonian Dido had wrought with her own hands. One vest arrayed the corpse; and the other they spread over his closed eyes, and wrapped around his head, so that when the yellow hair should fall in flame, the catching fire might burn the golden caul. Besides, the spoils of foes slain in battle, when he descended on the Latian plain—arms, trappings, horses—are led by the hearse in long array, the achievements of the dead. Then, pinioned with their hands behind, appear the unhappy captives, marching in the rear, appointed as offerings in the victor's name, to sprinkle with their blood the funeral flame. Inferior trophies are borne by the chiefs; gauntlets and helms adorn their loaded hands; and fair inscriptions are fixed, and the titles are read of Latian leaders conquered by the dead.

Acoetes attends his pupil's corpse, with feeble steps, supported by his friends. Pausing at every pace, drowned in sorrow, between their arms he sinks upon the ground; where, while he lies groveling in deep despair, he beats his breast, and rends his hoary hair. The champion's chariot is next seen to roll, besmeared with hostile blood, and honorably foul. To close the pomp, Aethon, the steed of state, is led, to wait upon the funerals of his lord. Stripped of his trappings, with a sullen pace he walks; and the big tears run rolling down his face. The lance of Pallas, and the crimson crest, are borne behind: the victor seized the rest. The march begins: the trumpets hoarsely sound; the pikes and lances trail along the ground. Thus, while the Trojan and Arcadian horse direct their course to the Pallantean towers, in long procession ranked, the pious chief stopped in the rear, and gave a vent to grief: "The public care," he said, "which war attends, diverts our present woes, or at least suspends them. Peace with the manes of great Pallas dwell! Hail, holy relics! And a last farewell!" He said no more, but inly though he mourned, he restrained his tears, and returned to the camp.

Now suppliants, sent from Laurentum, demand a truce, with olive branches in their hand. They implore his clemency, and beg leave to draw the bodies of their slain from the plain. They plead that none deny those common rites to conquered foes who die in fair battle. All cause of hate was ended in their death; nor could he war with bodies void of breath. A king, they hoped, would hear a king's request, whose son he once was called, and once his guest.

The hero grants their suit—too just to be denied—and further thus replied: "O Latian princes, how severe a fate has involved your state in causeless quarrels, and has armed you against an unoffending man, who sought your friendship before the war began! You beg a truce, which I would gladly give, not only for the slain, but for those who live. I did not come here but by Heaven's command, and sent by fate to share the Latian land. Nor do I wage unjust wars: your king denied my proffered friendship, and my promised bride; he left me for Turnus. Turnus, then, should try his cause in arms, to conquer or to die. My right and his are in dispute; the slain fell without fault, to maintain our quarrel. Let us alone contend in equal arms, and let him vanquish whom his fates befriend. This is the way (so tell him) to possess the royal virgin, and to restore the peace. Bear back this message, with ample leave, that your slain friends may receive funeral rites."

Thus having said, the ambassadors, amazed, stood mute a while, and gazed on each other. Drances, their chief, who harbored in his breast long hate to Turnus, as his professed foe, broke silence first, and to the godlike man, bowing with graceful action, thus began: "Auspicious prince, in arms a mighty name, but yet whose actions far transcend your fame—whether I should express your justice or your force, thought can but equal, and all words are less. We shall thankfully relate your answer, and the favors granted to the Latian state. If wished success shall attend our labor, think peace concluded, and the king your friend: let Turnus leave the realm to your command, and seek alliance in some other land; and you build the city your fates assign; we shall be proud to join in the great work."

Thus Drances; and his words so well persuade the rest who were empowered, that soon a truce is made. Twelve days was the term allowed; and, during those, Latians and Trojans, now no longer foes, mixed in the woods, to prepare funeral piles, to fell the timber, and to forget the war. Loud axes resounded through the groaning groves; oak, mountain ash, and poplar spread the ground; first they fall from high; and some receive the trunks in laden wagons; with wedges some they cleave.

And now the fatal news, that Pallas was slain, was blown by Fame through the short circuit of the Arcadian town—by Fame, which just before had borne his triumphs on distended pinions. Rushing from out the gate, the people stand, each with a funeral flambeau in his hand. Wildly they stare, distracted with amazement: the fields are lightened with a fiery blaze, which casts a sullen splendor on their friends, the marching troop that attends their dead prince. Both parties meet; they raise a doleful cry; the matrons from the walls with shrieks reply, and their mixed mourning rends the vaulted sky. The town is filled with tumult and with tears, till the loud clamors reach Evander's ears: forgetful of his state, he runs along with a disordered pace, and cleaves the throng; he falls on the corpse; and groaning there he lies, with silent grief, that speaks only through his eyes. Short sighs and sobs succeed; till sorrow breaks a passage, and at once he weeps and speaks:

"O Pallas! You have failed your plighted word, to fight with caution, not to tempt the sword! I warned you, but in vain; for well I knew what perils youthful ardor would pursue, that boiling blood would carry you too far, young as you were in dangers, raw to war! O cursed essay of arms, disastrous doom, prelude of bloody fields, and fights to come! Hard elements of unauspicious war, vain vows to Heaven, and unavailing care! Thrice happy you, dear partner of my bed, whose holy soul the stroke of Fortune fled, prescient of ills, and leaving me behind, to drink the dregs of life by fate assigned! Beyond the goal of nature I have gone: my Pallas set out late, but reached it too soon. If, for my league against the Ausonian state, I had found my fate amidst their weapons (a fate deserved from them), then I would have been returned a breathless victor, and my son would have mourned. Yet I will not upbraid my Trojan friend, nor grudge the alliance I so gladly made. It was not his fault that my Pallas fell so young, but my own crime, for having lived too long. Yet, since the gods had destined him to die, at least he led the way to victory: first for his friends he won the fatal shore, and sent whole herds of slaughtered foes before; a death too great, too glorious to deplore. Nor will I add new honors to your grave, content with those the Trojan hero gave: that funeral pomp which your Phrygian friends designed, in which the Tuscan chiefs and army joined. Great spoils and trophies, gained by you, they bear: then let your own achievements be your share. Even you, O Turnus, would have stood a trophy, whose mighty trunk had better graced the wood, if Pallas had arrived, with equal length of years, to match your bulk with equal strength. But why, unhappy man, do you detain these troops, to view the tears you shed in vain? Go, friends, relate this message to your lord: tell him, that, if I bear my bitter fate, and, after Pallas' death, live lingering on, it is to behold his vengeance for my son. I stay for Turnus, whose devoted head is owing to the living and the dead. My son and I expect it from his hand; it is all that he can give, or that we demand. Joy is no more; but I would gladly go, to greet my Pallas with such news below."

The morn had now dispelled the shades of night, restoring toils as she restored the light. The Trojan king and the Tuscan chief command to raise the piles along the winding strand. Their friends convey the dead to the funeral fires; black smoldering smoke expires from the green wood; the light of heaven is choked, and the new day retires. Then three times around the kindled piles they go (for ancient custom had ordained it so); three times horse and foot are led about the fires; and three times, with loud laments, they hail the dead. Tears, trickling down their breasts, bedew the ground, and drums and trumpets mix their mournful sound. Amid the blaze, their pious brethren throw the spoils, taken in battle from the foe: helms, embossed bits, and swords of shining steel; one casts a target, one a chariot wheel; some restore to their fellows their own arms: the falchions that they bore in luckless fight, their bucklers pierced, their darts bestowed in vain, and shivered lances gathered from the plain. Whole herds of offered bulls about the fire, and bristled boars, and woolly sheep expire. Around the piles a careful troop attends, to watch the wasting flames, and to weep their burning friends; lingering along the shore, till dewy night newly decks the face of heaven with starry light.

The conquered Latians, with like pious care, prepare piles without number for their dead. Some are laid in the places where they fell; and some are conveyed to the neighboring fields. The corpses of kings and captains of renown, borne off in state, are buried in the town; the rest, unhonored, and without a name, are cast in a common heap to feed the flame. Trojans and Latians vie with like desires to make the field of battle shine with fires, and the promiscuous blaze aspires to heaven.

Now the morning had three times renewed the light, and three times dispelled the shadows of the night, when those who remained around the wasted fires performed the last sad office to the slain. They rake the yet warm ashes from below; these, and the unburned bones, they bestow in earth; they grace these relics with the rites of their country, and raise a mount of turf to mark the place.

But, in the palace of the king, a scene more solemn appears, and a pomp of tears. Maids, matrons, widows, mix their common moans; orphans lament their sires, and sires their sons. All share in that universal sorrow, and curse the cause of this unhappy war: a broken league, a bride unjustly sought, a crown usurped, bought with their blood! These are the crimes with which they load the name of Turnus, and exclaim against him alone: "Let him who lords it over the Ausonian land engage the Trojan hero hand to hand: his is the gain; our lot is but to serve; it is just that he should deserve the sway he seeks." This Drances aggravates; and adds, with spite: "His foe expects, and dares him to the fight." Nor does Turnus lack a party, to support his cause and credit in the Latian court. His former acts secure his present fame, and the queen shades him with her mighty name.

While their factious minds thus burn with fury, the legates return from the Aetolian prince: they bring sad news, that, after all the cost and care employed, their embassy is lost; that Diomedes refused his aid in war, unmoved by presents, and deaf to prayer. Some new alliance must be sought elsewhere, or peace with Troy must be bought on hard conditions.

Latinus, sunk in sorrow, finds too late that a foreign son is pointed out by fate; and till Aeneas shall wed Lavinia, the wrath of Heaven is hovering over his head. The gods, he saw, espoused the juster side, when their titles were lately tried in the field: witness the fresh laments, and funeral tears undried. Thus, full of anxious thought, he summoned all the Latian senate to the council hall. The princes come, commanded by their head, and crowd the paths that lead to the palace. Supreme in power, and reverenced for his years, he takes the throne, and appears in the midst. Majestically sad, he sits in state, and bids his envoys relate their success.

When Venulus began, the murmuring sound was hushed, and sacred silence reigned around. "We have," said he, "performed your high command, and passed with peril a long tract of land: we reached the place desired; filled with wonder, we beheld the Grecian tents and rising towers. Great Diomede has compassed round with walls the city which he calls Argyripa, named from his own Argos. We touched with joy the royal hand that razed unhappy Troy. When introduced, we first brought our presents, then craved an instant audience from the king. With his leave obtained, we named our native soil, and told the important cause for which we came. He heard us attentively, while we spoke; then, with soft accents, and a pleasing look, made this return: 'Ausonian race, of old renowned for peace, and for an age of gold, what madness has possessed your altered minds, to change hereditary rest for war, to solicit unknown arms, and tempt the sword, a needless ill your ancestors abhorred? We—for I speak for myself, and for all the name of Grecians, who came to Troy's destruction (omitting those who were slain in battle, or borne by rolling Simois to the main)—not one but suffered, and too dearly bought the prize of honor which he sought in arms; some were doomed to death, and some were driven in exile, outcasts, abandoned by the care of Heaven; so worn, so wretched, so despised a crew, as even old Priam might with pity view. Witness the vessels tossed by Minerva in storms; the vengeful Capharean coast; the Euboean rocks! The prince whose brother led our armies to revenge his injured bed, lost in Egypt! Ulysses with his men have seen Charybdis and the Cyclops' den. Why should I name Idomeneus, in vain restored to scepters, and expelled again? Or young Achilles, slain by his rival? Even he, the King of Men, the foremost name of all the Greeks, and most renowned by fame, the proud revenger of another's wife, yet by his own adulteress lost his life; fell at his threshold; and the foul polluters of his bed enjoy the spoils of Troy. The gods have envied me the sweets of life, my much loved country, and my more loved wife: banished from both, I mourn; while in the sky, transformed to birds, my lost companions fly: hovering about the coasts, they make their moan, and cuff the cliffs with pinions not their own. What squalid specters, in the dead of night, break my short sleep, and skim before my sight! I might have promised myself those harms, mad as I was, when I, with mortal arms, presumed to move against immortal powers, and violate with wounds the Queen of Love. Such arms this hand shall never more employ; no hate remains with me to ruined Troy. I do not war with its dust; nor am I glad to think of past events, either good or bad. I return your presents: whatever you bring to buy my friendship, send to the Trojan king. We met in fight; I know him, to my cost: with what a whirling force he tossed his lance! Heavens! What a spring was in his arm, to throw! How high he held his shield, and rose at every blow! Had Troy produced two more his match in might, they would have changed the fortune of the fight: the invasion of the Greeks would have been returned, our empire wasted, and our cities burned. The long defense the Trojan people made, the war protracted, and the siege delayed, were due to Hector's and to this hero's hand: both brave alike, and equal in command; Aeneas, not inferior in the field, in pious reverence to the gods excelled. Make peace, you Latians, and carefully avoid the impending dangers of a fatal war.' He said no more; but, with this cold excuse, refused the alliance, and advised a truce."

Thus Venulus concluded his report. A jarring murmur filled the factious court: as, when a torrent rolls with rapid force, and dashes over the stones that stop the course, the flood, constrained within a scanty space, roars horribly along the uneasy race; white foam floats around in gathering eddies; the rocky shores rebellow to the sound.

The murmur ceased: then from his lofty throne the king invoked the gods, and thus began: "I wish, you Latins, what we now debate had been resolved before it was too late. It would have been much better for you and for me, unforced by this our last necessity, to have been earlier wise, than now to call a council, when the foe surrounds the wall. O citizens, we wage unequal war with men not only Heaven's peculiar care, but of Heaven's own race; unconquered in the field, or, when conquered, yet unknowing how to yield. Lay down what hopes you had in Diomedes: our hopes must now center on ourselves alone. Yet you see too well how feeble, and, indeed, how vain those hopes are; nor need my words explain. Vanquished without resource; laid flat by fate; factions within, a foe without the gate! Not but I grant that all performed their parts with manly force, and with undaunted hearts: we waged the war with our united strength; we engaged with equal numbers, equal arms. You see the event. Now hear what I propose, to save our friends, and to satisfy our foes. The Latins have possessed a tract of land along the Tiber, stretching to the west, which the Rutulians and Auruncans now till, and their mixed cattle graze the fruitful hill. Those mountains filled with firs, that lower land, if you consent, the Trojan shall command, called into part of what is ours; and there, on agreed terms, the common country share. There let them build and settle, if they please; unless they choose once more to cross the seas, in search of seats remote from Italy, and to set us free from unwelcome inmates. Then let us build twice ten galleys with speed, or twice as many more, if more they need. Materials are at hand; a well-grown wood runs equal with the margin of the flood. Let them assign the number and the form; the care and cost of all the stores shall be mine. To treat the peace, a hundred senators shall be commissioned from here with ample powers, who shall bear the presents with olive branches: a purple robe, a royal ivory chair, and all the marks of sway that Latian monarchs wear, and sums of gold. Debate this great affair among yourselves, and save the sinking state."

Then Drances took the word, who had long since grudged the rising glories of the Daunian prince. Factious and rich, bold at the council board, but cautious in the field, he shunned the sword; a close caballer, and a tongue-valiant lord. His mother was noble, and near the throne; but his father's parentage was unknown. He rose, and took advantage of the times, to load young Turnus with invidious crimes. "Such truths, O king," said he, "your words contain, as strike the sense, and render all replies vain. Nor are your loyal subjects now at a loss to know what common needs require, but they fear to speak. Let that haughty man give leave of speech, whose pride began this unauspicious war; for whose ambition (let me dare to say, fear set apart, though death is in my way) the plains of Latium run with blood around. So many valiant heroes bite the ground; dejected grief appears in every face; a town in mourning, and a land in tears; while he, the undoubted author of our harms, the man who menaces the gods with arms, yet, after all his boasts, forsook the fight, and sought his safety in ignoble flight. Now, best of kings, since you propose to send such bounteous presents to your Trojan friend, add yet a greater, at our joint request, one which he values more than all the rest: give him the fair Lavinia for his bride; with that alliance let the league be tied, and for the bleeding land a lasting peace provide. Let insolence no longer awe the throne; but, with a father's right, bestow your own. For this maligner of the general good, if we still fear his force, he must be wooed; we must implore his haughty godhead with prayers, that he release your scepter, and restore our just rights. O cursed cause of all our ills, must we wage unjust wars, and fall in fight, for you? What right have you to rule the Latian state, and send us out to meet our certain fate? It is a destructive war: from Turnus' hand we demand our peace and public safety. Let the fair bride remain to the brave chief; if not, the peace, without the pledge, is vain. Turnus, I know you do not think me your friend, nor will I much contend with your belief: I beg your greatness not to give the law in others' realms, but, beaten, to withdraw. Pity your own, or pity our estate; nor twist our fortunes with your sinking fate. Your interest is that the war should never cease; but we have felt enough to wish for peace: a land exhausted to the last remains, depopulated towns, and driven plains. Yet, if desire of fame, and thirst of power, and a beauteous princess, with a crown in dower, so fire your mind, assert your right in arms, and meet your foe, who dares you to the fight. Mankind, it seems, is made for you alone; we, but the slaves who mount you to the throne: a base ignoble crowd, without a name, unwept, unworthy of the funeral flame, bound by duty to forfeit each his life, that Turnus may possess a royal wife. Permit not, mighty man, that so mean a crew should share such triumphs, and detain from you the post of honor, your undoubted due. Rather, alone, employ your matchless force to merit what alone you must enjoy."

These words, so full of malice mixed with art, inflamed with rage the youthful hero's heart. Then, groaning from the bottom of his breast, he heaved for wind, and thus expressed his wrath: "You, Drances, never lack a stream of words, in the very hour when the public need requires our swords. First in the council hall to steer the state, and ever foremost in a tongue-debate, while our strong walls secure us from the foe, before yet our ditches overflow with blood. But let the potent orator declaim, and blot my name with the brand of coward; free leave is given him, when his fatal hand has covered the sanguine strand with more corpses, and his towering trophies stand as high as mine. If any doubt remains who dares the most, let us decide it at the Trojan's cost, and issue abreast, where honor calls—foes are not far to seek without the walls—unless his noisy tongue can only fight, and feet were given him only to speed his flight. I, beaten from the field? I, forced away? Who, but so known a dastard, dares to say? Had he but even beheld the fight, his eyes would have witnessed for me what his tongue denies: what heaps of Trojans were slain by this hand, and how the bloody Tiber swelled the main. All but he saw the Arcadian troops retire in scattered squadrons, and their prince expire. The giant brothers, in their camp, have found that I was not forced with ease to quit my ground. Not such the Trojans tried me, when, enclosed, I singly opposed their united arms: first I forced an entrance through their thick array; then, glutted with their slaughter, freed my way. It is a destructive war? So let it be, but to the Phrygian pirate, and to you! Meanwhile proceed to fill the people's ears with false reports, their minds with panic fears: extol the strength of a twice-conquered race; encourage our foes, and debase our friends. Believe your fables, and the Trojan town stands triumphant; the Grecians are overthrown; suppliant at Hector's feet Achilles lies, and Diomede flees from fierce Aeneas. Say rapid Aufidus, with awful dread, runs backward from the sea, and hides his head, when the great Trojan appears on his bank; for that is as true as your dissembled fears of my revenge. Dismiss that vanity: you, Drances, are below a death from me. Let that vile soul rest in that vile body; the lodging is well worthy of the guest.

"Now, royal father, to the present state of our affairs, and of this high debate: if you so early distrust your arms, and think your fortune already tried; if one defeat has brought us down so low as never more to meet the foe in fields; then I conclude for peace: it is time to treat, and to lie like vassals at the victor's feet. But, O! If any ancient blood remains, one drop of all our fathers', in our veins, that man would I prefer before the rest, who dared his death with an undaunted breast; who fell comely, by no dishonest wound, to shun that sight, and, dying, gnawed the ground. But if we still have fresh recruits in store, if our confederates can afford us more; if the contended field we bravely fought, and a bloodless victory was not bought; their losses equaled ours; and, for their slain, they filled the shining plain with equal fires—why, unforced, should we so tamely yield, and, before the trumpet sounds, resign the field? Good unexpected, and evils unforeseen, appear by turns, as fortune shifts the scene: some, raised aloft, come tumbling down amain; then fall so hard, they bound and rise again. If Diomede refuses to lend his aid, the great Messapus yet remains our friend: Tolumnius, who foretells events, is ours; the Italian chiefs and princes join their powers; nor least in number, nor last in name, your own brave subjects have embraced your cause. Above the rest, the Volscian Amazon contains an army in herself alone, and heads a squadron, terrible to sight, with glittering shields, bright in brazen armor. Yet, if the foe demand a single fight, and I alone withstand the public peace; if you consent, he shall not be refused, nor shall he find a hand unused to victory. Let this new Achilles take the field, with fated armor, and with Vulcanian shield! For you, my royal father, and my fame, I, Turnus, not the least of all my name, devote my soul. He calls me hand to hand, and I alone will answer his demand. Drances shall rest secure, and neither share the danger, nor divide the prize of war."

While they debate, and neither these nor those will yield, Aeneas draws his forces to the field, and moves his camp. The scouts with flying speed return, and through the frighted city spread the unpleasing news, that the Trojans are descried, marching in battle along the river side, and bending toward the town. They take the alarm: some tremble, some are bold; all arm in confusion. The impetuous youth press forward to the field; they clash the sword, and clatter on the shield: the fearful matrons raise a screaming cry; old feeble men reply with fainter groans; a jarring sound results, and mingles in the sky, like that of swans remurmuring to the floods, or of differing kinds of birds in hollow woods.

Turnus takes the occasion, and cries aloud: "Talk on, you quaint haranguers of the crowd: declaim in praise of peace, when danger calls, and the fierce foes approach the walls in arms." He said, and, turning short, with speedy pace, casts back a scornful glance, and quits the place: "You, Volusus, command the Volscian troops to mount; and lead our Ardean band yourself. Messapus and Catillus, post your force along the fields, to charge the Trojan horse. Some guard the passes, others man the wall; drawn up in arms, let the rest attend my call."

They swarm from every quarter of the town, and with disordered haste crown the ramparts. Good old Latinus, when he saw, too late, the gathering storm just breaking on the state, dismissed the council till a fitter time, and owned his easy temper as his crime, who, forced against his reason, had complied to break the treaty for the promised bride.

Some help to sink new trenches; others aid to ram the stones, or to raise the palisade. Hoarse trumpets sound the alarm; around the walls runs a distracted crew, whom their last labor calls. A sad procession is seen in the streets, of matrons who attend the mother queen: high in her chair she sits, and, at her side, with downcast eyes, appears the fatal bride. They mount the cliff where Pallas' temple stands; prayers in their mouths, and presents in their hands. With censers they first fume the sacred shrine, then join in this common supplication: "O patroness of arms, unspotted maid, propitious hear, and lend your Latins aid! Break short the pirate's lance; pronounce his fate, and lay the Phrygian low before the gate."

Now Turnus arms for fight. His back and breast are invested with well-tempered steel and scaly brass; the cuisses that enfold his brawny thighs are of mingled metal damasked over with gold. His faithful falchion sits upon his side; nor does casque, nor crest, hide his manly features: but, bare to view, amid surrounding friends, with godlike grace, he descends from the tower. Exulting in his strength, he seems to dare his absent rival, and to promise war. Freed from his keepers, thus, with broken reins, the wanton courser prances over the plains, or in the pride of youth overleaps the mounds, and sniffs the females in forbidden grounds. Or he seeks his watering in the well-known flood, to quench his thirst, and cool his fiery blood: he swims luxuriant in the liquid plain, and over his shoulder flows his waving mane: he neighs, he snorts, he bears his head on high; before his ample chest the frothy waters fly.

As soon as the prince appears outside the gate, the Volscians, with their virgin leader, await his last commands. Then, with a graceful mien, the warrior queen alights from her lofty steed: her squadron imitates her, and each descends; whose common suit Camilla thus commends: "If sense of honor, if a soul secure of inborn worth, that can endure all tests, can promise anything, or rely on itself greatly to dare, to conquer or to die; then, I alone, sustained by these, will meet the Tyrrhene troops, and promise their defeat. Let the danger be ours, the sole renown ours: you, general, stay behind, and guard the town."

Turnus stood mute a while, with glad surprise, and fixed his eyes on the fierce Virago; then thus replied: "O grace of Italy, with what becoming thanks can I reply? Not only words lie laboring in my breast, but thought itself is oppressed by your praise. Yet do not rob me of all; but let me join my toils, my hazard, and my fame, with yours. The Trojan, not unskilled in stratagem, sends his light horse before to scour the field; he himself, through steep ascents and thorny brakes, takes a larger compass to the city. My scouts confirm this news, and I prepare to foil his cunning, and to dare his force; with chosen foot to forelay his passage, and to place an ambush in the winding way. You, with your Volscians, face the Tuscan horse; the brave Messapus shall enforce your troops, with those of Tibur, and the Latian band, all subjected to your supreme command." This said, he warns Messapus to the war, then exhorts every chief with equal care. All thus encouraged, he joins his own troops, and hastens to prosecute his deep designs.

Enclosed with hills, a winding valley lies, formed by nature for fraud, and fitted for surprise. A narrow track, untrodden by human steps, leads, through perplexing thorns, to this obscure abode. High over the vale a steepy mountain stands, from which the surveying sight commands the nether ground. The top is level, an offensive seat of war, and a safe retreat from the war: for, on the right and left, there is room to press the foes at hand, or from afar to distress; to drive them headlong downward, and to pour a stony shower on their descending backs. Thither young Turnus took the well-known way, possessed the pass, and lay in blind ambush.

Meanwhile Latonian Phoebe, from the skies, beheld the approaching war with hateful eyes, and called light-foot Opis to her aid, her most beloved and ever-trusty maid. Then, with a sigh, she began: "Camilla goes to meet her death amidst her fatal foes: the one nymph I loved of all my mortal train, invested with Diana's arms, in vain. Nor is my kindness for the virgin new: it was born with her; and with her years it grew. Her father Metabus, when forced away from old Privernum, for tyrannic sway, snatched up, and saved from his prevailing foes, this tender babe, the companion of his woes. Casmilla was her mother; but he drowned one hissing letter in a softer sound, and called her Camilla. Through the woods he flies; the royal infant lies wrapped in his robe. His foes in sight, he mends his weary pace; with shout and clamor they pursue the chase. At length he gains the banks of the Amasene:

"The raging flood restrains his further flight, raised over the borders with unusual rains. Prepared to plunge into the stream, he fears, not for himself, but for the charge he bears. Anxious, he stops a while, and thinks in haste; then, desperate in distress, resolves at last. He bore a knotty lance of well-boiled oak; the middle part he covered over with cork: he enclosed the child within the hollow space; he bound the case with twigs of bending osier; then he poised the spear, heavy with human weight, and thus invoked my favor for the freight: 'Accept, great goddess of the woods,' he said, 'sent by her sire, this dedicated maid! Through air she flies a suppliant to your shrine; and the first weapons that she knows are yours.' He said; and with full force he threw the spear: above the sounding waves Camilla flew. Then, pressed by foes, he stemmed the stormy tide, and gained, by stress of arms, the further side. He pulled his fastened spear out of the ground, and, victor of his vows, unbound his infant nymph. Nor, after that, in towns that walls enclose, would he trust his hunted life amidst his foes; but, rough, in open air he chose to lie; earth was his couch, his covering was the sky. On unshorn hills, or in a desert den, he shunned the dire society of men. He led a shepherd's solitary life; he fed his daughter with the milk of mares. The dugs of bears, and of every savage beast, he drew, and pressed the liquor through her lips. The little Amazon could scarcely walk: he loads her with a quiver and a bow; and, that she might command her staggering steps, he fills her hand with a slender javelin. No golden fillet bound her flowing hair; nor did her trailing robe sweep the dusty ground. Instead of these, a tiger's hide overspread her back and shoulders, fastened to her head. She first attempts to fling the flying dart, and tosses the sling round her tender temples; then, as her strength increased with years, she began to pierce aloft in air the soaring swan, and to fetch the heron and the crane from the clouds. The Tuscan matrons vied with each other to bless their rival sons with such a bride; but she disdains their love, to share with me the sylvan shades and vowed virginity. And, O! I wish, content with my cares of wild spoils, she had not sought the wars! Then she would have been of my celestial train, and would have shunned the fate that dooms her to be slain. But since, opposing Heaven's decree, she goes to find her death among forbidden foes, haste with these arms, and take your steepy flight where, with the gods averse, the Latins fight. I bequeath to you this bow, this quiver, this chosen arrow, to revenge her death: by whatever hand Camilla shall be slain, whether of the Trojan or Italian train, let him not pass unpunished from the plain. Then, in a hollow cloud, I myself will aid to bear the breathless body of my maid: her arms shall be unspoiled, and her holy limbs unprofaned by any human hand, and she shall be laid in a marble tomb in her native land."
She said. The faithful nymph descends from on high with rapid flight, and cuts the sounding sky: black clouds and stormy winds fly around her body.

By this, the Trojan and the Tuscan horse, drawn up in squadrons, with united force, approach the walls: the sprightly coursers bound, press forward on their bits, and shift their ground. Shields, arms, and spears flash horribly from afar; and the fields glitter with a waving war. Opposed to these, Messapus, Coras, and the Latian horse come on with furious force; these, placed in the body, on either hand are sustained and closed by fair Camilla's band. Advancing in a line, they couch their spears; and less and less the middle space appears. Thick smoke obscures the field; and scarcely are seen the neighing coursers, and the shouting men. At the distance of their darts they stop their course; then man to man they rush, and horse to horse. The face of heaven their flying javelins hide, and deaths unseen are dealt on either side. Tyrrhenus and Aconteus, void of fear, borne in full career by mettled coursers, first meet opposed; and, with a mighty shock, their horses' heads knock against each other. Far from his steed fierce Aconteus is cast, as with an engine's force, or a lightning's blast: he rolls along in blood, and breathes his last. The Latin squadrons take a sudden fright, and sling their shields behind, to save their backs in flight. Spurring at speed to their own walls they drew; close in the rear the Tuscan troops pursue, and urge their flight: Asylas leads the chase; till, seized with shame, they wheel about and face, receive their foes, and raise a threatening cry. The Tuscans take their turn to fear and fly. So swelling surges, with a thundering roar, driven on each other's backs, insult the shore, bound over the rocks, encroach upon the land, and eject the sand far upon the beach; then backward, with a swing, they take their way, repulsed from the upper ground, and seek their mother sea; with equal hurry they quit the invaded shore, and swallow back the sand and stones they spewed before.

Twice were the Tuscans masters of the field, twice by the Latins, in their turn, repelled. Ashamed at length, they ran to the third charge; both hosts resolved, and mingled man to man. Now dying groans are heard; the fields are strewn with falling bodies, and are drunk with blood. Arms, horses, men, lie together in heaps: the fight is confused, and the cry more confused. Orsilochus, who did not dare to press too near strong Remulus, drove his spear at a distance, and stuck the steel beneath his horse's ear. The fiery steed, impatient of the wound, curvets, and, springing upward with a bound, casts his helpless lord backward on the ground. Catillus first pierced Iolas; then he drew his reeking lance, and threw it at Herminius, the mighty champion of the Tuscan crew. His neck and throat were unarmed, his head was bare, but shaded with a length of yellow hair: secure, he fought, exposed on every part, a spacious mark for swords and for the flying dart. The feathered wound came across his shoulders; transfixed he fell, and doubled to the ground. The sands are sanguine dyed with streaming blood, and death with honor sought on either side.

Resistless through the war Camilla rode, unappalled in danger, and pleased with blood. One side was bare for her exerted breast; one shoulder was pressed with her painted quiver. Now from afar her fatal javelins play; now with her axe's edge she hews her way: Diana's arms sound upon her shoulder; and when, too closely pressed, she quits the ground, from her bent bow she sends a backward wound. Her maids, in martial pomp, ride on either side, Larina, Tulla, fierce Tarpeia: Italians all; in peace, their queen's delight; in war, the bold companions of the fight. So marched the Thracian Amazons of old, when Thermodon rolled with bloody billows: such troops as these in shining arms were seen, when Theseus met their maiden queen in fight; such Penthesilea led to the field, when the Grecians fled from the fierce virgin; with such she returned triumphant from the war; her maids with cries attend the lofty car; they clash with manly force their moony shields; with female shouts they resound the Phrygian fields.

Who first, and who last, heroic maid, were laid by your courage on the cold earth? Your spear of mountain ash, driven with fury, transpierced Eumenius first, from side to side: a purple stream came spouting from the wound; bathed in his blood he lies, and bites the ground. Liris and Pegasus she slew at once: the former, as he drew the slackened reins of his faint steed; the latter, as he stretched his arm to prop his friend, the javelin reached. Both fall together by the same weapon, sent from the same hand, and both spurn the sand. Amastrus next is added to the slain: she follows the rest in rout over the plain: Tereus, Harpalycus, Demophoon, and Chromis, all shun her fury at full speed. Not one of her deadly darts was lost; each was attended with a Trojan ghost. Young Ornithus bestrode a hunter steed, swift for the chase, and of Apulian breed. Him from afar she spied, in unknown arms: over his broad back an ox's hide was thrown; his helm was a wolf, whose gaping jaws were spread as a covering for his cheeks, and grinned around his head; he clenched in his hand an iron prong, and towered above the rest, conspicuous in the throng. She soon singled him out from the flying train, and slew him with ease; then she thus insults the slain: "Vain hunter, did you think to chase through woods the savage herd, a vile and trembling race? Here cease your vaunts, and own my victory: a woman warrior was too strong for you. Yet, if the ghosts demand the conqueror's name, confess it was great Camilla, to save your shame." Then Butes and Orsilochus she slew, the bulkiest bodies of the Trojan crew; but Butes breast to breast: the spear descends above the gorget, where his helmet ends, and over the shield which defends his left side. Orsilochus and she ply their courses: he seems to follow, and she seems to flee; but in a narrower ring she makes the race; and then he flees, and she pursues the chase. Gathering at length on her deluded foe, she swings her axe, and rises to the blow full on the helm behind, with such a sway the weapon falls, the riven steel gives way: he groans, he roars, he sues in vain for grace; brains, mingled with his blood, besmear his face.

Astonished Aunus just arrives by chance, to see his fall; nor does he dare further advance. But, fixing his eye on the horrid maid, he stares, and shakes, and finds it vain to flee; yet, like a true Ligurian, born to cheat (at least while fortune favored his deceit), he cries out aloud: "What courage have you shown, who trust your courser's strength, and not your own? Forego the vantage of your horse, alight, and then on equal terms begin the fight: it shall be seen, weak woman, what you can do, when, foot to foot, you combat with a man." He said. She glows with anger and disdain, dismounts with speed to dare him on the plain, and leaves her horse at large among her train; with her drawn sword she defies him to the field, and, marching, lifts aloft her maiden shield. The youth, who thought his cunning did succeed, reins round his horse, and urges all his speed; adds the remembrance of the spur, and hides the goring rowels in his bleeding sides. "Vain fool, and coward!" cries the lofty maid, "Caught in the train which you yourself have laid! Practice your Ligurian arts on others; thin stratagems and tricks of little hearts are lost on me: nor shall you safely retire, with vaunting lies, to your fallacious sire." At this, she sped her flying feet so fast that she soon strained beyond his horse's head: then, turning short, at once she seized the rein, and laid the boaster groveling on the plain. Not with more ease the falcon, from above, trusses in middle air the trembling dove, then plumes the prey, bound in her strong pounces: the feathers, foul with blood, come tumbling to the ground.

Now mighty Jove, from his superior height, with his broad eye surveys the unequal fight. He fires the breast of Tarchon with disdain, and sends him to redeem the abandoned plain. Between the broken ranks the Tuscan rides, and these he encourages, and those he chides; he recalls each leader by name from flight; he renews their ardor, and restores the fight. "What panic fear has seized your souls? O shame, O perpetual brand of the Etrurian name! Incurable cowards, a woman's hand drives, breaks, and scatters your ignoble band! Now cast away the sword, and quit the shield! What use of weapons which you dare not wield? Not thus you flee your female foes by night, nor shun the feast, when the full bowls invite; when the glad augur calls to fat offerings, and the shrill hornpipe sounds to bacchanals. These are your studied cares, your lewd delight: swift to debauch, but slow to manly fight." Thus having said, he spurs amid the foes, not managing the life he meant to lose. The first he found he seized with headlong haste, in his strong grip, and clasped around the waist; it was Venulus, whom he tore from his horse, and, laid athwart his own, bore in triumph. Loud shouts ensue; the Latins turn their eyes, and view the unusual sight with vast surprise. The fiery Tarchon, flying over the plains, sustains the ponderous prey pressed in his arms; then, with his shortened spear, he explores around his jointed arms, to fix a deadly wound. Nor less does the captive struggle for his life: he writhes his body to prolong the strife, and, fencing for his naked throat, exerts his utmost vigor, and averts the point. So the yellow eagle stoops from on high, and bears a speckled serpent through the sky, fastening his crooked talons on the prey: the prisoner hisses through the liquid way; resists the royal hawk; and, though oppressed, she fights in coils, and erects her crest; turned to her foe, she stiffens every scale, and shoots her forky tongue, and whisks her threatening tail. Against the victor, all defense is weak: the imperial bird still plies her with his beak; he tears her bowels, and gores her breast; then claps his pinions, and soars securely. Thus, through the midst of circling enemies, strong Tarchon snatched and bore away his prize. The Tyrrhene troops, that shrunk before, now press the Latins, and presume the like success.

Then Aruns, doomed to death, essayed his arts to murder, unespied, the Volscian maid: this way and that he bends his winding course, and, wherever she turns, his steps attend. When she retires victorious from the chase, he wheels about with care, and shifts his place; when, rushing on, she seeks her foes in fight, he keeps aloof, but keeps her still in sight: he threatens, and trembles, trying every way, unseen to kill, and safely to betray. Chloreus, the priest of Cybele, from afar, glittering in Phrygian arms amidst the war, was viewed by the virgin. The steed he pressed was proud with trappings, and his brawny chest was covered over with scales of gilded brass; the rider wore a robe of Tyrian dye. With deadly wounds he galled the distant foe; Gnossian were his shafts, and Lycian his bow: a golden helm surrounded his front and head; a gilded quiver sounded from his shoulder. Gold, woven with linen, he wore on his thighs, distinguished with flowers of needlework, bound with golden buckles, and gathered up before. The fierce maid beheld him with ardent eyes, fond and ambitious of so rich a prize, either that the temple might hold his trophies, or else that she herself might shine in Trojan gold. Blind in her haste, she chases him alone, and seeks his life, regardless of her own.

This lucky moment the sly traitor chose: then, starting from his ambush, he rose, and threw, but first addressed his vows to Heaven: "O patron of Soracte's high abodes, Phoebus, the ruling power among the gods, whom first we serve, whole woods of unctuous pine are felled for you, and shine for your glory; by your protection, with our naked soles, through unsinged flames we march, and tread the kindled coals. Grant me, propitious power, to wash away the stains of this dishonorable day: I do not claim spoils or triumph from the deed, but entrust my fame to my future actions. Let me, by stealth, overcome this female plague, and return inglorious home from the field." Apollo heard, and, granting half his prayer, shuffled the rest in winds, and tossed it in empty air. He gives the death desired; his safe return is borne by southern tempests to the seas.

Now, when the javelin whizzed along the skies, both armies turned their eyes toward Camilla, directed by the sound. Of either host, the unhappy virgin, though most concerned, was only deaf; so greedy was she, bent on golden spoils, and intent on her prey, till in her breast the winged weapon stood infixed, and deeply drank the purple blood. Her sad attendants hasten to sustain their dying lady, drooping on the plain. Far from their sight the trembling Aruns flies, with beating heart, and fear confused with joys; nor does he dare further to pursue his blow, or even to bear the sight of his expiring foe. As, when the wolf has torn a bullock's hide at unawares, or gored a shepherd's side, conscious of his audacious deed, he flies, and claps his quivering tail between his thighs: so, having sped once, the wretch no more attends, but, spurring forward, herds among his friends.

She wrenched the javelin with her dying hands, but the weapon stands wedged within her breast; she draws the wood, the steely point remains; she staggers in her seat with agonizing pains; a gathering mist overclouds her cheerful eyes, and from her cheeks the rosy color flies. Then she turns to her, whom of her female train she trusted most, and thus speaks with pain: "Acca, it is past! He swims before my sight, inexorable Death; and claims his right. Bear my last words to Turnus; flee with speed, and bid him timely to succeed in my charge, to repel the Trojans, and to relieve the town: farewell! And in this kiss receive my parting breath." She said, and, sliding, sunk upon the plain: dying, her opened hand forsakes the rein; short, and more short, she pants; by slow degrees her mind is freed from the passage of her body. She drops her sword; she nods her plumy crest, her drooping head declining on her breast: in the last sigh her struggling soul expires, and, murmuring with disdain, retires to Stygian sounds.
A shout, that struck the golden stars, ensued; despair and rage renewed the languished fight. The Trojan troops and Tuscans, in a line, advance to charge; the mixed Arcadians join.

But Cynthia's maid, high seated, from afar surveys the field, and the fortune of the war, unmoved a while, until, prostrate on the plain, weltering in blood, she sees Camilla slain, and, around her corpse, a fighting train of friends and foes. Then, from the bottom of her breast, she drew a mournful sigh, and these sad words ensue: "Too dear a fine, ah, much lamented maid, have you paid for warring with the Trojans! Nor did Diana's sacred arms avail to save your life, in this unhappy strife. Yet unrevenged your goddess will not leave her votary's death, nor grieve with vain sorrow. Let the wretch be branded, and his name abhorred; but after ages shall record your praise. The inglorious coward soon shall press the plain: thus vows your queen, and thus the Fates ordain."

High over the field there stood a hilly mound, a sacred place, spread with oaks around, where Dercennus lay in a marble tomb, a king that once in Latium bore the sway. The beauteous Opis bent her flight there, to mark the traitor Aruns from the height.
