Soon she spied him in refulgent arms, swollen with success; and loudly she cried: "Your backward steps, vain boaster, are too late; turn like a man, at length, and meet your fate. Charged with my message, go to Camilla, and say I sent you to the shades below—an honor undeserved from Cynthia's bow."

She said, and from her quiver chose with speed the winged shaft, predestined for the deed; then she applied her strength to the stubborn yew, till the far distant horns approached on either side. The bowstring touched her breast, so strongly she drew; whizzing in air, the fatal arrow flew. At once the twanging bow and the sounding dart the traitor heard, and felt the point within his heart. His flying friends bequeath him, beating with his heels in the pangs of death, to foreign fields. The conquering damsel, with expanded wings, brings the welcome message to her mistress.

Their leader lost, the Volscians quit the field, and, unsustained, the chiefs of Turnus yield. The frighted soldiers, when their captains flee, rely more on their speed than on their strength. Confused in flight, they bear each other down, and spur their horses headlong to the town. Driven by their foes, and resigned to their fears, not once they turn, but take their wounds behind. These drop the shield, and those forgo the lance, or bear the slackened bow on their shoulders. The hoofs of horses, with a rattling sound, beat short and thick, and shake the rotten ground. Black clouds of dust come rolling in the sky, and fly over the darkened walls and ramparts. The trembling matrons, from their lofty stands, rend heaven with female shrieks, and wring their hands. All pressing on, pursuers and pursued, are crushed in crowds, a mingled multitude. Some few, happy, escape: the throng, too late, rushes on for entrance, till they choke the gate. Even in the sight of home, the wretched sire looks on, and sees his helpless son expire. Then, in a fright, they close the folding gates, but leave their friends excluded with their foes. The vanquished cry; the victors loudly shout; it is terror all within, and slaughter all without. Blind in their fear, they bounce against the wall, or, pursued to the moats, precipitate their fall.

The Latian virgins, valiant with despair, armed on the towers, share the common danger: so much did zeal for their country's cause inspire them; so much did Camilla's great example fire them. Poles, sharpened in the flames, they throw from on high, with imitated darts, to gall the foe. They bequeath their lives for godlike freedom, and crowd one another to be first in death. Meanwhile to Turnus, ambushed in the shade, the unhappy maid came with heavy tidings: "The Volscians overthrown, Camilla killed; the foes, entirely masters of the field, come rolling on like a resistless flood; the cry goes off the plain, and thickens to the town."

Inflamed with rage (for so the Furies fire the Daunian's breast, and so the Fates require), he leaves the hilly pass, the woods possessed in vain, and issues downward onto the plain. Scarcely was he gone when the Trojan troops succeed to the straits, now freed from secret foes. Through the black forest and the ferny brake, unknowingly secure, they take their way; from the rough mountains they descend to the plain, and there, drawn up in order, extend their line. Both armies are now seen in open fields; nor far the distance of the space between. Both bend to the city. Aeneas sees his hastening enemies through smoking fields; and Turnus views the Trojans in array, and hears the approaching horses proudly neigh. Soon their hosts would have joined in bloody battle, but westward to the sea the sun declined. Entrenched before the town, both armies lie, while night with sable wings involves the sky.

chapters.title: Book XII
paragraphs: Turnus challenges Aeneas to single combat. The terms are agreed, but the Rutulians break them and wound Aeneas. He is miraculously healed by Venus, forces Turnus into a duel, and the poem concludes with Turnus's death.

When Turnus saw the Latins leave the field, their ranks broken and their courage crushed, and saw himself become the target of public scorn, his honor called into question over the promised fight — the more he was oppressed by the common hatred, the more his fury boiled within his breast. He roused his strength for the final debate and lifted his haughty soul to meet his fate.

As when hunters chase the Libyan lion, he makes a sullen retreat and does not quicken his pace; but if the pointed javelin pierces his side, the lordly beast turns back with double pride. He wrenches out the steel, he roars with pain; he lashes his sides and raises his mane. So it is with Turnus. His eyes flash with fire, and from his wide nostrils clouds of smoke pour out.

Trembling with rage, he strode through the court, and at last came to the king and began: “No more excuses, no more delays. I stand armed and ready to fight hand to hand with this base deserter from his own country. The Trojan is bound by his own word to accept the very conditions he himself proposed. Renew the truce, prepare the solemn rites, and entrust the war to my single valor. The Latians shall watch the fight with no stake in it; this arm alone shall defend your right. Then, if my body lies stretched on the plain, let the crown and the beautiful bride pass to him.”

To which the king replied calmly: “Brave youth, the more your courage has been tested, the more it becomes us to weigh the chance of war with due respect — which you neglect. You do not lack wealth, nor an inherited throne, nor cities your arms have made your own. My towns and treasures are at your command, and my land is stocked with blooming beauties. Laurentum holds more than one Lavinia — unmarried, fair, of noble family. Now let me speak, and listen patiently to things that may grate on a lover's ear but come as honest counsel from a heart sincerely yours, free from any fraud. The gods, by clear signs, have shown that no Italian-born prince should inherit my throne. Our augurs, skilled in prediction, and our priests have again and again revealed a foreign son. Yet, won over by worth not to be withstood, bribed by my affection for my own blood, and urged by my wife who would not be denied, I promised Lavinia to you as your bride. I took her by force from the man she was pledged to; I broke every tie of treaty and of honor. For your sake I waged an impious war — with what result, there is no need to say. I and my people feel it, and you have had your share. Twice defeated while we strove in bloody fields, we scarcely keep our hopes alive within our walls. The river runs warm with human blood; the bones of Latians whiten the neighboring shore. Why am I not putting an end to this, still undecided, still a slave to fate? If Turnus's death can give us lasting peace, why should I not secure peace while you still live? Should I betray your youth to the chances of arms — what would my kinsmen the Rutulians say? And if you fell in battle (may heaven forbid!), how they would curse the cause that hastened the daughter's lover and the father's friend to his end. Weigh in your mind the many turns of war; pity your parent's age, and ease his cares.”

Such soothing words he poured out, but all in vain. The medicine offered only inflamed the pain. The furious youth, refusing the relief, spoke out his grief in broken sobs: “The care, O best of fathers, that you take for my concerns — set it aside, at my request. Do not let me drag out my days; let me make the best exchange, life for glory. This arm, this lance, can surely win the prize; and blood follows wherever the weapon strikes. His goddess mother is not here to shroud the fleeing coward in an empty cloud.”

But now the queen, who feared for Turnus's life and hated the harsh terms of the duel, held him back by force, and, as if dying in his death, gave voice to her grief: “O Turnus, I implore you by these tears, and by whatever Amata's honor still weighs within your heart — since you are all my hope, the repose of my sick mind, the prop of my sinking age; since on the safety of your life alone depend both Latinus and the Latian throne — refuse me not this one, this single prayer: waive the combat and continue the war. Whatever outcome attends this fatal struggle, know that yours includes Amata's life. I cannot live as a slave, or watch my throne usurped by strangers or by a Trojan son.”

At this, a flood of tears fell from Lavinia; a crimson blush spread over her lovely face, and her cheeks shifted by turns between white and red. The shifting colors, never settling, ran here and there and flushed and faded. What a lovely change! So Indian ivory gleams when bordered with purple paint, or lilies look damasked beside the rose.

Her lover gazed, and burning with desire, the more he looked, the more he fed the fire. Revenge, jealous rage, and secret resentment rolled in his breast and roused him to the fight. Then, fixing his ardent eyes on the queen, firm in his first intent, he replied: “O mother, do not with your tears prepare such ominous signs, or prejudge the war. Resolved to fight, I am no longer free to avoid my death if heaven has decreed it.” Then turning to the herald, he continued: “Go, greet the Trojan with unwelcome news: announce from me that when tomorrow's light gilds the sky, he need not urge his troops to battle. The Trojan and Rutulian armies shall no longer stain the Latian shore with each other's blood. Our swords alone shall settle the quarrel, and the beautiful bride shall go to the victor.”

He spoke, and striding on with rapid pace, he sought out his horses of Thracian breed. At his approach they tossed their heads high and, neighing proudly, promised victory. Their sires had been sent from afar by Orithyia to honor Pilumnus when he went to war. The drifts of Thracian snow were hardly so white, nor could the north winds match their swift flight. Attendants stood ready at his side; some combed out their flowing manes, others stroked their chests and gently soothed their pride.

He sheathed his limbs in armor: a tempered mass of gold and mountain bronze. Then he tied his glittering helmet to his head and buckled his trusty sword at his side. In his Aetnean forge the God of Fire had labored that blade for the hero's father, endowing it with immortal keenness and plunging it, hissing, into the Stygian flood. Propped against a pillar that held up the ceiling stood the lance that Auruncan Actor once carried — a weapon he used to brandish with such force that the tough ash trembled like a slender willow wand. Then he cried: “O heavy spoil of Actor slain, never yet wielded by Turnus in vain — fail not today your accustomed force! Go, sent by this hand, to pierce the Trojan foe! Let me tear his corslet from his breast, rip the crest from that eunuch head, and drag his curled hair in the dust, still hot from the vexing iron and smeared with fragrant oil!”

Thus he raved, while from his wide nostrils a fiery steam flew and sparks flashed from his eyes. So a bull fares in sight of his beloved cow: proudly he bellows and rehearses the fight; he tries his goring horns against a tree and practices against his absent enemy. He strikes at the winds, he digs the sand with his black hoofs, and paws the yellow ground.

No less did the Trojan, in his Lemnian armor, warm his manly courage for the coming fight. He sharpened his fury and prepared gladly to bring the lingering war to an end at last. He cheered his chiefs and his tender son, telling them what heaven had promised and expounding the fates. Then he sent word to the Latian king to halt the rage of arms and ratify the peace.

The next morning from the height of the mountain had scarcely spread its rosy light across the skies — the heavenly horses, bounding up from the sea, breathed the new day from their flaming nostrils — when the Trojan and Rutulian guards, working together in friendly labor, prepared the lists. Beneath the walls they measured out the space, then raised sacred altars on turfs of grass, where they set up the common gods with proper rites. The priests, in purest white, covered their heads; they carried living waters and holy fire; and over their linen hoods and shadowed hair they wore long twisted wreaths of sacred vervain.

In due order the Latin legion issued from the town, armed with pointed spears; and from the fields, advancing in a line, the Trojan and Tuscan forces joined them. Their various arms made a pleasing sight; they looked like a peaceful procession, peace-ready yet prepared for battle. Between the ranks the proud commanders rode, glittering in gold, their vests dyed in purple: here Mnestheus, ancestor of the Memmian line, and there Messapus, of divine seed. The signal was given, and around the marked-off space each man took his proper place. Leaning on their broad shields, they stood with pointed lances fixed in the sand. Now, eager to see the spectacle, a crowd of every sort — men and women, old and young — swarmed the town. Those who stayed behind lined the gates and walls and the tops of houses. Meanwhile the Queen of Heaven watched the scene with displeased eyes from the height of Mount Albano (later called Alban by repute, but then an empty hill without a name). From there she surveyed the field, the Trojan forces, the Latin squadrons, and the towers of Laurentum. Then the goddess of the skies spoke with sighs and tears to the goddess of the lake — King Turnus's sister, once a lovely maid, before she was betrayed to the lust of lawless Jove, forced by him but, by the grateful god, now made the naiad of the nearby stream: “O nymph, the pride of living lakes,” she said, “most renowned and most beloved by me, you have long known — I need not recite — the wanton affairs of my wandering lord. Of every Latian woman whom Jove led astray to steal into my violated bed, you alone I did not begrudge his embrace: I gave you a portion of heaven and an unenvied place. Now learn from me the grief coming near you, and do not think my wishes fail you in relief. While fortune favored and heaven's king did not deny my aid to the Latian side, I saved your brother and the sinking state. But now he struggles with unequal fate, and with the gods against him, overmatched in strength, goes to meet inevitable death in battle. I may not break the truce, nor can I bear the sight. You — if you dare to lend him your aid now, it well becomes a sister's care to try.”

At this the lovely nymph, overcome with grief, three times tore her hair and beat her comely breast. To her Saturnia said: “Your tears are too late. Hurry, snatch him, if he can still be snatched from fate. Stir up new disturbances; violate the truce. Who knows what changeable fortune may produce? It is no crime to attempt what I decree — or if it is, lay the crime on me.” She spoke, and sailing away on the winged wind, she left the sad nymph suspended in her mind.

And now in pomp the peaceful kings appeared. Four horses drew the chariot of Latinus; twelve golden rays played about his temples, marking his descent from the God of Day. Two snowy horses drew Turnus's chariot, and in his hand he shook two heavy spears. Then Aeneas, founder of the Roman line, issued from the camp in divine armor, and beside him took his place Ascanius, the second hope of Rome's immortal race. A reverend priest, clothed in white, approached and brought offerings to the flaming altars: a young pig and a lamb that had never been sheared. Then he turned his eyes to the rising sun and sprinkled the beasts appointed for sacrifice with salt and meal. With equal attention he marked their foreheads and clipped their hair. Between their horns he poured purple wine, and fed the flame with the same generous drink.

Then Aeneas unsheathed his shining sword and adored the gods with pious prayers: “All-seeing Sun, and you, Ausonian earth, for which I have endured so long a toil; you, King of Heaven, and you, Queen of Air, propitious now and reconciled by prayer; you, God of War, whose unresisted rule the labors and events of arms obey; you living fountains, you running rivers, all powers of the ocean, all gods of the sky — hear, and bear witness. If I fall in battle, or prove a coward and yield to Turnus, my Trojans shall swell Evander's town, and Ascanius shall renounce the Ausonian crown. All claims, all disputes shall cease; he and his shall not disturb the peace by force. But if my juster cause prevails in the fight (as it surely will, if I judge rightly), the Trojans shall not rule over the Italians. Both shall be equal, both unconquered, joined in laws, lands, and homes. I ask only altars for my weary gods. The care of those sacred rites shall be mine; the crown I leave to King Latinus. His shall be the sovereign sway. And I will not share his power in peace, nor his command in war. For myself, my friends shall build another town, and bless the rising walls with the name of my fair Lavinia.”

Thus he spoke. Then, with uplifted eyes and hands, the Latian king stood before his altar. “By the same heaven,” he said, “and earth and sea, and all the powers that all three contain; by hell below, and by that upper god whose thunder ratifies peace and whose nod seals it; so let Latona's twin offspring hear, and double-faced Janus, what I swear: I touch the sacred altars, I touch the flames, and I call all those powers to witness, and all their names. Whatever happens on either side, no term of time shall break this union. No force, no fortune shall loosen my vows, or shake the steadfast course of my mind — not though the encircling seas should burst their bounds, overflow the shores, or undermine the solid ground; not though the lamps of heaven should leave their spheres, hurled down to hiss in the lake below. Just as this royal scepter” — for he held a scepter in his hand — “shall never again put out branches, or renew its growth: an orphan now, cut by the keen axe from its mother earth, stripped of its foliage, sheathed in bronze for Latian kings to bear.”

When in public view the peace was thus sealed with solemn vows sworn on both sides, and all the dues that sacred rites require had been performed, the victim beasts were slain before the fire, their trembling entrails torn from their bodies and carried in chargers to the fattening flames.

But the Rutulians already judged their champion overmatched before the fight began. At first, whispered fears ran through the crowd; then, gathering volume, they murmured more loudly. Side by side they measured with their eyes the two champions' bulk, their sinews and their size — and the closer they compared, the more their own man's disadvantage showed. Turnus himself, in full view of the people, appeared conscious of fate and despondent of the fight. He moved slowly and stood at his altar with eyes downcast and trembling hands, and while he muttered unintelligible prayers, a livid paleness crept into his cheeks.

When Juturna saw the rising alarm of the mad multitude, heard their short sighs and gathering sobs, and found their minds ready for a change, she disguised her immortal form and took the features, dress, and look of Camertus — a chief of ancient blood whose great father had been renowned in arms, and he an even greater son. In that shape she ran among the ranks, and playing on their first impulses, she began: “For shame, Rutulians! Can you bear to see one man alone exposed for all of us in single combat? Shall we, before the face of heaven, admit that our courage is colder, our numbers smaller? Look over the whole Trojan host, the Arcadian band, the Tuscan army — count them as they stand. If we advanced undaunted to battle, hardly every second man would find an enemy to face. True, Turnus in this unequal strife will lose his devoted life with honor, or rather exchange it for immortal fame, joining the gods from whom he came. But you, a servile and inglorious mob, shall sow your native land for foreign masters — the very fields your fighting fathers won, which have so long sustained their lazy sons.” With such words she carried her design. A rising murmur ran along the line. Even the city troops and the Latians, tired of the long war, seemed inspired with new souls. They lamented their champion's fate with pity and repented of the league so lately sworn.

Nor did the goddess fail to feed the rage with lying wonders and a false omen. She added a sign, there before their eyes, that inspired fresh courage and glad surprise. Suddenly, in the burning tracts above, appeared in pomp the imperial bird of Jove. He spied a flock of waterfowl swimming the lakes and shook his sounding wings over their heads. Then, stooping on the fairest of the flock, he clutched a silver swan in his strong talons. The Italians marveled at the unusual sight; but as he labored, lagging in his flight, look — the timid birds returned and pursued him with united force. Clamorous around the royal hawk they flew, thickening into a cloud that shaded the sky. They struck, they scratched, they crossed his airy course; the burdened bird could not endure their force. Vexed but not vanquished, he dropped the heavy prey, and, lightened of his burden, winged his way off.

The Ausonian ranks greeted the sight with shouts, eager for action and clamoring for the fight. Then King Tolumnius, versed in the art of augury, cried out and made his boasted skill known: “At last, what I have long desired is granted! This, this is what my frequent vows required. You gods, I take your omen and obey. Advance, my friends, and charge — I lead the way! These are the foreign foes, whose impious band, like that rapacious bird, infests our land. But like him they shall soon be forced to sea by our united strength, and forego their prey. Bring your timely help to your country; hurry to the rescue and save your king.”

He spoke, and pressing forward through the crowd, poised his lance in his lifted arm and threw it. The winged weapon, whistling in the wind, drove on and did not miss its intended mark. At once the cornel shaft rattled in the sky; at once tumultuous shouts and cries rose up. Nine brothers stood in a fine band, born of Arcadian mingled with Tuscan blood — the sons of Gylippus. The fatal javelin flew, aimed at the midmost of that friendly group. It found a passage through the jointed armor just where the belt was bound to the body, and struck down the gentle youth, stretched on the ground. Then, fired with pious rage, his generous brothers rushed forward madly to avenge the slain. Some hurled their javelins in eager haste; some assailed the enemy sword in hand.

The Latin troops welcomed the desired insult, meeting their ardor in the middle space. The Trojans, Tuscans, and Arcadian line opposed their design with equal courage. Peace deserted the violated fields, and hate drove both armies to their mutual fate. With impious haste the altars were overturned, the sacrifice half-roasted and half-unburned. Thick storms of steel flew from either army, and clouds of clashing weapons obscured the sky. Brands from the fire were seized as missile weapons, along with chargers, bowls, and all the priestly gear. Latinus, frightened, hurried from the fray, carrying away his unregarded gods. Some leaped onto horseback, others yoked their chariots; the rest, with swords held high, ran headlong into war.

Messapus, eager to wreck the peace, spurred his hot horse through the press of fighters at King Aulestes — known by his purple and his royal crown as a Tuscan prince — and, charging, bore him down. He fell backward; and as fate arranged, the ruins of an altar were behind him. There, pitching onto his shoulders and his head, he lay stretched out amid the scattered fires. Then the heavy spear came descending from above, pierced his cuirass, and drove through his body. With a scornful smile the victor cried: “The gods have found a fitter sacrifice.” Greedy for spoils, the Italians stripped the dead man of his rich armor and uncrowned his head.

The priest Corynaeus armed his better hand with a blazing brand from his own altar, and as Ebusus advanced to battle with thundering stride, he dashed it in his face. His bristly beard blazed up in sudden fire; the crackling crop gave off a noisome stench. Following the blow, he seized Ebusus's curling crown with his left hand and threw him down with the other. He pressed the prostrate body with his knees and plunged his holy dagger in his breast.

While Podalirius pursued the shepherd Alsus with his sword through the fleeing crowd, Alsus turned swiftly and aimed a deadly blow straight at the forehead of his unwary foe. The broad axe entered with a crashing sound and split the chin with one continuous wound. Warm blood and mingled brains smeared the arms around him; an iron sleep pressed down his dazed eyes and sealed their heavy lids in endless rest.

But good Aeneas rushed in among the ranks, his head bare and his hands naked, in sign of truce. Then he cried aloud: “What sudden rage, what new thirst for blood inflames your altered minds? O Trojans, stop these impious arms — do not violate the peace! By human agreement and by divine law the terms are all agreed; the war is mine. Dismiss your fears, and let the single combat go forward. This hand alone shall set right the gods and you. To this avenging sword the faithless Turnus owes a debt for our injured altars and their broken vow.”

While he spoke, heedless of defense, a winged arrow struck the pious prince. Whether it came from some human hand or from a hostile god, fame has not recorded. No human hand or hostile god was ever found to boast of so base a wound.

When Turnus saw the Trojan quit the plain, his chiefs dismayed, his troops a fainting crew, his unhoped-for turn of events lifted his spirit. At once he called for his arms and his horses, then with a leap gained his lofty chariot and took the reins with a ready hand. He drove on impetuously, and wherever he went he left behind a lane of slaughtered foes. Some he reached with his lance; over others he rolled his rapid chariot, crushing out their lives. In vain the conquered fled; the victor hurled the dead men's weapons at their living friends. So on the banks of the frozen Hebrus, the God of Battles in his angry mood, clashing his sword against his brazen shield, let the reins loose and scoured across the field. Before the wind his fiery horses flew; the sad earth groaned, and the rattling sky resounded. Wrath, Terror, Treason, Tumult, and Despair — dire and deformed faces — surrounded his car, friends of the god and followers of war. With fury not unlike his, no less disdain, exulting Turnus flew across the plain. His smoking horses, at their utmost speed, he lashed on and urged over the dead. Their fetlocks ran with blood, and when they bounded, gore and gathering dust were flung around. Thamyris and Pholus, masters of war, he killed up close, and Sthenelus from afar. From afar he also slew the sons of Imbracus, Glaucus and Lades of the Lycian company, both trained to fight on foot in close battle, or to mount the horse that outstrips the wind.

Meanwhile Eumedes, boasting on the field, fired up the Trojans anew and drove back their enemies. This son of Dolon bore his grandsire's name, but emulated his father's fame even more. His guileful father had gone as a night scout to spy out the Greek camp and its dispositions — a hard enterprise, and he might well demand the chariot and horses of Achilles as his reward. But caught in the scouting, the Aetolian prince paid him a juster recompense in death. Fierce Turnus saw the Trojan from afar and launched his javelin from his lofty car; then lightly leaping down, he followed up the blow, pressed his foot on the fallen foe, wrenched the shining sword from his feeble grip, and plunged it into the owner's breast. “Possess,” he said, “the reward of all your pains. Measure out, at full length, our Latian plains! Thus are my foes rewarded by my hand; thus may they build their town, and thus enjoy the land!”

Then he slew Dares, Butes, and Sybaris, whom his stumbling horse had thrown over its neck. As when loud Boreas, with his blustering train, stoops from above and bears down on the sea — wherever he flies, he drives the rack before him and rolls the billows onto the Aegean shore — so, where irresistible Turnus took his course, the scattered squadrons bent before his force. His crest of horsehair streamed out behind him, tossed by the opposing air and rustling in the wind.

Haughty Phegeus saw this with great disdain, and as the chariot rolled along the plain, he leapt light from the ground and seized the reins. Hanging in the air, he still held on, frightening the horses and controlling their course. Turnus's lance reached him as he hung there and pierced his plated armor, but passed along it and only grazed the skin. He turned and held his broad shield up against his menacing foe, then called for help — but while he cried in vain, the chariot bore him backward on the plain. He lay overturned; the victor king descended and struck so squarely where his helmet ended that he lopped off the head. The Latian fields were drenched with the streams that issued from the bleeding trunk.

While Turnus triumphed and the Trojans gave way, the wounded prince was forced to leave the field. Strong Mnestheus, tested Achates, and young Ascanius, weeping by his side, led him back to his tent. He could barely lift his limbs from the ground, supported on his spear. Resolved in mind, indifferent to the pain, he tugged with both hands and broke off the shaft. The steel remained. He found no quicker way to draw out the weapon than to enlarge the wound. Eager to fight, impatient of delay, he urged them on, and his unwilling friends obeyed.

Iapis was at hand to exercise his skill — Iapis, whose youthful beauty had so fired Apollo's heart that the god had offered to bestow on him his tuneful lyre and his unerring bow. The pious young man, more intent on saving his aging father who was sinking toward the grave, preferred the power of herbs and the silent praise of the healing art to Apollo's laurel bays.

Propped on his lance, the pensive hero stood, and heard and saw the mourning crowd unmoved. The famed physician tucked his robes around him with ready hands and hurried to the wound. With gentle touches he performed his part, working the dart this way and that, and plied all his heavenly art. All softening simples known for sovereign use he pressed out, pouring their noble juice. These first, infused, to ease the pain; then he tugged with pincers — but tugged in vain. Then he prayed to the patron of his art; the patron of his art refused his aid.

Meanwhile the war drew closer to the tents; the alarm grew hotter, and the noise augmented. The driving dust proclaimed the danger near; first their friends appeared, then their foes. Their friends retreated; their foes pursued the rear. The camp filled with terror and alarm. Hissing shafts fell within the trench; a confused noise rose to the sky — the shouts of those who killed, the groans of the dying.

But now the goddess mother, moved by grief and pierced with pity, hastened to his relief. She brought a branch of healing dittany, carefully sought in the fields of Crete — its stem rough, surrounded by woolly leaves, the leaves crowned with flowers, the flowers with purple; well known to wounded goats as a sure remedy to draw out the pointed steel and ease the pain. This Venus brought, wrapped in clouds, and she infused the extracted liquor with ambrosial dews and fragrant panacea. Unseen, she stood tempering the mixture with her heavenly hands, and poured it into a bowl already filled with the juice of medicinal herbs prepared to bathe the wound. The healer, unaware of the superior art that was aiding the cure, bathed the wound with this — and in a moment the raging pain ceased. The blood was staunched and settled in the bottom. The steel, barely touched by tender hands, worked upward and came out of its own accord, and health and strength were restored at once. Iapis was the first to notice the wound closing, and the first to recognize the footsteps of a god. “Arms, arms!” he cried. “Prepare the sword and shield, and send the willing chief, renewed, to war! This is no mortal work, no cure of mine, no effect of art — it is done by divine hands. Some god is sending our general into battle; some god preserves his life for greater ends.”

The hero armed himself in haste. His hands wrapped his thighs in greaves of refulgent gold. Inflamed for the fight and rushing to the field, one hand sustaining the celestial shield, the other gripped his lance and shook it with such vigor that the heavy weapon quivered along its length. Then he strained his son to him in a close embrace and, kissing him through his helmet, began: “My son, learn war from my example — to endure in camps and to dare in battle. But may happier fortune than mine attend your efforts. This day my hand shall shield your tender age and crown you with the honors of the conquered field. You, when riper years shall send you forth to the toils of war, remember my worth. Assert your birthright, and in arms be known as Hector's nephew and Aeneas's son.” He spoke, and striding, went out onto the plain. Anteus and Mnestheus, and a numerous retinue, attended his steps. The rest took up their weapons and, crowding to the field, abandoned the camp. A cloud of blinding dust was raised around them; the ground trembled and labored beneath their feet.

Now Turnus, posted on a hill, watched from a distance the progress of the moving war. With him the Latins viewed the covered plains, and their chill blood ran backward in their veins. Juturna saw the advancing troops appear, heard the hostile sound, and fled in fear. Aeneas led on, drawing a sweeping train, closed in their ranks and pouring onto the plain. As when a whirlwind rushing to the shore from the open sea drives the waves before it — the unhappy farmer with a heavy heart foresees his flattened fields and the slaughter of his trees — with a like impetuous rage the prince appeared before his doubled front, bearing no less destruction. And now both armies clashed in the open field. Osiris was killed by strong Thymbraeus. Archetius, Ufens, and Epulon were slain (all famed in arms, and of the Latian train) by the hands of Gyas, Mnestheus, and Achates. The fatal augur fell — he by whose command the truce had been broken, whose lance, smeared with Trojan blood, had renewed the unhappy fight. Loud shouts and cries rent the liquid sky, and across the field the frightened Latins fled. The prince disdained to pursue the cowards, nor did he move to meet in arms the handful still fighting. Turnus alone, amid the dusky plain, he sought, and called in vain to combat. Juturna heard, and seized with mortal fear, she forced her brother's charioteer from the pole. She took on his shape, his armor, and his bearing, and, like Metiscus, was seen in his seat.

As the black swallow flies about a mansion — over empty courts and under arches, now soaring aloft, now skimming along the water, to stock her noisy nest with food — so the rapid goddess drove over the plain; the smoking horses ran with loosened reins. She steered a varied course among the foes; now here, now there, she showed her conquering brother; now in a straight course, now wheeling in flight, she turned and bent but shunned the single combat. Aeneas, fired with fury, broke through the crowd, sought out his foe, and called him by name aloud. He ran in a narrower ring and tried to stop the chariot — but the chariot flew on. If he only caught a glimpse, Juturna took fright and bore the Daunian hero far away.

What was he to do? Neither tricks nor arms availed, and various cares troubled his mind in vain. Great Messapus, thundering across the field, held in his left hand two pointed javelins. Encountering the prince, he drew one dart and threw it with unerring aim and utmost force. Aeneas saw it coming and, stooping low beneath his shield, dodged the threatening blow. The weapon hissed above his head and tore away the waving plume he wore on his helmet. Forced by this hostile act, and fired with spite that Turnus still refused the fight, the prince — whose piety had long held back his inborn fire — now invaded the field. He invoked the powers of violated peace, to redress their rites and their injured altars. Then, giving his rage free rein, he filled the plain with blood and slaughtered bodies.

What god can tell, what numbers can display the various labors of that fatal day — what chiefs and champions fell on either side, killed in combat or by what kinds of death; whom Turnus and whom the Trojan hero killed; who shared the fame and fortune of the field? Jove, could you watch, and not avert your sight, two jarring nations joined in cruel fight, whom bonds of lasting love would soon unite!

Aeneas first came upon the Rutulian Sucro, whose valor had made the Trojans yield their ground. He drove the javelin so accurately between his ribs that it reached his heart and required no second thrust. Meanwhile Turnus, with two blows, killed two brothers. First he threw fierce Amycus from his horse; then, leaping to the ground, on foot he attacked Diores and prevailed in equal fight. He left their lifeless trunks upon the place; their heads, dripping with gore, adorned his chariot.

The Trojan hero threw three men cold on the earth, slain without respite at a single charge: Cethegus, Tanais, and Tagus fell overborne, and sad Onythes was added to the rest — of Theban blood, whom Peridia had borne.

Turnus overthrew two brothers from the Lycian shore, sent to battle from Apollo's shrine; Phoebus could not prevent their fate. After them he killed peaceful Menoetes, who had long shunned the dangers of battle. He had led a silent life on the lake of Lerna, earning his bread with his nets and his fishing rod, knowing neither pompous cares nor palaces, wisely withdrawing from the infectious world. His house was poor; his father's hard-working hands paid the rent and plowed another man's land.

As flames are thrown into lofty woods on opposite sides, both driven by winds — the laurels crackle in the sputtering fire; the frightened woodland spirits retreat from their shades — or as two neighboring torrents fall from high ground, running rapidly, their foamy waters seething, rolling to the sea with irresistible force and plunging their course down over the rocks: with no less rage the rival heroes took their different ways, and made no less destruction. With spears from afar, with swords at close quarters, they struck; and zeal for slaughter fired both souls alike. Like them, their dauntless men held the field, hearts pierced but unwilling to yield. They returned blow for blow and wound for wound, and heaps of bodies rose to level the ground.

Murranus, boasting of his blood that sprang from a long royal line of Latian kings, was thrown from his chariot by the Trojan, crushed by the weight of an unwieldy stone. He fell between the wheels; the wheels that had borne his living weight tore his dying body. His startled horses, shying from the glittering sword, trampled his limbs under their hoofs, forgetting their lord.

Fierce Hyllus threatened loudly and face to face confronted Turnus in the middle space. The prince met him in full career and aimed the deadly spear at his temples. So fatally sped the flying weapon that it pierced through his brazen helmet into his head. Nor, Cisseus, could you escape Turnus's hand, though you were the strongest of the Arcadian band. Nor could Cupentus's gods afford availing aid against the Aenean sword, which drove its course into his naked heart — nor could his plated shield withstand the force.

Iolas fell, whom neither the Grecian powers nor the great overthrower of the Trojan towers had been fated to kill while heaven prolonged his days. But who can cross the bounds set by fate? In high Lyrnessus, and in Troy, he had held two palaces, and had been expelled from each. Of all the mighty man, what remains at the last is a little spot of foreign earth.

And now both armies united their broken troops in equal ranks and mingled in mortal fight. Seresthus and undaunted Mnestheus joined the Trojan, Tuscan, and Arcadian line. Sea-born Messapus, with Atinas, led the Latin squadrons into battle. They struck, they pushed, they thronged the narrow space, resolved on death, impatient of disgrace; and where one fell, another filled his place.

Now the Cyprian goddess inspired her son to leave the unfinished fight and storm the town. For while he was rolling his eyes around the plain in search of Turnus, whom he sought in vain, he saw from afar the unguarded city, careless and at rest, secure from war. The opportunity roused his mind to dare more than the task he had first designed. Resolved, he summoned his chiefs; they left the fight. Accompanied, he took a nearby height; his crowding troops stood around their general, all under arms, awaiting his high command. Then the lofty prince spoke: “Hear and obey, you Trojan bands, without the least delay. Jove is with us; and what I have decided demands our utmost vigor and our speed. Prepare your weapons at once against the town, the source of mischief and the seat of the war. This day those Latian towers that rival the sky shall be leveled with the plain in ashes. The people shall be slaves, unless in time they kneel for pardon and repent their crime. Twice our foes have been beaten on the plain — am I to wait until Turnus chooses to be slain? Turn your force against the perjured city. There it began, and there the war shall end. The peace profaned demands our righteous arms; cleanse the polluted place with purging fires.”

He finished, and one spirit inspiring them all, the foot soldiers, formed in a wedge, approached the wall. Outside the town, an unprepared crowd of gaping, staring citizens was slain. Some bore firebrands, others scaling ladders — these they tossed aloft, and those they reared up. The flames were launched, the feathered arrows flew, and clouds of missiles darkened the sky. Advancing to the front, the hero stood, stretching his pious hands to heaven, calling the gods to witness his innocence, reproaching the Ausonian prince with breach of faith, declaring the royal honor doubly stained and the rites of holy peace twice profaned.

Discordant cries arose within the town. Each one wanted to be heard, and all advised at once. One party contended for peace, one for war; some would shut out their enemies, some would admit their friends. The helpless king was hurried along in the throng, carried by whatever tide prevailed. So when a countryman, within a hollow rock, attacks the bees with suffocating smoke, they run about, or struggle on their wings, unused to flight, and shoot their sleepy stings; in vain they try to shun the bitter fumes; black vapors issuing from the vent envelop the sky.

But now fate and envious fortune prepared to plunge the Latins into final despair. The queen, who saw the enemies invading the town, brands thrown onto the tops of burning houses, cast her eyes round, distracted with fear — no troops of Turnus appearing in the field. Once more she stared about, but still in vain, and then concluded that the royal youth was slain. Mad with her anguish, unable to bear the mighty grief, she came to loathe the very air. She called herself the cause of all the evil, and owned the dire effects of her ungoverned will. She raged against the gods, she beat her breast, she tore her purple robe with both hands; then she tied a running noose around a beam, and, fastened by the neck, died obscenely.

As soon as the fatal news was spread by Fame and made known to her women and her daughter, sad Lavinia tore her yellow hair and her rosy cheeks; the others shared her sorrow. The palace rang with shrieks and the madness of despair. The spreading rumor filled the public square. Confusion, fear, distraction, and disgrace, and silent shame were seen on every face. Latinus tore his garments as he went, for both his public and his private woes. He smeared his venerable beard with filth, and sordid dust disfigured his silver hair. He blamed himself much for the softness of his mind — susceptible to the charms of womankind, and too easily persuaded to change what he had so well designed; to break the long-desired solemn league, and to fail to fulfill what his own fates, and those of Troy, required.

Now Turnus wheeled his chariot far out over empty plains, and here and there picked off some straggling foes. His flying horses pleased him less and less, ashamed of easy fighting and cheap success. Half-content, anxious in his mind, he heard distant cries driven in on the wind — shouts from the walls, but shouts drowned in murmurs, a jarring mixture and an ominous sound. “Alas!” he said. “What do these dismal cries mean? What doleful clamor rises from the town?” In confusion he stopped and pulled the reins back. She who now served as his charioteer replied: “My lord, leave these new alarms to others; fight here, and press the fortune of your arms. There are others to defend the wall. If by your rival's hand the Italians fall, so let your fatal sword oppress his friends — equal in honor, equal in success.”

To this the prince replied: “O sister — for I knew the peace was first broken by you. I recognized you when you first mixed in the fighting, and you would deceive my sight in vain now. Why, goddess, this unprofitable care? Who sent you down from heaven, wrapped in air, to take your share of mortal sorrows and see your brother bleeding on the plain? To what power can Turnus now have recourse, or how can he resist his fate's prevailing force? These eyes saw Murranus bite the ground — a mighty man, a mighty wound. I heard my dearest friend with dying breath call on my name to avenge his death. Brave Ufens fell with honor on the spot, to avoid the shameful sight of my disgrace. Flat on his back he lies, a manly corpse; his clothes and armor are the victor's prize. And shall I see Laurentum in flames, the one thing lacking to complete my shame? How the Latins will hoot at their champion's flight! How Drances will exult and point them to the sight! Is death so hard to bear? Powers below — since those above show so little compassion — receive a soul yet unsullied by shame, one that does not disgrace my great forefather's name!”

He said; and while he spoke, Saces came flying on his foamy horse, a shaft fixed in his wounded face, seeking Turnus and sending his voice before him: “Turnus, on you — on you alone — depends our last relief! Take pity on your friends! Like lightning, fierce Aeneas rolls on, invests the town with arms, invades it with flames. The brands are hurled on high; the winds conspire to drive the deluge of fire along. Every eye is fixed on you; your foes rejoice; even the king wavers and holds off his choice, unsure whether to surrender or defend the town, whom to reject, or whom to call his son. The queen, on whom your utmost hopes were placed, has suborned her own death and breathed her last. It is true, Messapus, fearless of his fate, with fierce Atinas's help, defends the gate. Surrounded on every side by the enemy, the more they kill, the greater their numbers grow; an iron harvest sprouts up, still to be mown. But you, far aloof from your forsaken men, drive your rolling chariot over empty sands.”

Stunned he sat, his eyes cast down at the earth, turning various cares over in his mind. Rage boiling from the bottom of his breast, and sorrow mingled with shame, oppressed his soul; and conscious worth labored in his thoughts, and love driven by jealousy into madness. By slow degrees his reason drove away the mists of passion and resumed her sway. Then, rising in his car, he turned his eyes and saw the town wrapped in fire and smoke. A wooden tower was already blazing — one he had raised himself on beams and rafters, with bridges laid above to join the space and wheels below so it could roll from place to place. “Sister, the fates have conquered. Let us go the way that heaven and my hard fortune show. The fight is settled; the branded name of a base coward shall not blot your brother's fame. I choose death; but let me try my strength and vent my rage before I die.” He spoke, and leaping down without delay, he cut his way through the scattered foes. Striding on, impetuous as the wind, he left the grieving goddess far behind. As when a fragment, torn from a mountain by raging storms, or carried by torrents, or undermined by time, or loosened at the roots, shoots down through the void in rocky ruin, rolling from crag to crag, from steep to steep; down sink at once the shepherds and their sheep; together they rush to the ground below, stunned at the shock, and, stunned, rebound from the earth: so Turnus, hastening headlong to the town, shouldering and shoving, bore down the squadrons. Still pressing onward, he came up to the walls, where shafts and spears and arrows flew in confusion, and streams of blood drenched the slippery ground. First stretching out his arm in sign of peace, he cried aloud to make the combat cease: “Rutulians, hold! Latin troops, withdraw! The fight is mine, and the gods require me. It is just that I alone should vindicate the broken truce, or atone for its breach. This day shall free the Ausonian state from war, or finish my misfortunes in my fate.”

Both armies broke off their bloody work and, drawing back, formed a spacious ring. The Trojan hero, who heard through Fame the welcome sound and the champion's name, soon left the captured works and the mounted walls, eager for a war where greater glory called. He sprang forward, exulting in his force; his jointed armor rattled as he ran. Like Eryx, or like Athos, he loomed great — or like Father Apennine, when, white with snow, he hides his divine head in the clouds and shakes the sounding forest on his sides. The nations, overawed, halted the fight; their bodies froze, their eyes fixed. Even death stood still. They no longer threw down their darts from above, nor drove their battering-rams below. In silent order each army stood, their swords dropping unknowingly from their hands. The Ausonian king looked on in wonder at two mighty champions matched in single fight — born under distant skies, brought by fate, to settle their claims to the state with the sword.

Now in the closed arena they viewed each other from a distance, and rushing on, began the war. They launched their spears; then they met hand to hand. The trembling ground resounded beneath their feet. Their shields clashed; thick blows came down from on high, and flakes of fire flew from their hard helmets. Courage and chance conspired together, and both engaged with equal fortune still, and mutual rage. As when two bulls fight for their fair mate in the shades of Sila or on the heights of Taburnus, meeting with horns thrust forward — the keeper runs; the herd stands silent; the heifers roll their eyes and await the outcome, wondering which will carry off the victory and rule as lord of the lusty year. The jealous rivals burn with the rage of love, and return push for push, wound for wound; their dewlaps gored, their sides bathed in blood, loud bellowings and roars echo through the woods: such was the combat in the marked-off ground, so clashed their swords, so rang their shields.

Jove set up the scales; into each pan he laid the champions' fate, and weighed them precisely. On this side, life and lucky chance rose; loaded with death, the other pan descended. Stretching for it, young Turnus aimed a blow full on the helmet of his unguarded foe. Shrill shouts and cries rang on either side, as hopes and fears divided their panting hearts. But the treacherous sword shattered into pieces, deserting its lord in the middle of his stroke. Now nothing remained but death or flight — disarmed, he fled when he saw an unfamiliar hilt in his hand. Fame says that Turnus, when yoking his horses and hurrying to war with a disordered mind, had snatched up the first weapon his haste could find. It was not the fated sword his father bore, but the one his charioteer Metiscus wore. While the Trojans were in flight, its toughness had held; but against the great Vulcanian shield, the mortal-tempered steel failed in his hand. The shivered fragments shone amid the sand.

Seized with fear, he fled along the field, now running straight, now wheeling in circles; for here the Trojan troops surrounded the ring, and there the way was closed by pools and marshy ground. Aeneas hastened after him, though at a heavier pace — his wound so newly knit hindered the chase, and often his trembling knees refused their aid — yet, pressing foot to foot, he pursued his foe.

Thus when a fearful stag is hemmed in by crimson nets, or finds himself caught against a river, the deep-mouthed hound appears high on the bank, still baying, still following wherever he turns. The persecuted creature turns this way and that to escape his Umbrian foe. The bank is steep, and if he gains the land, the purple death is pitched along the shore. His eager pursuer, set on the chase, stretched at full length, gains ground with every step. Now he reaches for the stag's antlered head, and now he holds, or thinks he holds, his prey. At the very pinch, the stag leaps clear in fear; the hound bites the wind and fills his sounding jaws with air. The rocks, the lakes, the meadows ring with cries; the mortal tumult mounts and thunders in the skies. So the Daunian prince fled, and as he fled, blamed his sluggish troops and, calling them by name, demanded his trusty sword. The Trojan threatened the realm with ruin, and to lay their ancient homes in ashes, if they dared to supply his vanquished enemy with arms or aid. So threatening, he still pursued the course with vigor, though with diminished strength. Ten times already around the marked-off space one chief had fled, and the other given chase. No trivial prize was in play; for on the life or death of Turnus now the whole struggle depended.

Within the arena an olive tree had stood, a sacred shade, a venerable wood, consecrated by vows to Faunus, the Latins' guardian god. On it hung the garments and carved tablets of sailors saved from shipwreck. With heedless hands the Trojans had felled the tree to clear the ground for combat. Deep into the root, whether by fate, by chance, or through hasty error, the Trojan had driven his lance; then he stooped and tugged with immense force to free the embedded spear from the tenacious tree, so that by flying weapon he might reach from afar the man his failing limbs could not catch.

Confounded with fear, bereft of human aid, Turnus then prayed to the gods, and first to Faunus: “O Faunus, pity me! And you, Mother Earth, where I, your foster son, received my birth — hold fast the steel! If my devout hand has honored your tree, which your enemies have profaned, hear my pious prayer favorably!” He spoke, and did not invoke their aid in vain. The straining hero wrenched and pulled and strained; but the stubborn earth still held the steel. Juturna took her chance; and while he struggled vainly, she assumed Metiscus's shape again, and in that imitated form restored the Daunian sword to the despairing prince. The Queen of Love, who with disdain and grief saw the bold nymph provide this prompt relief, to assert her offspring with a greater deed, freed the lingering weapon from the tough root.
Once more upright, the rival chiefs advanced — one trusting the sword, the other the pointed lance — both alike resolved to try their fatal chance.

Meanwhile imperial Jove spoke to Juno, who watched the clash from a shining cloud: “What new interference, Queen of Heaven, is sent to halt the fates now laboring toward the outcome? What further hopes have you left to pursue? Divine Aeneas — and you know it too — is destined for these celestial seats. What more can be attempted for Turnus, that you linger here in this lonely shade? Is it becoming to the due respect and awful honor of a god elect, to feel a wound unworthy of our state, patient of human hands and earthly steel? Or does it seem just that the sister should restore a second sword when one was lost before, and arm a conquered wretch against his conqueror? For what, without your knowledge and consent — no, more, your dictate — would Juturna dare? At last, out of deference to my love, cease to harbor this anxious care in your soul. Lean on my breast, unload your grief: who should relieve the goddess but the god? Now all things tend to their final issue, pushed by the fates to their appointed end. While permission was granted, and a lawful hour, for vengeance, wrath, and unresisted power, tossed on the seas you could afflict your foes, and, driven ashore, oppress them with hostile arms; deform the royal house; and from the side of the rightful bridegroom, tear away the plighted bride. Now cease, at my command.” So spoke the Thunderer. And Juno, with downcast eyes, made this answer: “Because I knew your dread decree too well, I withdrew from Turnus and from earth unwilling. Else you should not behold me here alone, wrapped in empty clouds, bewailing my friends — but, girded with vengeful flames, in open sight, engaged against my foes in mortal fight. It is true, Juturna mingled in the strife at my command, to save her brother's life — at least to try; but, by the Stygian lake (the most sacred oath the gods can take), with this restriction: not to bend the bow, or toss the spear, or fling the trembling dart. And now, yielding to your superior might, and tired of fruitless toils, I loathe the fight. Let me beg this one thing (and no fates withstand it), both for myself and for your father's land: that when the marriage bed shall seal the peace (which, since you ordain it, I consent to bless), the laws of each nation shall be the same; but let the Latins still keep their name, speak the same language they spoke before, wear the same customs their grandsires wore. Do not call them Trojans: let the renown and name of Troy perish with that detested town. Let Latium be Latium still; let Alba reign, and Rome's immortal majesty remain.”

Then the founder of mankind replied (his brow unruffled, his eyes serene): “Can Saturn's daughter, heaven's other heir, bear such endless anger in her breast? Be mistress, and gain your full desire; but quench the choler you foment in vain. The Ausonian people, sprung from ancient blood, shall keep their name, their dress, and their tongue. The Trojans shall be bound to their customs; I myself will provide their common rites. The natives shall command; the foreigners shall yield. All shall be Latium; Troy shall be no name; and her lost sons shall forget where they came from. From blood so mixed, a pious race shall flow, equal to the gods, excelling all below. No nation shall pay more respect to you, or lay greater offerings on your altars.” Juno consented, well pleased that her wishes had found success, and withdrew from the cloud.

The peace thus made, the Thunderer next prepared to force the water-goddess from the wars. Deep in the dismal regions without light, three daughters had been born at one birth to Night. These their brown mother, brooding over her charge, had endowed with windy wings to flit in the air, girded with serpents and crowned with hissing hair. In heaven they were called the Dirae, and they stood ever near the throne of angry Jove — his ministers of wrath, ever ready to fill the minds of mortal men with fears, whenever the moody father, to work his hatred on realms or towns that deserve their fate, hurls down diseases, death, and deadly care, and terrifies the guilty world with war. One of these sister plagues he sent from heaven to frighten Juturna with a dire portent. The pest came whirling down. Far more slowly springs the swift arrow from the Parthian bow, or from the Cydon yew, when, traversing the skies and drenched in poisonous juice, the sure destruction flies. With such sudden and unseen flight, the daughter of Night shot through the clouds. As soon as she had the enclosed field in view, and knew her appointed quarry from afar, she contracted herself into the boding bird that haunts ruined piles and hallowed urns, and beats about the tombs on nightly wings, and sings obscene songs on sepulchers. In that lesser form, with frightful cries, the Fury flew round unhappy Turnus — flapped on his shield and fluttered in his eyes.

A lazy chill crept along his blood; his voice was choked; his hair stood up in horror. Juturna saw her from afar and knew the ill omen by her screaming cry and the whirring of her wings. Amazed with fear, she beat her lovely breast and tore her flowing hair.

“Ah me!” she cried. “In this unequal strife what more can your sister do to save your life? Weak as I am, can I contend in arms with that inexorable fiend? Now, now I leave the field! Forbear to frighten my tender soul, you baleful birds of night! The lashing of your wings I know too well, the sounding flight, the funeral screams of hell! These are the gifts you bring from haughty Jove — the worthy recompense of ravished love! Did he for this exempt my life from fate? O hard conditions of immortal state — though born to death, not permitted to die, but forced to bear imposed eternity! Take back your envious gifts, and let me go to be companion to my brother's ghost below! The joys have vanished; nothing now remains of immortal life but immortal pain. What earth will open her devouring womb, to rest a weary goddess in the tomb?” She drew a long sigh; she said no more, but wrapped her head in her azure mantle, and plunged into her stream in deep despair, and her last sobs came bubbling up into the air.

Now stern Aeneas waved his heavy spear against his foe, and reproached his fear: “What further evasion can Turnus find? What empty hopes are harbored in his mind? Your swiftness cannot secure your flight; it is not with feet, but with hands, that brave men fight. Vary your shape into a thousand forms, and dare whatever skill and courage can attempt in war; wish for the wings of winds, to mount the sky, or to lie hidden in the hollow earth!” The champion shook his head and made this short reply: “Your threats cannot move my manly mind; it is hostile heaven I dread, and partial Jove.” He said no more, but with a sigh repressed the mighty sorrow swelling in his breast.

Then, as he rolled his troubled eyes around, he saw an ancient stone — the common boundary of neighboring fields, a marker of the land — so huge that twelve strong men of modern days could hardly lift its enormous weight from the earth. He heaved it up at a lift, and, poised on high, ran staggering forward against his enemy; but so disordered that he scarcely knew his way, or what unwieldy weight he was throwing. His knocking knees buckled beneath the load, and cold shivering chilled his vital blood. The stone dropped from his arms, and, falling short for want of strength, mocked his vain effort. And as, when heavy sleep has closed the sight, the sickly fancy labors in the night — we seem to run, and, deprived of strength, our sinking limbs fail us in the course; in vain we heave for breath, in vain we cry; the nerves, unbraced, refuse their usual strength; and on the tongue the faltering words die — so Turnus fared. Whatever means he tried, all force of arms and tricks of art he employed, the Fury flashed across and made all his efforts void.

A thousand varied thoughts confounded his soul. He stared about, found neither help nor escape. His own men blocked the way, and his own walls hemmed him in. Once more he paused and looked around, and sought the goddess-charioteer in vain. Trembling, he watched the thundering chief advance, brandishing aloft the deadly lance. Amazed, he cowered before his conquering foe, forgot to parry, and awaited the coming blow. Stunned as he stood, transfixed with fear, he saw the spear coming, aimed at his shield.

The hero first measured the destined mark with a narrow eye, and, rising as he threw, hurled the fatal weapon with his full force. Not with less rage the rattling thunder falls, or stones from battering engines break walls — swift as a whirlwind, from an arm so strong, the lance drove on, bearing death with it. His sevenfold shield did nothing to help the prince, nor did anything beneath his arms, the coat of mail. It pierced through all, and with a ghastly wound transfixed his thigh and doubled him to the ground. The Latins rent the vaulted sky with groans; the woods, hills, and valleys answered the voice.

Now the lofty chief lay low on the earth, his eyes cast upward, his arms spread out, and begged the proud victor, humbled: “I know my death is deserved, and I have no hope to live. Use what the gods and your good fortune give. Yet think, O think — if mercy can be shown — you once had a father, and you have a son. Pity my father, now sinking to the grave; for Anchises's sake, save old Daunus! Or, if your sworn revenge pursues my death, give my body, void of breath, to my friends. The Latian chiefs have seen me beg for my life; yours is the conquest, yours the royal wife. To strive against a yielded man is mean, ignoble strife.”

In deep suspense the Trojan seemed to stand, and, just prepared to strike, held back his hand. He rolled his eyes, and every moment felt his manly soul soften with more compassion — when, casting a casual glance downward, he spied the golden belt that glittered on Turnus's side, the fatal spoils that haughty Turnus had torn from dying Pallas, and wore in triumph. Then, roused anew to wrath, he cried aloud (flames, while he spoke, came flashing from his eyes): “Traitor! Do you, do you, dressed in the trophies of my friend, presume to beg for mercy? It is Pallas, Pallas, who gives this deadly blow, as a welcome offering to his sad soul!” He raised his arm aloft, and at the word drove the shining sword deep into his breast. The streaming blood stained his arms all around; and the disdainful soul came rushing out through the wound.
